Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1369. The numbers suggest Chelsea are pushovers as they slide down the Premier League table... and club legend GUS POYET says it's time to prove they're up for a fight

Published: 07:38 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 11:44 EST, 10 November 2026

Morgan Rogers insisted it was no intentional drive-by. That he did not mean to knee Trai Hume in the head while the Sunderland defender was sitting up after a foul. Just an accident, honest.

The history shared between these two particular players opened the incident to interpretation.

Hume had folded Rogers like a deckchair in a 1-1 draw for Aston Villa last season. The challenge went viral. Sunderland shared it on their social media, glamourising it. Rogers responded at the time by saying: 'Great message to send out. Dangerous tackles getting highlight reels.'

At the Stadium of Light on Sunday, Hume was starting to sit up when Rogers caught him. Chelsea were losing 1-0, and frustrated. Their £117million arrival from Villa apologised immediately, so we will believe him when he says it was an innocent collision rather than retribution.

Nevertheless, Rogers does have an aggressive side to him. He squared up with Declan Rice at Arsenal, and James Tarkowski at Everton, and was signed in the summer partially for that passion.

Rogers has contested more duels than any other Chelsea player this season. He loses more than he wins, but is involved, for better or worse. He is Xabi Alonso's most-fouled footballer, while nobody has committed more fouls than this 6ft 2in England international.

Morgan Rogers (right) showed some fight during Chelsea's loss at Sunderland that appears to be lacking across the whole squad

If Rogers' team-mates showed the same mentality they may have avoided defeat on Sunday

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso needs his side to develop an aggressive streak

So when we ponder whether Alonso's Chelsea are pushovers, Rogers is arguably an exception. He is a hard nut surrounded by a soft shell, and that was a problem at Sunderland.

It was not only that Brian Brobbey bullied Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana. Regis Le Bris' side were all at it, a team of bouncers ready to rough up the lads planning to party. Cole Palmer and Co ended up getting tossed out of the Stadium of Light on their rears. Chelsea recorded 69 per cent possession - their highest of the Premier League season so far - but were second-best throughout.

Gus Poyet saw that. He played for Chelsea, managed Sunderland, and was an assistant to Dennis Wise at Leeds, who will be the next visitors to Stamford Bridge after this international break.

Daniel Farke's side have won more duels and aerial duels than any other Premier League team this season, which, given what we witnessed on Sunday, should be a concern for Alonso.

Poyet can predict what is coming. Chelsea-Leeds is already a fixture with a narrative attached. It never needs a second invitation to be talked up as 'dirty'. Alonso's side will need to show a willingness to compete if that awaits, more than they managed when travelling to Sunderland.

'Sunderland went to the game with that old-fashioned mentality,' the 58-year-old Uruguayan told Daily Mail Sport. 'Pressure from the fans, noise, tackling, "I'm gonna run over you". Chelsea went on to try to play. There was quite a big difference in that aggression. We see teams that are looking so much for an identity that they forget the process to win games.'

Poyet brought up Chelsea's 2-0 win at Everton last month. We told him how Alonso had admitted it was his favourite performance of the season, describing it as 'solid' and 'serious'.

'There you go,' said Poyet, who thinks before travelling to the Stadium of Light, it would have been worth showing Chelsea's players videos from that victory at the Hill Dickinson. It was a rare showing of seriousness from Alonso's side. Only David Moyes' Everton, with 83, have committed fewer fouls than Chelsea's 95 in the Premier League this season. While giving away free-kicks is hardly a cause for celebration, it is not the worst way of measuring whether you are there to push or be pushed.

Sunderland striker Brian Brobbey (left) bulled Chelsea's Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana (right)

'For me that was a proper old-fashioned game, being able to win like that,' Poyet said about Chelsea's win at Everton. 'Put the video on and say, "Play the same".

'Now I know what the other side are going to say after watching the Sunderland game. Leeds will be saying, 'Let's go'. Leeds are very solid, and very aggressive, so it can be that kind of game.

'More and more, through the years, I think from the pandemic to now, the difference between the teams is mental. Identity, positions, shapes, blah, blah, blah, but when they are right in here (in the head), it's big. Right now, Leeds, as a team, are a little ahead mentally.'

Alonso is a polite manager. Given the chance to have a pop at the refereeing at the Stadium of Light - how Chelsea were not awarded a penalty when Cole Palmer was sandwiched, but Sunderland were when Brobbey dropped down in front of Colwill - he declined. The Blues boss chose instead to decry his team's defending as substandard. Colwill was hooked at half-time, while there were two new summer signings in the back line in Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria who need to get to grips with the Premier League, sooner rather than later.

Poyet's first appearance after signing for Chelsea in 1997 was in the Charity Shield. Roy Keane welcomed him to English football with a kick to the head - with a little less subtlety than Rogers' knee on Hume. It finished 1-1 before Manchester United won on penalties.

Ex-Chelsea midfielder Gus Poyet has warned them of the threat Leeds pose later this month

Poyet learned a harsh lesson in that match, and not only from Keane's high kick. 'I couldn't get in the pace of the game,' Poyet recalls. 'I was always late. Ruud (Gullit) at half-time told me, "Gus, you're not really in the front, not really at the back". I said, "I'm trying!" The game was too fast.'

In a weird way, an ACL injury suffered by Poyet helped. He used the recovery time to prepare for returning. 'I went to the stadium, I was watching, learning the language, listening to Dennis Wise in the dressing room, getting that mentality,' he said. 'Then when I came back, I knew everything.

'That was my mentality. Some players need time. Some adjust quickly. You need to use all the time. For example, use this game against Sunderland when you play against Leeds. You cannot say, 'We didn't expect it'. Expect it! It's going to be similar.'

#1367. The little-known new face called up by England: Can you name the star brought in to replace Ezri Konsa?

Published: 05:58 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel has made a first-time England call-up to replace Ezri Konsa - but casual fans could be forgiven if they do not recognise the latest Three Lions addition.

He is not a widely-recognised face among the stars from the Premier League and other top European leagues in Tuchel's selection but James Hill, 24, has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose this season.

The central defender, who started his career at Fleetwood Town, has enjoyed a dream few months: He married partner Tara Rose in June, welcomed his first child in August and has now had his maiden England call.

England announced today that Arsenal defender Konsa will not be in contention to face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night - although he will be fit to potentially face Spain away on Sunday - and Hill has been called up in his place.

Hill has played for England's Under 20s and Under 21s but this is his first senior call. He was signed by Bournemouth for just £1.2million in 2022 - beating Sheffield United, Burnley, Leeds, Southampton, Tottenham and even Barcelona, who all checked on his progress.

Bournemouth's official X account posted today: 'Congratulations, Hilly. Our defender has earned a first senior @England call-up.'

James Hill - pictured with new wife Tara - has been called up to the latest England squad (Source: Instagram/james_hill_10)

Hill has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose

Hill's route to the top is a fascinating one. He attended a trial day at Fleetwood as a 14-year-old and managed to impress them enough to earn place at their new academy.

Interestingly, Hill did not play for a football team of any kind before he was 10, simply kicking a ball around with friends and playing in the garden to hone his skills.

Blackpool opted against signing him after a trial and he was then dropped by Bolton after a short stint.

It proved to be a shrewd piece of talent identification from Fleetwood, with Hill later becoming the club's record sale, eclipsing the fee they received for Jamie Vardy.

And having signed for the Cherries in 2022, Hill has now established himself as a key member of Marco Rose's side.

He's played every minute of every Premier League match this season at the heart of the defence and clearly Tuchel has been impressed.

Speaking before his call-up, Hill said: 'It’s every kid’s dream, isn’t it? You grow up watching the Three Lions on TV, for the World Cup, the Euros. It’s one of the greatest honours you can have in football.'

Football is in the blood for Hill. His father, Matt, made more than 550 appearances in the Football League for the likes of Preston North End, Wolverhampton Wanderers, Sheffield United and Queens Park Rangers as a defender.

Hill played for England at age group level, pictured here kissing his now wife after a game

Hill's younger brother, Tyler, is also in the game, playing for Torquay United in National League South.

But Matt did not pressure his sons into the sport, with James previously telling the Times: 'He didn’t want me to feel as though it’s a job.

'He wanted me to feel like I’m wanting to be here because I love doing it. This is my passion. It brings me happiness. He wanted me to come to that conclusion, not for him to make that decision for me.'

Hill was a well-rounded sportsman and his secondary school did not even play football. Instead, he excelled as a fly-half for the rugby side and impressed as a javelin thrower.

He attributes his success as being aided by trying his hand at different disciplines and it is paying off in abundance having had to largely bide his time before earning a first-team spot under Andoni Iraola last term, with loans to Blackburn and Hearts helping him develop.

Hill's progress flew somewhat under the radar somewhat for many fans outside of Bournemouth and his career peak of an England call-up coincides with domestic bliss.

Having married Tara in the summer, they welcomed their daughter Edie two months later.

Hill, pictured, heading the ball away against Ipswich has become one of the best defenders in the Premier League

'Becoming a dad is one of the most special things I’ve ever experienced in my life,' he said. 'There isn’t a manual though, it’s just like, "Congratulations, you’ve got a baby". Then the door shuts! Hang on a minute. What am I supposed to do next? Is there a book for this? My wife has been absolutely incredible.'

He regularly shares pictures from both his professional and personal life on social media, putting wedding snaps alongside action shots of Bournemouth games.

Hill's England call-up will no doubt introduce him to a whole new audience previously unaware of the defender's capabilities, with only 34,000 Instagram followers at present.

The 24-year-old must now impress Tuchel enough to earn some game time when England play Croatia on Thursday in their next Nations League encounter.

#1365. Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints1,2. Achieving efficient operation at low supply voltages therefore requires new materials and gate-stack engineering strategies. Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer intrinsic advantages because their atomic thickness affords excellent gate control, and their sizable bandgaps suppress off-state current. However, a major obstacle is the imperfect interface between 2D channels and gate dielectrics, which degrades subthreshold swing, hysteresis and bias-temperature instability3. Here we demonstrate that a wafer-scale, transferable, single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric can be van der Waals integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The obtained pristine 2D-dielectric interface enables subthreshold swing close to the thermal limit, record-low hysteresis and well-matched transfer characteristics for both n- and p-type enhancement-mode field-effect transistors. Building on this, we demonstrate complementary field-effect transistors, whose inverters achieve high voltage gain and large noise margins with subpicowatt static power consumption. These results highlight the promise of 2D semiconductors for ultra-low-power operation.

Modern silicon transistors continue to improve with technological advancement. However, as scaling progresses, power efficiency has emerged as a critical constraint, especially for ultra-low-energy applications such as wearable electronics, implantable medical devices, Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, edge AI processors and distributed sensor networks. To achieve substantial power reductions, device operation at reduced supply voltages has been explored extensively4,5. Nevertheless, silicon’s relatively small bandgap inherently increases leakage, while maintaining strong electrostatic control at scaled dimensions remains challenging6. A recent simulation study that compares silicon transistors with planar 2D field-effect transistors (FETs) from 16 nm to 1 nm technology nodes highlighted the low-power potential of 2D FET-based circuits7. These observations motivate the investigation of 2D semiconductors for low-power operation8,9,10,11,12.

The sizable bandgaps of 2D semiconductors suppress off-state current, while their atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) structure enables excellent gate control, making them well suited for energy-efficient operation. Proof-of-concept inverters assembled from n- and p-type 2D semiconductors—including MoS2-WSe2 (refs. 13,14,15), MoS2-MoTe2 (ref. 16) and pseudo-complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) based on single transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD)17—have demonstrated low-voltage and subthreshold operation with reduced static power consumption (Extended Data Table 1). However, these demonstrations rely on non-scalable approaches, such as mechanically exfoliated flakes or lateral assembly of dissimilar materials and devices. Their voltage gains are also limited (Extended Data Table 1), primarily because of asymmetric n-channel FET (n-FET) and p-channel FET (p-FET) transfer characteristics. One major source of this asymmetry is the gate stack: an imperfect 2D/high-κ interface degrades subthreshold swing, whereas unintentional dielectric-induced doping shifts the threshold voltage (Vth), impairing inverter performance. Most critically, WSe2-based p-FETs often have pronounced bipolar transfer characteristics, which are incompatible with robust CMOS operation and integration. High-permittivity, crystalline dielectric or buffer layers have been used to improve gate controllability by increasing gate capacitance and suppressing defect-induced degradation18,19,20. Clean vdW integration of gate dielectrics with 2D semiconductors also minimizes interfacial traps caused by direct deposition processes21,22,23,24. Despite these advances, a scalable method for achieving pristine 2D/high-κ interfaces in both n- and p-type transistors remains elusive.

Here we show that standard amorphous HfO2 grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) contains prevalent charge traps that degrade WSe2 FETs by inducing unwanted bipolar transport, pronounced hysteresis, and compromised n- and p-type performance. Transitioning to a single-crystal dielectric mitigates these issues. Although crystalline dielectrics retain structural imperfections, their threading dislocations are spatially confined to one-dimensional defects with self-passivated cores, making them less detrimental to two-dimensional interfacial transport. We fabricated a -3-inch free-standing single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide (A-TiO2) membrane, a high-κ dielectric with κ ≈ 44–50 at a thickness of 18.2 nm. Patterned membranes are van-der-Waals-integrated with 2D semiconductors as top- or bottom-gate dielectrics, preserving pristine 2D/high-κ interfaces. The resulting MoS2 n-FETs and WSe2 p-FETs have ideal unipolar behaviour, well-matched enhancement-mode thresholds, near-ideal subthreshold swing and record-low hysteresis. Complementary inverters deliver high voltage gain, wide noise margins and record-low static power (subpicowatt) at low voltage. Furthermore, non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) simulations show that this architecture is scalable to a gate length (Lg) of 10 nm, comparable with the 1 nm technology-node specifications in the IRDS 2031 roadmap while maintaining stable operation at 0.3 V.

We use a laser scanning-assisted pulsed-laser deposition technique to fabricate free-standing 3-inch A-TiO2 dielectric layers (Methods). In brief, a SrTiO3 layer was first epitaxially grown on a 3-inch single-crystalline LaAlO3 (001) substrate, followed by a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer that served as a template for the subsequent epitaxial growth of single-crystal A-TiO2 dielectric layers. The optical image of the as-grown 3-inch LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure and its cross-sectional high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image profile with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mappings are shown in Fig. 1a,b. To enable wafer-scale vdW integration with 2D semiconductors, we develop a transfer process as schematically illustrated in Fig. 1c. The grown heterostructure is patterned into 100 × 100 μm2 squares using inductively coupled plasma etching to expose the underlying Sr3Al2O6 layer surrounding the defined squares. The sacrificial Sr3Al2O6 layer is then selectively removed by immersion in deionized water, leaving the A-TiO2 layer in direct contact with the LaAlO3//SrTiO3 substrate. Owing to the vdW interaction between A-TiO2 and the substrate, the 3-inchpatterned A-TiO2 can be lifted off using a polymer support layer and transferred onto target substrates. Acetone washing followed by a mild O2 plasma treatment was used to remove polymer residues from the transferred A-TiO2. A photograph of the as-released 3-inch A-TiO2 layer on a Si//SiO2 substrate is shown in Fig. 1d.

Uniformity and flatness of the gate dielectric are critical for 2D semiconductor devices. The thickness mapping of the transferred 3-inch A-TiO2 film (Supplementary Fig. 1) indicates the exceptionally low coefficient of variation of 1.15%. The thickness of the transferred A-TiO2 membrane is further supported by atomic force microscopy (AFM; Supplementary Fig. 2) and X-ray reflectometry (Supplementary Fig. 3) measurements. Meanwhile, the AFM image of the A-TiO2 transferred onto SiO2 reveals an atomically flat surface, with a minimum average roughness (Ra) of approximately 0.12 nm and an average roughness of 0.13 nm across the 3-inch A-TiO2 platform (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, AFM measurements support that the surface roughness for all thickness variants remains ≤0.2 nm (Supplementary Fig. 4). This roughness is comparable with that of atomically flat hexagonal boron nitride (around 0.19 nm), highlighting the exceptional smooth nature25,26. Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the as-grown LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure indicate coherent single-crystalline growth (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Azimuthal X-ray diffraction ϕ scanning along the (110) plane of free-standing A-TiO2 with different thicknesses further supported in-plane single-crystallinity without rotated domains (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The localized crystallinity is revealed by plan-view dark-field TEM imaging and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis (Fig. 1f), both of which support the local atomic-scale lattice registry and phase purity. X-ray diffraction characterization supports the single-crystalline quality of the A-TiO2 films. The symmetric (004) and asymmetric (107) rocking curves of the released A-TiO2 yield a screw dislocation density of 3.8 × 109 cm−2 and an edge dislocation density of 2 × 1010 cm−2, respectively (Methods). This dislocation density, which arises from the lattice mismatch inherent to the current sacrificial substrate, represents a lower bound for device performance that we expect to substantially improve by migrating to more closely lattice-matched systems. Moreover, asymmetric (107) reciprocal space mapping corroborates the structural homogeneity by tracking the strain state evolution post-release and verifying the absence of polycrystalline domains (Supplementary Fig. 5)27,28,29.

The metal–insulator–metal (MIM) capacitor structure is used to evaluate the capacitance of the as-prepared freestanding A-TiO2, where the A-TiO2 layer is transferred onto a gold-coated silicon substrate followed by the deposition of a top titanium/gold electrode (Extended Data Fig. 2). The inset of Fig. 1g demonstrates the dependence of the effective permittivity (εeff) on thickness, where each data point represents an average value obtained from multiple capacitors of the corresponding A-TiO2 thickness. Notably, the extracted εeff reflects the combined electrostatic contribution from both the single-crystal A-TiO2 layer and the interfacial vdW gap layer formed at the transferred interfaces. The effective value εeff is related to the measured capacitance (Ceff) through \({C}_{\mathrm{eff}}=A{\varepsilon }_{0}{\varepsilon }_{\mathrm{eff}}/t\), where \(A\) is the area of the top electrodes, t is the thickness of the A-TiO2 layer and ε0 is the vacuum permittivity. The εeff as a function of thickness can be well described by the typical dead layer model emerging in a high-κ nanocapacitor18. Figure 1g further summarizes the thickness dependence of equivalent oxide thickness (EOT), calculated as \(3.9t/{\varepsilon }_{\mathrm{eff}}\). The EOT scales nearly linearly with the A-TiO2 thickness, indicating that sub-1-nm EOT values can be achieved with films thinner than 7.7 nm. Meanwhile, the capacitance-equivalent thickness (CET) was determined using metal–oxide-semiconductor capacitors (Supplementary Fig. 6), demonstrating that an approximately 7.2-nm-thick A-TiO2 film achieves a CET of approximately 1 nm.

For practical device deployment, future high-κ dielectrics must simultaneously demonstrate minimal leakage current and high breakdown strength, for which single-crystal dielectrics represent a compelling high-κ solution for 2D electronics. Figure 1h shows the leakage current characteristics of the as-prepared A-TiO2 membranes with thicknesses of 5.8 nm and 18.2 nm. Both variants have excellent insulating behaviour, with leakage current densities (Jleak) remaining below the low-power limit (1.5 × 10−2 A cm–2) up to operating voltages of 1.5 V (2.6 MV cm–1) and 4.6 V (2.5 MV cm–1) for 5.8-nm and 18.2-nm A-TiO2, respectively. The breakdown field (Ebd) characteristics of the 5.8-nm and 18.2-nm A-TiO2 layers are statistically analysed in Fig. 1i. Furthermore, time-dependent dielectric breakdown analysis of A-TiO2 with an EOT ≈ 1.5 nm under constant-voltage stress projects a ten-year device lifetime at operating voltages below 4 V (Supplementary Fig. 7). These results demonstrate the suitability of transferred A-TiO2 for low-power electronic applications.

To examine the gate dielectric performance of A-TiO2 in 2D transistors, a 3-inch patterned A-TiO2 membrane is transferred onto an Si//SiO2 substrate incorporating patterned platinum back-gate electrodes (refer to Supplementary Fig. 8 for details on the fabrication process flow). A wafer-scale monolayer MoS2 (1L-MoS2) film grown by chemical vapour deposition (CVD) is subsequently transferred to the top of A-TiO2, where the quality of MoS2 is verified by Raman and photoluminescence spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 9). MoS2 channels are defined and contacted using antimony/gold metals to form local bottom-gate MoS2 FETs. Photographs of the 3-inch device array are shown in Fig. 2a,b, and a schematic of the device structure is presented in Fig. 2c. A cross-sectional HRTEM image at the contact area reveals two distinct vdW gaps at the 1L-MoS2/Sb and 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 interfaces (Fig. 2d). At the latter interface, the well-defined single-crystalline dielectric surface provides a clean interface contact with MoS2, minimizing charge-impurity scattering and doping. The clean interface is also attributed to the optimized transfer and polymer removal process (Methods). Furthermore, the vdW gap at the interface of the 2D materials and A-TiO2 also plays a key role in effectively suppressing fringing-induced barrier lowering caused by using high-κ dielectric, which in turn helps to mitigate drain-induced barrier lowering in scaled devices18. At the MoS2/Sb interface, a pristine and intimate contact free of metal-induced defects is observed30, enabling a low contact resistance of about 120 Ω μm, as extracted using the transfer length method from devices with channel lengths ranging from 80 nm to 0.8 μm (Supplementary Fig. 10).

To ensure an equitable assessment, only CVD-grown channels with single-gate configurations are included.

To assess transistor performance with A-TiO2 gate oxide, we measured 100 p- and 100 n-type devices across the wafer, randomly sampled from five representative regions (Supplementary Fig. 11), where the majority of devices have consistent electrical characteristics across the wafer. Devices were qualified by excluding those with abnormal Vth shifts, Ion/Ioff outside 106–5 × 107, or failed electrical characteristics. Figure 2e shows representative transfer characteristics (Ids – Vgs) of 80 qualified long-channel 1L-MoS2 FETs integrated with a 5.8-nm-thick A-TiO2 dielectric (EOT ≈ 0.88 nm; W/L = 2 μm/3 μm). The average subthreshold swing across the array is 68 mV dec–1, with the best device achieving 61 mV dec–1. Similarly, 84 qualified bilayer WSe2 (2L-WSe2) FETs (W/L = 2 μm/2 μm) with A-TiO2 dielectric show excellent performance (Fig. 2f), delivering average and minimum subthreshold swing values of 79 mV dec–1 and 65 mV dec–1, respectively. The subthreshold swing values as a function of Ids for selected 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices are presented in Supplementary Fig. 13. Statistical distributions of Ion/Ioff, subthreshold swing and Vth for the working p- and n-type transistors are summarized in Supplementary Fig. 12, with most n- and p-FETs (>98%) exhibiting over seven orders of magnitude in Ion/Ioff ratios, low gate leakage and minimal variation in Vth. Supplementary Fig. 14a and 14b further present representative transfer characteristics of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs integrated with thicker A-TiO2 gate dielectrics (18.2 nm; EOT ≈ 1.5 nm). Supplementary Fig. 14c–f show the corresponding gate leakage currents for 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with 18.2-nm and 5.8 nm A-TiO2 gate dielectrics, supporting that strong electrostatic control is maintained without increased leakage even under aggressive EOT scaling. Extended Data Fig. 3a compares the subthreshold swing versus EOT across various technologies using CVD-grown 2D channels. Extended Data Fig. 3b further compares Jleak at an applied gate voltage of 1 V for various gate-stack technologies with EOT or CET ≤ 1 nm. The A-TiO2 gate stack demonstrates low Jleak with sub-1-nm EOT, remaining well below the low-power limit (1.5 × 10−2 A cm−2). Recent studies have highlighted the trade-off between leakage-current suppression and electrostatic scaling in vdW-integrated 2D transistor interfaces31, and readers are referred to these works for broader discussions on EOT benchmarking and scaling considerations.

We further fabricated short-channel bottom-gated 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with channel lengths of about 50 nm to evaluate gate controllability at scaled dimensions. Even at this reduced channel length, both 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices exhibit near-ideal subthreshold swing (around 72 mV dec–1) and a high Ion/Ioff ratio (>108) without an increase in off-state current (Fig. 2g,h). The short-channel devices also have high Ion at Vds = 0.6 V. For the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 configuration, Ion reaches 227 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.6 V and 167 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.4 V. Similarly, the 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 device demonstrates Ion values of 136 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.6 V) and 86 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.4 V) at a drain bias of –0.6 V, where Vov = Vgs − Vth denotes the gate-overdrive voltage. The corresponding output characteristics are shown in Fig. 2i. These results can be attributed to the superior gate-to-channel electrostatic control enabled by the A-TiO2 high-κ gate stack (Extended Data Fig. 4). Figure 2j benchmarks the subthreshold swing versus channel length (Lch) for reported short-channel 2D FETs using different dielectric technologies, highlighting that the subthreshold swing values achieved with A-TiO2 gate dielectric are among the lowest reported for CVD-grown MoS2 and WSe2 devices with similar structures. Supplementary Table 1 benchmarks devices using amorphous or single-crystal gate dielectrics with CVD-grown 2D TMD channel materials. The proposed A-TiO2 integration achieves a sub-1-nm EOT, a subthreshold swing of below 65 mV dec–1 and a high Ion, metrics which align with the requirements for low-power, high-performance logic applications.

Hysteresis in the transistor transfer characteristics is a critical metric of operational stability. Here we systematically compare 2D transistors integrated with single-crystalline A-TiO2 to those using amorphous HfO2 and Al2O3 gate dielectrics deposited by the ALD approach (Methods). Extended Data Fig. 5 displays the Ids – Vgs characteristics for different types of dielectrics under forward and reverse gate-voltage sweeps. The hysteresis width (ΔVH) of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs reaches an exceptionally small value of around 1.5 mV at the sweeping frequency (f) of 0.028 Hz (f = 1/tsw, where tsw represents the total forward and backward sweeping time). The cyclostationary behavior of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET is further detailed in Supplementary Fig. 15. The minimal variation observed between the initial and 100th measurement cycles supports the robustness of the gate stack and ensures that our hysteresis characterization is reliable for future device benchmarking32. For a fair comparison, ΔVH is normalized by EOT33,34. Figure 3a summarizes the statistical distribution of normalized ΔVH extracted from devices employing different dielectrics (Supplementary Fig. 16), where A-TiO2 has the smallest hysteresis value among all the tested devices. Supplementary Fig. 17 further shows normalized ΔVH as a function of sweep frequency for a representative 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET measured under different gate sweeping ranges. The resulting hysteresis remains minimal across all measurement conditions, in sharp contrast to MoS2 transistors with conventional SiO2, Al2O3 or HfO2 gate dielectrics, which display pronounced hysteresis, particularly at low sweeping frequencies, due to slow charge trapping in oxide defect states35. Figure 3b benchmarks the normalized ΔVH of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs against literature values reported for a range of dielectric technologies. Notably, our unencapsulated devices achieve a normalized ΔVH of 0.5 mV nm–1, which not only outperforms those of unencapsulated 2D transistors but also demonstrates superior stability compared with channel-encapsulated devices. Furthermore, bias-temperature instability (BTI) measurements reinforce the stability of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 interface (Methods), revealing small threshold voltage shift (ΔVth) under both positive (ΔVth = 40 mV) and negative (ΔVth = 50 mV) gate bias stress (Supplementary Fig. 18). These results indicate the scarcity of border traps within the single-crystalline gate dielectric and a clean dielectric/2D semiconductor interface, even when integrated using conventional wet transfer technologies. Although the BTI of these 2D FETs currently exceeds that of established silicon technology3, further optimization of the interface and dielectric quality remains a clear path toward industrial parity.

a, Normalized hysteresis widths ΔVH with average (μ) and standard deviation (σ) values extracted from the MoS2 FETs with different gate dielectrics and thicknesses. b, Comparison of normalized ΔVH across high-κ dielectric technologies in 2D FETs18,19,22,49,50,51,52,53. Open and solid symbols denote amorphous and crystalline gate dielectrics, respectively. All benchmark values were extracted for 2 V < ΔVgs < 3.5 V and tsw ≤ 100 s. c, Typical cross-sectional STM topography image of the Au/TiO2 interface. Scale bar, 10 nm. d, Atomic-scale evolution of electronic properties of the subsurface of A-TiO2 and HfO2. e, Arrhenius plot of I-DLTS results extracted from 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 1L-MoS2/HfO2 devices, revealing two distinct trap states. The table in the inset lists the activation energy (Ec – Et) and the capture cross section (σn) of two trap states, obtained from the slope and intercept of the two Arrhenius curves. f, Transfer characteristics of 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 (green) and 2L-WSe2/HfO2 (purple) p-FETs. Both devices share identical channel dimensions (Lch = 2 μm, Wch = 2 μm), highlighting the impact of dielectric choice on FET devices.

The record-low hysteresis can be attributed to the clean channel–dielectric interface and crystalline dielectric with low concentration of traps, which together drastically suppress charge trapping to enable low hysteresis. The estimated interface trap density (Dit) is determined as approximately 5.74 × 1011 cm−2 eV−1, substantially lower than the values typically reported for devices incorporating CVD-grown MoS2 channels (Supplementary Table 2), although CVD-synthesized MoS2 inevitably contains point defects (1011–1012 cm–2) due to thermodynamic and growth chemistry constraints36. To understand the origin of hysteresis, we perform cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscope/spectroscopy (XSTM/S) measurements to directly probe the in-gap states in dielectric oxides (Supplementary Note 1). A representative XSTM topography of the metal–dielectric interface is shown in Fig. 3c, whereas spatially resolved XSTM-STS measurements acquired at sub-0.5 nm intervals from the interface into the dielectric are presented in Fig. 3d. Amorphous HfO2 has pronounced in-gap states near the band edges, particularly close to the interface, indicating a high density of charge-trapping centres. By contrast, no discernible in-gap states are detected in A-TiO2, supporting its intrinsically low trap density.

Moreover, current-mode deep-level transient spectroscopy (I-DLTS) reveals distinct trap characteristics at 1L-MoS2/dielectric interfaces (Fig. 3e). 1L-MoS2/HfO2 has a shallow trap (0.221 eV below Ec) with a large capture cross-section (σn = 1.40 × 10−13 cm2). Conversely, 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 shows a deeper trap at 0.293 eV below Ec with a capture cross-section that is three orders of magnitude smaller (σn = 6.40 × 10−17 cm2), substantially suppressing trapping (Supplementary Note 2). The close agreement between XSTM-STS and I-DLTS measurements indicates that shallow, Coulomb-attractive traps dominate the 1L-MoS2/HfO2 interface, whereas deeper, near-neutral traps in A-TiO2   exhibit substantially lower trapping probability. The influence of dielectric quality is further illustrated in Fig. 3f, which compares the transfer characteristics of WSe2 p-FETs fabricated with A-TiO2 and amorphous HfO2 gate dielectrics. The A-TiO2-gated device has clean unipolar p-type behaviour across the entire gate sweep; however, the HfO2-gated device shows pronounced bipolar transport, incompatible with robust CMOS operation. This contrast indicates that the bipolar response is linked to defect-induced Fermi-level modulation associated with in-gap states in the amorphous dielectric (Supplementary Note 3). These findings underscore the critical importance of using high-quality dielectrics with low-trap density to achieve stable, unipolar p-type operation in WSe2 FETs.

The stable and high-performance A-TiO2-gated 2D FETs motivate us to further demonstrate their scalable vertical integration into complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) (Fig. 4a). Fabrication begins with MoS2 n-FET arrays, using buried gold electrodes as source and drain contacts and single-crystalline A-TiO2 as the top-gate dielectric. A vertical CMOS architecture is then constructed by stacking 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 p-FET arrays directly above the n-type tier, sharing a common Pt gate electrode. After vertically interconnecting the drain electrodes of n- and p-FETs through the via-metal, where the output voltage (Vout) is measured, the CFET inverters are realized (the schematic structure is shown in Fig. 4b; refer to Extended Data Fig. 6 for detailed fabrication steps). Figure 4c shows the cross-sectional HRTEM images acquired at the channel region of a representative CFET inverter, revealing uniformly flat layers with atomically sharp vdW interfaces between the 2D semiconductors and the A-TiO2 gate dielectrics. An overview cross-sectional HRTEM image of the complete CFET stack, illustrating the vertical alignment of the top p-FET and bottom n-FET tiers, is provided in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The transfer curves of the bottom n-FETs and top p-FETs (Lch = 1 μm) measured from 16 CFETs are shown in Fig. 4d, exhibiting nearly symmetric behavior and limited device-to-device variation. Note that the voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) curves shown for the CFET inverters exclude abnormal devices (Supplementary Note 4). The yield of the CFET inverters is approximately 50% (25 functional devices out of 50 fabricated devices) and requires further engineering improvement. The standard deviations of normalized Ion are 21.8% for the n-FETs and 23.9% for the p-FETs. The average Vth is 0.9 V for the n-FETs and −1.1 V for the p-FETs, confirming enhancement-mode operation for both device types, which is essential for low-power logic applications. Both n- and p-FETs have steep subthreshold slopes, indicating high transconductance ( gm, defined as the change in drain current with respect to gate voltage, ∆Ids/∆Vgs) and transconductance efficiency (gm/Ids), which are essential for achieving large voltage gain in CFET inverters. Consistently, both device types maintain Ion/Ioff ratios exceeding 107 over a range of Vds while preserving a minimum subthreshold swing of about 75 mV dec–1 (Supplementary Fig. 19), enabling efficient inverter operation at reduced supply voltage (Vdd) with low power consumption. Figure 4e displays representative VTCs of the CFET inverters, demonstrating excellent full-rail logic swing across a range of Vdd from 0.1 V to 1 V. The voltage gain increases progressively with Vdd, from 12 V/V at 0.25 V to a peak value of 89 V/V at 1 V. Remarkably, even at the minimum Vdd of 0.1 V, the inverter maintains a gain value exceeding the minimum threshold (1 V/V) for functional logic operation37, highlighting the potential of this CFET architecture for ultra-low-voltage, energy-efficient circuits. Supplementary Fig. 20 summarizes the voltage gain, static power consumption (Pstatic) and estimated noise margins (NML, low-level noise margin; NMH, high-level noise margin) as functions of Vdd, extracted from 16 individual CFET inverters. Owing to the crystalline nature of the high-κ dielectric and well-matched characteristics of n/p-FETs, the CFET inverters had ultralow gate and channel leakage currents during operation, resulting in exceptionally low Pstatic. At Vdd = 0.25 V, Pstatic is measured to be 38 fW, and even at Vdd = 1 V it remains as low as 1 pW. As summarized in Fig. 4f, the achieved Pstatic is the lowest reported among 2D material-based CMOS inverters, while simultaneously maintaining high gain.

Figure 4g compares the voltage gain values versus switch point (VM/Vdd), where VM denotes the input voltage at which Vout equals Vin. A switching point near 0.5 is critical for maximizing noise margins and ensuring symmetric logic operation. The CFET inverters demonstrated here not only achieve high voltage gains but also maintain VM/Vdd values close to the ideal 0.5. To further evaluate the noise tolerance of our CFET inverters, we estimated the noise margin (NM% = NML% + NMH%) values from the VTCs for 16 individual devices. The average NM% values are 67.5%, 82.5%, 87.5% and 89.2% at Vdd values of 0.25 V, 0.5 V, 0.75 V and 1 V, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 20), exceeding previously reported CFET implementations (Extended Data Table 1).

Beyond inverter operation, logic gate networks, including NAND and NOR gates, were implemented using CFET-based pull-up and pull-down configurations comprising two p-FETs and two n-FETs (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 21). Both logic gates operate reliably at a low Vdd of 0.5 V, demonstrating the feasibility of CFET-based logic beyond single-inverter circuits. The thermal stability of A-TiO2-integrated CFETs was evaluated at both material and device levels (Supplementary Note 5). The results support that the A-TiO2 dielectric and its interfaces with TMD channels retain electrical and crystallographic integrity under  back-end-of-line (BEOL) thermal conditions (up to 400 °C). However, extended high-temperature exposure beyond conventional limits causes noticeable device degradation.

Furthermore, the electrical performance of short-channel CFET inverters with about 50 nm channel lengths in both the bottom- and top-tier FETs was also evaluated (Extended Data Fig. 8a). The transfer characteristics of the p-FET and n-FET show well-matched threshold voltages and on-currents (Extended Data Fig. 8b). This electrical symmetry enables a high inverter voltage gain (gain = 97 V/V at Vdd = 1 V). The improvement is attributed to the higher switching current enabled by the short channels, as illustrated in the VTC and corresponding gain curve in Extended Data Fig. 8c,d. As expected, the static power consumption of these short-channel devices is higher than that of long-channel (Lch = 1 μm) CFETs, as a result of increased short-circuit current and Ioff during switching (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Further work on integrating Vth-tuning techniques is needed to achieve the critical balance of high gain and low power consumption in our CFET technology. Furthermore, we estimate dynamic power (Pdyn) (Supplementary Note 6), where the analysis indicates that the scaled CFET achieves a 39% reduction in dynamic power (Pdyn ≈ 230.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V), compared with the long-channel counterpart (Pdyn ≈ 378.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V). This improvement arises from reduced intrinsic and Miller capacitances associated with the scaled geometry, which outweighs the additional parasitic coupling introduced by the vertical stacking38,39.

In summary, this work demonstrates a 3-inch freestanding A-TiO2 membrane as a gate dielectric that delivers exceptional thickness uniformity and favourable dielectric metrics. The atomically clean interface formed between A-TiO2 and 2D materials enables low subthreshold swing, record-low hysteresis and well-balanced enhancement-mode operation for both n- and p-type transistors. Building on this gate-stack platform, vertically stacked CFET inverter arrays have high voltage gain, wide noise margins and ultralow static power consumption. Density functional theory (DFT) combined with NEGF (NEGF-DFT) simulations further project that the proposed 2D CFET architecture can be scaled to the 1-nm node while sustaining stable operation (Supplementary Note 7). Together, these results establish wafer-scale single-crystal high-κ dielectrics integrated with 2D semiconductors as viable and promising platforms for energy-efficient logic technologies, positioning them as compelling candidates for the post-silicon electronics roadmap.

The AlO2-terminated surface of single-crystalline 3-inch LaAlO3 (001) substrates was prepared by wet etching of LaAlO3 (001) for 30 s with dilute HCl (pH ≈ 4.5), followed by 1,000 °C annealing in a pure oxygen atmosphere. The atomically sharp step and terraces of substrates were examined by AFM. The SrTiO3, Sr3Al2O6 and A-TiO2 films were grown by pulsed laser deposition using a 248-nm krypton fluoride excimer laser with a laser fluence of 48 mJ cm–2. A laser-scanning system capable of depositing films on wafers up to 4-inch in diameter was used, in which a linear translation stage, rather than a galvanometer, was used to scan the laser beam across a rotating target. This configuration eliminates optical distortions and maintains consistent ablation conditions, thereby ensuring uniform film growth. The SrTiO3 buffer layer and water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 layers were deposited at 850 °C with an oxygen partial pressure (\({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\)) of 1 × 10−6 torr. The in situ RHEED patterns indicated the highly crystalline nature for the as-grown A-TiO2 layer, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The epitaxial growth of the A-TiO2 layer on the Sr3Al2O6 thin film was then conducted at 800 °C and \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−4 torr. On the completion of film deposition, the sample was cooled down to room temperature under \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−1 torr to prevent non-stoichiometry in A-TiO2 film.

The 1L-MoS2 film was synthesized via a CVD method on C/M sapphire substrates (supplied by Crystal-wise Technology), which had undergone surface reconstruction. Molybdenum trioxide (MoO3, 99.5%) and sulfur (S, 99.5%) powders (both from Sigma-Aldrich) were positioned in separate zones of a quartz tube furnace. A heating belt regulated the sulfur evaporation at 160–180 °C, whereas the substrate and MoO3 were heated to 700 °C. An argon gas flow facilitated the transport of vapourized precursors. The growth process lasted 15 min, after which the system was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The 2L-WSe2 film was provided by Nexstrom, where the samples were grown by CVD methods. The transfer procedures of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 follow the common polymethyl-methacrylate-assisted wet transfer method.

X-ray diffraction measurements were conducted using a Rigaku SmartLab thin-film XRD system with a rotating copper anode X-ray source. The dislocation density (\(\rho \)) is evaluated using the Vannas (Halliwell–Hirsch) model:

where \(\beta \) is the FWHM in radians and \(b\) is the Burgers vector. The surface morphologies were examined by AFM (Bruker Dimension Icon SPM). The film thickness uniformity was measured by an ellipsometer (J.A. Woollam RC2). Raman and Photoluminescence spectra of MoS2 and WSe2 were collected in a confocal Raman microscopy system (WITec alpha 300 R) with a 532-nm laser. The cross-sectional STM measurement was conducted under ultrahigh vacuum (5 × 10−11 torr) at room temperature. Plan-view dark-field TEM image and SAED pattern of A-TiO2 membrane were captured using a Thermo Scientific Talos F200X STEM at 200 kV from a top-view sample suspended on a holey carbon grid. Cross-section lamellas for LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure, single FET and CFET devices were prepared with a focused-ion-beam system (Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX). Cross-section STEM images and EDS mapping were conducted by the same STEM system at 200 kV. The surface topography and structure of CFET logic gates were examined by SEM (Zeiss Sigma 300 VP).

For MIM capacitors, the A-TiO2 membranes were transferred onto Au-coated Si substrates; subsequently, 10 nm Ti and 80 nm Au electrodes were fabricated through the shadow mask by electron-beam evaporation. For ALD-grown amorphous dielectric oxides, we used trimethylaluminum and water as the precursors for Al2O3 deposition, whereas tetrakis (dimethylamido) hafnium and water served as the precursors for HfO2, with the growth temperature of 150 °C. For FET fabrication (Supplementary Fig. 8), the A-TiO2 membranes and 1L-MoS2/2L-WSe2 layers were sequentially transferred onto a Ti/Pt (1 nm/8 nm) local back-gate array. The channel area was defined using electron-beam lithography followed by O2 reactive-ion etching (10 mTorr, 100 W). After patterning the source/drain regions using electron-beam lithography, Sb/Au (20 nm/40 nm) and Pt/Au (5 nm/15 nm) contacts were deposited to form n-type 1L-MoS2 and p-type 2L-WSe2 FETs, respectively. The metals were deposited using thermal and e-beam evaporation, and the chamber pressure was maintained at around 10−8 Torr throughout the metal deposition process. For CFET devices (Extended Data Fig. 6), a 12-nm Au layer was first deposited on the substrate to serve as the bottom contact for the n-FET. A 1L-MoS2 film was transferred and patterned, followed by the transfer of an A-TiO2 membrane as the gate dielectric. A 10-nm Pt mid-gate was then defined on A-TiO2 to serve as the shared gate for both bottom n-FET and top p-FET. The top device was then completed by sequential transfer of a second A-TiO2 membrane and a 2L-WSe2 film, which was intentionally adopted to improve device-to-device uniformity and process tolerance during multilayer CFET fabrication, supported by independent statistical comparison of 1L-WSe2 and 2L-WSe2 devices (Supplementary Note 8). To remove surface polymer residue, a mild O2 plasma treatment (15 W, 20 s) and hot-acetone vapour (80 °C, 30 min) were applied after transferring the A-TiO2 and 2D material layers, respectively. After electron-beam lithography alignment of the active regions, 5 nm Pt/20 nm Au were deposited to form the p-FET contacts. Finally, the CFET inverter was formed by interconnecting the two pads respectively from n- and p-FETs through a via opening defined by O2/SF6 inductively coupled plasma etching, followed by Au metallization. The same via process was used for NAND and NOR logic demonstrations.

Electrical characterization of the devices was performed using a Keysight B1500A semiconductor parameter analyser mounted in a closed-cycle cryogenic probe station (at a base pressure of about 10−6 Torr). Capacitance measurements were conducted with the Keysight E5288A C-V Measurement System integrated into the B1500A platform. All devices were measured under vacuum conditions within a probe station featuring a shielded enclosure to reduce electromagnetic interference. where \({C}_{\mathrm{ox}}\) is the gate dielectric capacitance obtained from MIM capacitance measurements (Extended Data Fig. 2), \(q\) is the elementary charge, \({k}_{{\rm{B}}}\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the absolute temperature. Pstatic is calculated as \({{V}}_{{\rm{dd}}}\times ({I}_{{{\rm{Static}}}_{{\rm{low}}}}+{I}_{{{\rm{Static}}}_{{\rm{high}}}})/2\) in the static regime (Vin = 0 V or Vin = Vdd).

Bias-temperature instability measurements were performed at room temperature by applying gate biases of –1 V and +2 V, respectively, for 1,000 s. After removal of the stress bias, Vth recovery was monitored through transfer measurements at Vds = 1 V. The same extraction criterion was used throughout, and the Vth shift was calculated relative to the initial value as ΔVth = Vth,t – Vth,0.

The transport properties of the 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs were investigated using DFT combined with the NEGF formalism, as implemented in the QuantumATK package60. Here, \({V}_{\mathrm{gs}}\) and \({V}_{\mathrm{dd}}\) were set to be 0.6 V. All calculations were performed using linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) basis set with high accuracy and PseudoDojo pseudopotential61. The exchange-correlation functional was treated at the GGA-PBE level. For the MoS2 DG-FET, a 15 × 1 × 173 Monkhorst–Pack k-point grid is used. For the 2L-WSe2 DG-FET, a 33 × 1 × 165 grid is adopted and vdW-D3 correction is used for vdW interaction62. The gate length of both devices is set to 10 nm. Two gate dielectrics are examined for electrostatic control: SiO2 with a permittivity of 3.9 and thickness of 0.9 nm, and TiO2 with a high-κ value of 25 and thickness of 5.8 nm. The atomic compensation-charge method is used to control the doping distribution in the source and drain extensions.

#1364. Everton Women Welcome JYSK As Official Home Furnishing Retail Partner

Everton Women has announced a new partnership with international home furnishing retailer JYSK, which will become the Club's ‘Official Home Furnishing Retail Partner’.

The agreement brings together Everton and the Danish retailer, renowned for its Scandinavian-inspired furniture and homeware, in a partnership that will enhance facilities at Goodison Park and support community initiatives across Merseyside.

JYSK (pronounced 'YOOSK') operates more than 3,600 stores worldwide, with a presence in the Liverpool City Region through its outlets in Hunts Cross and St Helens. The Scandinavian retailer will provide furniture and homeware to create welcoming spaces for players, staff and supporters at Goodison Park.

The announcement marks Everton Women's third dedicated commercial partnership, following agreements with GGM Gastro and, most recently, Nestlé Confectionery, further demonstrating the growing appeal of the Club to leading international businesses.

Everton Women's move to Goodison Park has provided a distinctive platform for commercial growth, combining the Club's rich footballing heritage with new opportunities for partners to play a meaningful role in the future of women's football.

JYSK will also support the work of Everton in the Community, with furniture featured in the partnership's launch campaign donated to the charity's 'Home Is Where The Heart Is' programme, which supports young adults experiencing or at risk of homelessness.

The donated items will make a valuable contribution to the charity's four-bedroom residential property in the L4 area of Liverpool, further enhancing the welcoming and supportive environment provided for young people as they develop the skills and confidence needed to live independently.

Andrew Middleton, President of Business Operations at Everton, said: "We're delighted to welcome JYSK to Everton Women. There's a natural connection between a business that helps people make a house a home and the next chapter we're creating at Goodison Park, and we're looking forward to bringing that to life for our players and supporters.

"What particularly stands out is JYSK's commitment to making a positive difference beyond football. Their support for Everton in the Community is a fantastic example of how we want our partnerships to deliver meaningful benefits, both for the Club and the communities we represent.

"There's a growing recognition among businesses of the opportunities around Everton Women, and we're focused on building partnerships that go beyond traditional sponsorship. JYSK is another great addition to that journey and we're excited about what we can achieve together."

Roni Tuominen, Country Director, JYSK Ireland & UK, said: "Everton Women has an incredible story with a rich heritage and community roots. The team has made a positive start to the season and we can’t wait to support them at Goodison Park and help turn this legacy stadium into a home."

JYSK's partnership will be visible at Goodison Park for the first time when Everton Women host Durham Women in the Subway Players Cup on Wednesday 11 November (7pm GMT kick-off), with branding featuring on the stadium's big screens and pitchside LED advertising.

To celebrate the announcement, JYSK will also give away limited-edition JYSK x Everton tote bags at its Hunts Cross Retail Park store on Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November.

The bags will be available to customers making a purchase, with no minimum spend, on a first-come, first-served basis while stocks last.

For more information about JYSK, visit jysk.co.uk.

#1363. Hearts boss Vrancken is playing with fire by turning the guns on his own players

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:17 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Not for the first time this season under Wouter Vrancken, Hearts suffered a complete and utter implosion as they were thrashed 5-2 at home to Falkirk last weekend.

This is a team who lost 6-0 to Sturm Graz over two legs in the Champions League qualifiers back at the start of the campaign.

A team who were then battered 6-1 away against Benfica in Lisbon in the Europa League qualifiers – and a team who were also thumped 7-1 against Celtic at Parkhead a few weeks ago.

Hearts also lost the derby to Hibs just over a week ago in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup at Hampden.

Now comes an annihilation against Falkirk where Hearts were 4-0 down by half-time. What a shambolic way to lose a long unbeaten record at home.

Even accounting for what had gone before in some of those matches this season, what happened on Sunday at Tynecastle felt like a new low.

Hearts were a shambles. But what was even more alarming was the manager's inability to stop the bleeding and make any changes from the touchline.

All of which poses a very simple question. Have Hearts and Jamestown made a mistake with Vrancken? At the moment, he looks hopelessly one-dimensional.

But it was his post-match comments on Sunday afternoon which actually became even more alarming than the performance itself.

Wouter Vrancken was 'embarrassed' by Hearts' 5-2 home loss to Falkirk

Vrancken branded it 'embarrassing' and a 'disgrace'. He called his players 'childish' and basically insinuated that they lacked any spirit or character until the youngsters came off the bench.

In the midst of a horrendous injury crisis and with players dropping like flies, that is a very dangerous game for any manager to play. He threw them under a bus.

By publicly slaughtering his players like that during a time of adversity and when many of them are being asked to play out of position, he is playing with fire.

Those are the type of comments that could very easily lose a dressing room. His comments would have gone down like a lead balloon among the squad.

Hearts have had the best part of a dozen players missing through injury. Vrancken himself has branded it an injury crisis unlike any other he has experienced throughout his career.

But what is most curious in all of this is that Vrancken seems totally unwilling to engage in any self-reflection throughout all of this.

After the shellacking at Celtic Park a few weeks ago, he lamented the fact his team had made too many individual errors.

There was no acknowledgment that his system had set them up to fail. No acceptance that pressing Celtic man-for-man and leaving players one-v-one at the back was a huge part of the problem.

Since he arrived in the summer, Vrancken's preferred style of play has been front-foot attacking football. There have been times when it has clicked reasonably well.

When he had his key players fit, Hearts were a good watch. But when the guts of a full team were then ripped out due to injury, it has quickly disintegrated into chaos.

Continuing to demand the same high-pressing and attacking style of play without meaningful adjustment is not principled. It is naive, inflexible, and tactically illiterate.

When the structure collapses, as it did against Falkirk and in the 7-1 defeat at Celtic, the emphasis returns to individual mistakes rather than collective vulnerability created by the system itself.

It is a classic example of a manager publicly hanging his players out to dry rather than choosing to accept his own part in the wider failings.

Hearts are not in crisis yet. They still sit fourth in the table, just a point behind Falkirk. But this is a team who have clearly regressed from where they were last season.

Vrancken was hired on the basis that he could bring a more dynamic style of play and move the team forward from the platform left behind by Derek McInnes.

As written in these pages a few weeks ago after the defeat to Celtic, there is absolutely no prospect whatsoever of this Hearts team challenging for the title this time around.

The current combination of a horrendous injury list, a rigid tactical approach and increasingly pointed public criticism of the players is a dangerous mixture that threatens to undermine everything.

Scottish football's fixture congestion, the demands of European competition and the physical toll of the season have exposed the limits of Vrancken's one-dimensional plan.

Adaptation is not a betrayal of principles. It is a basic requirement of the job when circumstances change this dramatically.

The international break offers a brief window. A handful of bodies may return for Hearts' next fixture against Dundee at Dens Park.

The more important return would be a change in tone and a willingness to adapt the demands placed on those players left still standing.

Publicly branding his players as 'a disgrace' while refusing to acknowledge that the system itself is contributing to their vulnerability is a sure-fire way to get himself sacked.

Vrancken's Hearts squad has been ravaged by injuries this season

The manager is entitled to be angry. He is entitled to demand better. He is not entitled to ignore the context he is operating in or the effect his words will have on a group already stretched to breaking point.

Vrancken arrived with a clear identity and early promise. The test now is whether he can evolve that identity under pressure or whether he remains locked into one way of playing regardless of the resources available.

Hearts cannot afford the latter. Much more of this public slaughtering and the players will switch off. Vrancken will have lost them completely.

Players will run for a manager who shows understanding of their situation even while criticising their standards.

They will begin to switch off for one who appears to place the preservation of his methods above the protection of the group.

That is the risk Vrancken is running. It is a risk no manager in the middle of a crippling injury crisis can afford to take.

#1362. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

It’s been a feisty game so far. Newcastle fans are unhappy with the number of fouls given against them. The hosts are being very aggressive with their press as Gonzalez dispossesses Kamara to force a corner, but nothing comes from the set piece.

Newcastle fans can breathe a huge sigh of relief as Botman’s card stays as a yellow. The defender is a very lucky man.

Referee Gillett shows two yellow cards in incredibly quick succession as Joelinton and Botman both fly into forceful challenges on Manzambi and Jackson respectively. The crowd furiously boo both decisions. Botman’s tackle on Jackson was wild and over the top of the ball, with VAR checking for a possible red card.

Villa are finding holes in Newcastle’s defence as Manzambi plays in Cash, who fires into the side netting from a tight angle. Emery and his players are convinced they should of had a corner.

Once again, Villa hit Newcastle on the counter. This time, Jackson turns provider and tries to thread a pass into Alysson’s path. However, Hall is on high alert and defends diligently to intercept and clear.

Huge chance for Villa! Out of nowhere, Villa counter from a Newcastle corner. It’s excellent play from Alysson, who powers past his marker before slipping a pass to the onrushing Jackson. The striker is through and chops inside of Botman, before shooting straight at Hornicek with the outside of his boot. Given the ruthless form he’s been in, you’d expect more from Jackson there.

Villa are penned in at the moment, with Newcastle having made a fast start in these early stages. Suzuki has the ball and he’s put under tremendous pressure from Wissa. The goalkeeper is calmness personified as he coolly passes to Cash.

Fernandez-Pardo drives at Wan-Bissaka and tries to find Willock with a low delivery. The cross is intercepted by Lindelof, but it’s positive play from Newcastle’s summer recruit, who is lining up in his preferred position out wide.

Early signs reveal that Fernandez-Pardo is playing on the right wing, with Wissa operating as the central striker and Willock pushed up as the most advanced midfielder. Barnes is on the left.

Villa get us under way at St James’ Park.

Both line-ups are out on the pitch. St James’ Park is absolutely buzzing as the Premier League anthem rings around the stadium after a modified edition of Blaydon Races, with kick-off minutes away.

There is a new version of the Blaydon Races, reworked by Newcastle United in order to become their club’s official pre-match anthem. It is slower than the original and lacks a bit of oomph. But, you know what, I wanted to hate it and it was actually okay. Once supporters get used to the new pace of the song they should start joining in with the singing. Newcastle will be relieved that this game is at St James’ Park, with the club having lost their previous two away fixtures 4-1 against both Coventry and Leeds.

Summer signing Nicolas Jackson has five goals in his previous six games for Aston Villa in all competitions and looks to be brimming with confidence as he leads the line for Unai Emery. The striker dispatched both finishes for his brace against Fenerbahce with unerring composure and will target more goals at St James’ Park.

One of the interesting subplots to this evening’s game will be watching Johan Manzambi playing for Aston Villa.

The Switzerland international’s decision to reject Newcastle in order to sign for Villa helped convince Eddie Howe to quit in the summer.

Having already missed out on Victor Munoz, who decided to join Liverpool at the last moment, losing Manzambi - their first-choice target across the position board - was a blow Howe did not feel he could recover from.

In short, he was not convinced the alternatives would give him the tools to do the job this season. Aladji Bamba, who was signed instead, has not started a game for Newcastle this season and appears to be well down the pecking order in the centre midfield under Howe’s successor Matthias Jaissle.

Manzambi had a slow start to his Villa career because of injury but he was hugely impressive at the World Cup for Switzerland and is expected to become one of the best midfield players in Europe over the next few years. Nobody can say with any degree of confidence that will be the same for Bamba.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage as Newcastle United welcome Aston Villa to St James’ Park in the Premier League.

Newcastle endured a hellish Monday night as they were condemned to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Coventry City in their previous top-flight outing. Matthias Jaissle’s rebranded Newcastle outfit have notably lacked consistency in the early weeks of the season, with the loss to Coventry another abrupt reminder of how this is expected to be a challenging campaign for his freshly assembled squad. The new arrivals are yet to fully settle and Newcastle are undoubtedly still adapting following a turbulent summer transfer window where they lost several key players.

Meanwhile, Villa arrive up north in tremendously high spirits following their 6-0 thumping of Fenerbahce in midweek Champions League action, thereby recording their biggest European win in the club’s history. However, in a similar vein to Newcastle, Villa have struggled to impose themselves in the Premier League, triumphing just once in their opening six matches of the season. Unai Emery’s men conceded a 79th-minute equaliser to Brentford’s Kristoffer Ajer last time out in the Premier League to draw 2-2 and deepen their domestic frustration.

Despite how this week’s results have shaped contrasting moods in the two camps, Newcastle are currently three points ahead of Villa in the Premier League, with today’s visitors aiming to make it back-to-back top-flight away wins after beating Tottenham 3-2 in the capital last month.

Jaissle is still trying to find his feet in English football, and hosting Villa is yet another tough test of his credentials. Meanwhile, it’s a question of when Emery’s new-look Villa will click, not if, given his unbelievable impact at the club. The Spaniard is fast approaching his four-year anniversary as Villa’s head coach, and what a journey it has been.
