In the absence of O-GlcNAcylation (fgly = 0), FG-NUPs collapsed into a dense surface condensate surrounding the NPC scaffold (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Video 6), leaving a large central void and producing NUP98 chain extensions inconsistent with previous in situ FLIM–FRET measurements26 (Fig. 5e). Increasing O-GlcNAcylation progressively expanded FG domains into the central channel (Fig. 5b–d and Supplementary Videos 7–9). An O-GlcNAcylation level of fgly = 0.3 reproduced the experimentally measured RE of NUP98 FG domains particularly well (Fig. 5e) and yielded 48 predicted O-GlcNAcylation sites, closely matching the 46 sites identified experimentally in Xenopus NUP9848. Higher O-GlcNAcylation levels yielded progressively more extended chains.

O-GlcNAcylation also accelerated bond-vector relaxation, mirroring the experimental trend in which NUP98 FG domains exhibit faster segmental dynamics inside the NPC than in unglycosylated in vitro condensates, yet slower dynamics than isolated chains (Figs. 1h and 5f and Supplementary Fig. 15). The effect of explicit O-GlcNAcylation on FG-NUPs can be reproduced by implicitly weakening FG-NUP attractive interactions through an interaction-rescaling parameter, α (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Fig. 15). Remarkably, by then matching the RE of NUP98 to the FLIM–FRET measurements, we find the FG-NUPs to be near the critical point for phase separation in the Martini model, where relatively small changes in effective interactions can strongly alter FG-NUP organization, confirming our earlier observations from the residue-level coarse-grained FG-NUP models26.

Because O-GlcNAcylation weakens effective FG–FG interactions, we next asked whether differences in modification state could also influence mixing between FG assemblies. Simulations and selective-partitioning experiments showed that differences in O-GlcNAcylation promote demixing between otherwise similar FG assemblies (Supplementary Figs. 16–18 and Methods). Thus, differences in FG-NUP PTMs, including O-GlcNAcylation in metazoans and potentially O-mannosylation or phosphorylation in yeast, may tune FG–FG interaction strengths in ways that oppose mixing21.

Together, the combination of Martini and residue-level coarse-grained simulations recapitulates key mesoscopic and microscopic features—from chain extension and apparent segmental motion to importin-β partitioning and transport behaviour—and bridges simplified in vitro studies with the crowded environment of the intact NPC. These results highlight how O-GlcNAcylation and importin-β make complementary contributions to maintaining liquid-like FG-domain conformational dynamics and generating the spatial and dynamic heterogeneity characteristic of the permeability barrier.

By combining site-specific labelling with picosecond TRFA, we directly monitored conformational dynamics of FG-NUPs in living cells. NUP98 retained rapid apparent segmental motion even in regions that aggregate readily in vitro, sharply contrasting with aged FG condensates that transition into solid-like hydrogels. Their progressive loss of apparent segmental motion is consistent with amyloid-like interactions observed by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and electron microscopy12,36.

The discrepancy raises a key question: why do FG domains rapidly age into hydrogels in vitro4,5,13, yet remain dynamic in one of the cell’s longest-lived protein assemblies19,51? Nucleocytoplasmic transport depends on ultrafast, reversible FG–FG and FG–NTR interactions, with thousands of transient sequential contacts supporting millisecond cargo passage24,25. The apparent segmental motion detected by TRFA therefore provides a dynamic context for the rapid exchange of transient FG–NTR contacts during transport. We identify importin-β and O-GlcNAcylation as two factors that tune this behaviour. Each partially suppresses molecular ageing in vitro, whereas together they reproduce the apparent segmental-motion trends measured in living cells (Extended Data Fig. 8f).

Molecular-dynamics simulations further showed how importin-β contributes to this stabilization. Importin-β dilutes aggregation-prone FG segments, swells condensates and enhances apparent segmental motion. Although chaperone-like properties of importin-β have been proposed previously36,37,38, our work demonstrates how it modulates FG-domain dynamics at the segmental level, particularly when FG–FG interactions are strengthened, consistent with the karyopherin-centric model of the NPC barrier10,52.

PTMs provide another regulatory layer. Phosphorylation has been proposed to modulate FG-domain dynamics53, and NUP98 hyperphosphorylation promotes NPC disassembly54. However, selectively perturbing NUP98 phosphorylation in live cells remains challenging. By contrast, the extensive O-GlcNAcylation of NUP9847,48 allowed direct perturbation here. Altering O-GlcNAc levels changed both apparent segmental motion of FG domains and nuclear transport (Fig. 4e,f), linking O-GlcNAc–dependent tuning of FG-NUP dynamics to NPC function.

Serendipitously, our simulations also show the radial organization of the NPC barrier. Under experimentally matched interaction strengths (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42), importin-β was enriched near the pore periphery, whereas extended FG domains occupied the centre; increasing FG–importin-β affinity instead drove importin-β to cluster in the pore centre (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.5; Fig. 3b,c and Supplementary Videos 3 and 4). The peripheral distribution agrees with recent three-dimensional MINFLUX tracking of NTR-bound cargos14 and with our two-dimensional MINFLUX measurements. Our simulations further indicate that this organization emerges naturally from FG-NUP grafting geometry39 and locally elevated FG density near the pore wall. Consequently, importin-β exposure may vary along NUP98, potentially leading to position-dependent rescue of apparent segmental motion (Fig. 4c).

These findings provide a complementary perspective on central plug-like densities reported by electron microscopy55,56 and high-speed AFM studies21. Differences in NPC conformation may partly underlie these observations, as in situ cryo-electron tomography shows a wider central channel in native cellular NPCs than in isolated preparations39. Because our MINFLUX measurements use NUP96 as a scaffold reference without directly resolving the inner-ring diameter, we cannot exclude effects of NPC dilation or constriction on the apparent importin-β distribution. Moreover, the central plug shown by AFM is highly mobile21, consistent with a dynamic transport-associated assembly rather than a rigid structure. Our data do not exclude importin-β from central plug-like densities, but indicate that the central axis is not its predominant location. One possible framework is a dual-route organization in which small and medium-sized cargos that interact efficiently with NTRs preferentially use the periphery, whereas larger or more slowly transported cargos occupy the central channel. In this view, some central densities could represent transient cargo or transport complexes rather than a permanent plug.

More broadly, our study illustrates how cellular context can preserve functional dynamics of IDPs in crowded environments, with implications for diseases linked to FG-NUP dysfunction, including cancer, viral infection and neurodegenerative disease57,58. Combining in-cell fluorescence measurements with multiscale computational modelling provides a general strategy for probing IDP conformational dynamics in their native cellular environment.

COS-7 cells (Sigma, 87021302) and HEK293T cells (Beyotime, C6008) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (Thermo Fisher, 41965-039) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sigma, F7524), 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher, 15140-122), 1% l-glutamine (Thermo Fisher, 25030-081) and 1% sodium pyruvate (Thermo Fisher, 11360-070). U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells originally obtained from Cytion (300174) and provided by Y. Li were maintained in McCoy’s 5A (Procell, PM150710) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO2 and were passaged every 2–3 days. All experiments were performed using cells in 20 passages.

To generate a doxycycline-inducible U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cell line expressing importin-β, lentiviral particles were produced in HEK293T cells by cotransfection of pTRIPZ-importin-β-3×FLAG-ALFA-P2A-tagBFP (derived from the pTRIPZ; Addgene, 206981), psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259) at a plasmid ratio of 4:3:1. Viral supernatants were collected 48 and 72 h after transfection and concentrated by polyethylene-glycol-8000 precipitation. U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells were transduced for 48 h and selected with puromycin (1 μg ml−1; Yeasen, 727136ES03) for 4 days. For MINFLUX imaging, expression of importin-β was induced with doxycycline (0.5 μg ml−1; MCE, HY-N0565) for 24 h before fixation.

Cell morphology was routinely monitored during culture. The engineered U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP/importin-β cell line was also verified by NUP96-mEGFP fluorescence and doxycycline-inducible importin-β expression. No in-house short tandem repeat profiling was performed. All cell lines were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination by PCR and with the MycoBlue Mycoplasma Detector Kit (Vazyme, D101-01), with negative results.

COS-7 cells were seeded on 35-mm glass-bottom imaging dishes (ibidi, 81158) 24 h before transfection to reach 60–70% confluency. Cells were transfected with plasmids listed in Supplementary Table 1 using jetPRIME (Polyplus) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. At 4–5 h post-transfection, the medium was replaced with fresh culture medium supplemented with 10 mM HEPES and either 50 μM BCN for site-specific labelling or 50 μM BOC for control experiments. Where indicated, 10 μM Thiamet-G (MCE, HY-12588) or 10 μM OSMI-4 (MCE, HY-114361) was added at this stage and maintained throughout the experiment.

At 20–24 h following transfection, cells were washed with medium containing 50 μM BOC and 10 mM HEPES and incubated for 2 h at 37 °C to allow excess BCN to clear. Cells were then labelled with 2 μM HD653 in serum-free medium for 30 min at 37 °C. For O-GlcNAc perturbation experiments, 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 was included during labelling to maintain treatment conditions. Where indicated, SiR-tetrazine (Spirochrome, SC008) or JF646-tetrazine (Tocris, 7279) was used following the same protocol. After labelling, cells were washed with 1× PBS and imaged immediately in FluoroBrite Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (Thermo Fisher, A1896701) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% l-glutamine, 1% sodium pyruvate and 10 mM HEPES. Imaging was performed at room temperature with the dish sealed to ensure stable conditions during the roughly 2-h acquisition period.

COS-7 cells labelled with HD653 were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 10 min, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 min and blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin in PBS for 90 min. Cells were incubated with an anti-KPNB1 antibody (Abcam, ab2811; 1:1000 dilution) followed by an Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated anti-mouse secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:1000 dilution). Immunofluorescence imaging confirmed localization of endogenous importin-β at the nuclear envelope following live-cell labelling (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

To estimate the local concentration of importin-β at the nuclear pore, solutions containing free Alexa Fluor 488 at known concentrations (1 μm–1 mM) were added to immunostained cells. Nuclear pore fluorescence remained distinguishable from the background in the presence of up to 100 μM free dye but became indistinguishable at 1 mM (Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that the effective local concentration of importin-β at the nuclear pore is in the millimolar range.

The doxycycline-inducible U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cell line described above was treated with doxycycline (0.5 μg ml−1) for 0, 6, 10, 15 or 24 h. Non-transduced U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells without doxycycline treatment were used as a parental control. Cell lysates were collected at the indicated time points and analysed by immunoblotting using an anti-FLAG antibody (Proteintech, 66008-4-Ig; 1:1,000 dilution) to detect exogenous importin-β and an anti-KPNB1 antibody (1:2,500 dilution) to detect both endogenous and exogenous importin-β. α-Tubulin detected with an anti-α-Tubulin antibody (ABclonal, AC012; 1:5,000 dilution) was used as a loading control. Doxycycline induction resulted in detectable FLAG-tagged importin-β expression, whereas the total KPNB1 signal showed no substantial increase compared with the parental control, consistent with near-endogenous expression of the exogenous protein (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20).

To verify modulation of cellular O-GlcNAcylation, COS-7 cells were treated with 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 as described above and lysed directly in Laemmli sample buffer. Proteins were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE), transferred to nitrocellulose membranes and probed with the anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 (Invitrogen, MA1-072; 1:1,000 dilution). Bound antibody was detected using an IRDye 800CW goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (LI-COR Biosciences, 926-32210; 1:10,000 dilution) and visualized using an Odyssey imaging system (Fig. 4b).

Live-cell nuclear-import assays were performed as described previously49 with minor modifications. COS-7 cells expressing NES–mCherry–LINuS were treated with 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 and imaged 24 h after transfection following Hoechst 33342 staining (10 μg ml−1, 10 min). Imaging was performed on a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope. Nuclear import was induced by 488-nm illumination and monitored by mCherry fluorescence using 561-nm excitation. Images were acquired every 10 s for 820 s. Nuclear regions were segmented using Hoechst fluorescence, and nuclear mCherry intensity was quantified over time and normalized to the pre-activation signal. Apparent nuclear-import rate constants were obtained by fitting fluorescence accumulation curves to y = 1 + (b − 1)(1 − e−kt), where b is the plateau fluorescence intensity and k is the apparent nuclear-import rate constant.

The human NUP98 FG domain (residues 1–505) was cloned into a pQE-14his-TEV vector. As described previously26,59, the GLEBS domain (residues 157–213) was excluded to avoid misfolding of this structured region on rapid dilution from denaturant during phase separation (see ‘In vitro phase separation assay’ below); intrinsically disordered FG regions, by contrast, readily regain their dynamic ensemble under native buffer conditions. The construct was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21-AI cells and grown in terrific broth supplemented with kanamycin (50 µg ml−1) at 37 °C with shaking at 200 rpm. Protein expression was induced when optical density at 600 nm (OD600) ≈ 0.6 with 0.02% (w/v) arabinose and 1 mM iIsopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation for 16 h at 18 °C.

Cells were collected and lysed using a high-pressure cell disruptor (CF1, Constant Systems) in lysis buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride (GdmCl), 0.2 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), 20 mM imidazole and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Following clarification by centrifugation (12,000g, 1 h, 4 °C), lysates were incubated with nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) resin for 2 h at 4 °C. Bound protein was washed with 2 M GdmCl buffer and eluted with 500 mM imidazole in 2 M GdmCl and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). After dialysis into 0.5 M GdmCl and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), the N-terminal His-tag was removed by overnight TEV protease digestion. The cleaved protein was separated from uncleaved protein and TEV protease by a second Ni-NTA purification step and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL, Cytiva, 28990944) in 2 M GdmCl, 0.2 mM TCEP and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Purity was confirmed by SDS–PAGE and Coomassie staining. Protein fractions were concentrated to about 15 mg ml−1, quantified using a bicinchoninic acid assay and stored at −80 °C.

The purified NUP98 FG domain was enzymatically glycosylated using recombinant OGT1 and UDP-GlcNAc (Sigma, U4375). The reaction mixture contained 10 µM NUP98 FG domain, 1 µM OGT1 and 1 mM UDP-GlcNAc in glycosylation buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 20 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM TCEP and 1% Tween-20). Samples were incubated for 16 h at room temperature with gentle rotation. Following O-GlcNAcylation, His-tagged OGT1 was removed using Ni-NTA resin. O-GlcNAcylated NUP98 FG domain was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200) in 2 M GdmCl, 0.2 mM TCEP and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and concentrated to about 40 mg ml−1. O-GlcNAcylation efficiency was assessed by mass spectrometry, confirming successful modification of the NUP98 FG domain (Extended Data Fig. 8c).

For experiments requiring higher levels of O-GlcNAc modification, the purified glycosylated protein was subjected to a second round of enzymatic O-GlcNAcylation under identical reaction conditions. Unless otherwise stated, all experiments were performed using NUP98 FG domains that had undergone a single round of O-GlcNAcylation. Proteins subjected to two rounds of O-GlcNAcylation were used only for the experiments shown in Supplementary Fig. 18.

NUP98 FG-domain variants containing a single cysteine substitution (residue 36, 100, 221, 312, 387 or 482) were exchanged into 4 M GdmCl, 1× PBS, 0.1 mM EDTA and 0.2 mM TCEP (pH 7.0). Proteins were labelled overnight at 4 °C with Cy3B maleimide (GE Healthcare, PA63131) or Alexa Fluor 594 maleimide (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A10256) at a protein/dye molar ratio of 1:2. Excess dye was quenched with 10 mM dithiothreitol and removed by ultrafiltration (3 kDa molecular-weight cutoff), followed by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200). Protein concentrations and labelling efficiencies were determined spectroscopically using a Duetta fluorometer (Horiba). Labelled proteins were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

The human importin-β coding sequence was cloned into a pTXB3-intein-CBD-12His vector and transformed into E. coli BL21-AI cells. Cultures were grown in terrific broth supplemented with kanamycin (50 μg ml−1) at 37 °C with shaking (200 rpm). Protein expression was induced at OD600 = 0.4–0.6 with 0.02% (w/v) arabinose and 1 mM iIsopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation for 5–6 h at 37 °C. Cells were lysed by high-pressure homogenization in 50 mM Tris, 650 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 5 mM imidazole, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride and 0.2 mM TCEP (pH 7.0). After clarification by centrifugation (12,000g, 1 h, 4 °C), lysates were incubated with Ni-NTA resin for 2 h at 4 °C. Bound protein was washed with lysis buffer containing 10 mM imidazole and 1.5 M NaCl and eluted with 400 mM imidazole. The eluate was dialysed into imidazole-free buffer and subjected to a second Ni-NTA purification step. Importin-β was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200) in 50 mM Tris, 650 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2 and 0.2 mM TCEP (pH 7.0). Purity was confirmed by SDS–PAGE. Purified protein was concentrated to about 500 μM, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Purified NUP98 FG domains stored in 2 M GdmCl were induced to phase separate by rapid dilution into transport buffer (20 mM HEPES, 110 mM KOAc, 5 mM NaOAc, 2 mM Mg(OAc)2, 1 mM EGTA and 2 mM dithiothreitol, pH 7.3). Unless otherwise indicated, 1 μl protein solution was mixed with 24 μl transport buffer on a chambered coverslip (ibidi, 81507) immediately before imaging. Wild-type NUP98 FG domains were used at a final concentration of 10 μM mixed with 2 nM labelled FG domain. The residual GdmCl concentration after dilution was about 80 mM and did not interfere with condensate formation.

Because O-GlcNAcylated FG domains exhibited reduced phase-separation propensity, a final concentration of 25 μM was used for the experiments in Fig. 4g–i to generate condensates of comparable size and morphology to those formed by wild-type FG domains.

For cophase separation assays, importin-β was diluted into transport buffer to the desired concentration before mixing with FG domains. Wild-type FG domains were used at 10 μM unless otherwise indicated. Glycosylated FG–importin-β condensates were prepared from 25 μM glycosylated FG domains and 10 μM importin-β to obtain condensates comparable to those formed by wild-type FG domains. The final concentration of GdmCl was maintained at 80 mM across all conditions.

Dense- and dilute-phase concentrations of NUP98 FG condensates were determined using trace amounts of Alexa Fluor 594-labelled NUP98 FG domain. Condensates were formed from mixtures of unlabelled wild-type NUP98 FG domain and labelled tracer protein at molar ratios of 2,000:1, 5,000:1 or 10,000:1, as described above. Immediately after formation, condensates were sedimented by centrifugation at 4,300g for 5 min.

Dense-phase fluorescence was measured on a custom-built confocal microscope equipped with a 560-nm pulsed laser. Dense-phase regions were identified from their high fluorescence intensity and characteristic condensate morphology. Fluorescence intensities were converted to protein concentrations using calibration curves generated from known concentrations of free Alexa Fluor 594 measured under matched buffer conditions. Differences in fluorescence quantum yield between free dye and dye-conjugated protein were measured independently using a Duetta fluorometer and used to correct the calculated protein concentrations.

Dilute-phase concentrations were measured by focusing well above the condensate layer and applying the same calibration and quantum-yield correction. An unlabelled/labelled protein ratio of 20:1 was used to increase dilute-phase signal while minimizing perturbation of phase behaviour. Small dynamic nanoclusters were occasionally observed in the dilute phase of wild-type NUP98 FG condensates in the absence of importin-β (Extended Data Fig. 3d).

The experimentally determined dense- and dilute-phase concentrations were used to constrain FG–importin-β interaction strengths in the coarse-grained molecular-dynamics simulations (Extended Data Fig. 3e).

To examine the effect of O-GlcNAcylation on FG-domain partitioning, NUP98 FG domains containing a cysteine substitution at residue 221 were site-specifically labelled with fluorescent maleimide dyes. Unglycosylated NUP98 FG domains were labelled with Alexa Fluor 488 maleimide, whereas unglycosylated, modestly O-GlcNAcylated (single-round glycosylation) and highly O-GlcNAcylated (two-round glycosylation) NUP98 FG domains used as probe molecules were labelled with LD655 maleimide.

Preformed condensates were generated from unglycosylated NUP98 FG domains (final concentration roughly 10 μM supplemented with 4 nM Alexa Fluor 488-labelled protein) as described above. Samples were incubated for 30 min at room temperature to allow condensate maturation before probe addition. LD655-labelled probe proteins (unglycosylated, modestly glycosylated or highly glycosylated NUP98 FG domains) were then added to the chamber at a 1:1 volume ratio, yielding a final probe concentration of 20 nM. The incorporation of probe molecules into preformed condensates was monitored by time-lapse confocal microscopy using a Zeiss LSM 980 microscope (Supplementary Fig. 18).

TRFA measurements were conducted on a custom-built confocal microscope equipped with picosecond pulsed laser diodes (560 nm: LDH-D-TA-560, PicoQuant; 660 nm: LDH-D-C-660, PicoQuant) controlled by a Sepia II PDL 828 multichannel laser driver26. The excitation beam was delivered through a single-mode polarization-maintaining optical fibre (KineFLEX-P-2-S-405/640-2.5-2.5-p2), passed through a Glan-laser polariser (Thorlabs), directed through a FLIMbee laser scanning system (PicoQuant) and focused onto the sample through a ×60 water immersion objective lens (SR Plan Apo IR, 1.27 NA, Nikon). Fluorescence emission was collected through the same objective, spatially filtered using a pinhole (100 μm for live-cell measurements and 50 μm for in vitro measurements) and separated into parallel and perpendicular polarization components using a polarizing beam splitter. Each component was further separated spectrally by dichroic filters (ZT561 RDC and T647 LPXR, Chroma), passed through bandpass filters (Cy3B: 612/69 BrightLine HC, Semrock; HD653: ET700/75m, Chroma) and detected with hybrid photon-counting detectors (PMA Hybrid 40, PicoQuant). Photon arrival times were recorded with a HydraHarp 400 time-correlated single-photon-counting module at 16-ps resolution. Data were acquired using SymPhoTime 64 software (v.2.6, PicoQuant).

Instrument response functions (IRFs) were measured daily using Erythrosine B in saturated potassium iodide solution and used for reconvolution analysis. Detection channels were aligned using the measured IRFs. We note that a small discontinuity around 4 ns is observed in the raw anisotropy-decay curves; this arises from weak optical reflections in the time-correlated single-photon-counting setup and is accounted for in the analysis by reconvolution with the measured IRFs.

HD653 fluorescence intensity at the nuclear rim was first verified under 660-nm laser excitation (optimized to 50 μW average power at 40 MHz) to assess the expression level, ensuring comparable expression levels and avoiding overexpression artefacts. Data acquisition was performed using T3 mode, with fluorescence photons collected separately by parallel and perpendicular detectors. Imaging parameters included a pixel size of 100 nm, an image size of 256 pixels × 256 pixels, a pixel dwell time of 150 µs and an imaging time of 5 min. Regions of interest corresponding to the nuclear rim were selected, where thresholding algorithms were applied to identify regions of interest on the basis of pixel intensity and average fluorescence lifetime. The time-resolved intensity curves for parallel and perpendicular channels were extracted for further analysis.

Condensates were imaged immediately after formation as described above. Fluorescence photons were collected in T3 mode using 560-nm excitation (40 MHz repetition rate). To minimize photobleaching and ensure representative sampling, the imaging field was changed every 5 min to examine different condensates throughout the measurement period. Imaging parameters included a pixel size of 150 nm, an image size of 256 pixels × 256 pixels, a pixel dwell time of 203 μs and a time resolution of 16 ps. Condensates were identified on the basis of fluorescence intensity and morphology, and time-resolved intensity curves were extracted from condensate regions using SymPhoTime 64 software.

For measurements of individual FG chains in solution, purified and labelled FG domains were diluted in transport buffer to a final concentration of 10 nM. Data acquisition and analysis were performed as described above for condensate measurements.

TRFA decay, r(t), was calculated from fluorescence emissions collected parallel (\({I}_{\parallel }(t)\)) and perpendicular (\({I}_{\perp }(t)\)) to the excitation polarization according to60

where L1 and L2 are polarization mixing factors caused by the high numerical aperture of the objective lens and G accounts for the differential detection efficiencies between the parallel and perpendicular polarization components:

To determine L1 and L2, the fluorescence decays of a reference sample, yellow fluorescent protein (YFP), were measured. YFP has a known fluorescence rotational relaxation time (ρ = 16 ns) (ref. 61). The fluorescence decays for the parallel and perpendicular components of YFP were globally fitted using the following equations61:

where I0 is the initial fluorescence intensity, τ is the fluorescence lifetime and ρ is the rotational correlation time of YFP. The G factor was determined by measuring the ratio of the average intensities in the perpendicular and parallel channels using a solution of tris(2,2’-bipyridyl)dichlororuthenium(II) chloride ([Ru(bpy)3]Cl2), which exhibits isotropic rotational motion.

For IDPs, r(t) can be modelled using a double-exponential decay32:

where r0 is the fundamental anisotropy of the fluorophore, ρfast is the fitted rotational correlation time associated primarily with local dye/linker motion, rp is the residual anisotropy remaining after fast local motion and reflecting slower, larger-scale chain motions and ρslow is the fitted slow-component timescale used here as an apparent segmental-motion parameter. Values approaching the upper fitting bound of 1,000 ns were interpreted as indicating very slow apparent segmental motion and were not considered well resolved.

When ρfast is much smaller than ρslow, equation (5) can be approximated and simplified to

where βfast = 1 − rp/r0 and βslow = rp/r0 represent relative amplitudes of the fast (local) and slow (segmental) components, respectively.

The fluorescence lifetime (τ) was first determined by fitting the total fluorescence decay obtained from the parallel and perpendicular emission channels. The resulting τ value was then fixed during the subsequent global fitting of the parallel and perpendicular fluorescence decays using the 2_exp_rot model implemented in TauFit in the PAM package62, where IRFs were included through reconvolution analysis. Here we interpret ρslow primarily as an apparent segmental-motion parameter for relative comparisons rather than as a precise absolute rotational correlation time. Rotational components slower than the fluorescence lifetime can nevertheless influence the measured anisotropy decay and be estimated by model-based fitting, with precision depending strongly on photon statistics and decreasing as the correlation time increasingly exceeds the fluorescence lifetime63,64. Although three-exponential models were also evaluated, the additional component was consistently negligible or degenerate with existing components and therefore did not improve the fits.

To calculate steady-state anisotropy (rss), the integrated intensities of the fluorescence emissions collected in the parallel (\({I}_{\parallel }\)) and perpendicular \(({I}_{\perp }\)) channels were used. The steady-state anisotropy was computed using the equation

The steady-state anisotropy value provides a single, time-averaged measurement of the overall fluorescence anisotropy, which complements the dynamic information obtained from TRFA decay analysis.

For live-cell measurements, single-cell anisotropy-decay traces were used for subsequent analysis. In Fig. 1i, the fitted slow-component parameter (ρslow) was calculated on a per-cell basis to capture relative temporal trends in apparent segmental motion. For all other experiments, a non-parametric bootstrap strategy was applied to improve signal-to-noise and ensure robust curve fitting.

For each condition, 200 bootstrap replicates were generated by resampling single-cell decay traces with replacement, summing photon counts and fitting the resulting decays in TauFit62. Bootstrap depth was selected on the basis of convergence analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2). Differences between conditions were assessed using two-sided bootstrap tests. P values were calculated as the proportion of null resamples with absolute differences greater than or equal to the observed effect. Percentile confidence intervals were derived from the empirical distribution of independent bootstrap differences.

For in vitro measurements, anisotropy decays were analysed every 5 min and fitted individually. Reported values represent the mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments.

To assess the suitability of HD653 as a probe for TRFA, control experiments were performed using a globular protein with known rotational properties. Purified EGFP containing a single BCN at residue 39 was site-specifically labelled with either HD653 or the rigid, well-characterized anisotropy dye Cy3B30,31. TRFA measurements were conducted on both unlabelled and labelled EGFP at 10 nM in 1× PBS. The rotational correlation times were obtained by fitting TRFA decay curves using the 2_exp_rot model function in TauFit62. For globular EGFP, the fitted slow component, ρslow, corresponds to its overall rotational correlation time and was used to determine the hydrodynamic radius:

where kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature and \(\eta \) is the solvent viscosity. Hydrodynamic radii determined for labelled EGFP were consistent with wild-type EGFP and previously reported values65,66, confirming HD653 as a reliable anisotropy probe and supporting its use for segmental dynamics measurements in live-cell and in vitro assays.

Doxycycline-induced U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells expressing importin-β-3×FLAG-ALFA were prepared as described above. Cells were fixed with 4% PFA for 10 min, washed three times with 1× PBS containing 100 mM glycine and permeabilized and blocked for at least 30 min at room temperature in blocking buffer consisting of 3% bovine serum albumin, 10% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in 1× PBS.

DNA docking strand-conjugated anti-GFP and anti-ALFA nanobodies (Massive Photonics) were diluted 1:200 in antibody incubation buffer (Massive Photonics) and incubated with cells for 1 h at room temperature. Samples were washed three times with washing buffer (Massive Photonics) and post-fixed with 2.4% PFA for 8 min. Gold nanoparticles (250 nm diameter; BBI Solutions) were then added for 10 min as fiducial markers for active drift correction, followed by extensive washing with 1× PBS.

Cy3B-labelled DNA-PAINT imager strands (Massive Photonics) were diluted in imaging buffer (Massive Photonics) to a final concentration of 200–500 pM. Samples were mounted in custom imaging chambers, and imager solution was added immediately before imaging. All MINFLUX measurements were completed within 2 days of sample preparation.

Two-colour DNA-PAINT MINFLUX measurements were performed on a commercial MINFLUX microscope (Abberior Instruments) based on an Olympus IX83 inverted microscope equipped with a ×100 UPlanXApo objective and controlled by Imspector software. The excitation beam pattern and pinhole position were calibrated daily using fluorescent calibration nanoparticles (Gold 150 nm and 2C Fluor 120 nm; Abberior Instruments).

Cells expressing the inducible importin-β construct were identified by tagBFP fluorescence. Imaging was performed at the basal surface of the nucleus adjacent to the coverslip. Transient DNA-PAINT binding events were verified by rapid confocal imaging before MINFLUX acquisition. At least three gold fiducials were present in each field of view and were used by the active stabilization system to correct real-time drift, maintaining subnanometre lateral stability throughout acquisition.

Regions of interest were imaged using the standard two-dimensional MINFLUX acquisition sequence with a pinhole diameter of 0.83 Airy units. Following acquisition of the first target, imager strands were exchanged using a custom perfusion system while maintaining uninterrupted MINFLUX acquisition and active stabilization. Buffer exchange was performed at about 10 μl s−1 until DNA-PAINT binding events were no longer detected, indicating complete removal of the first imager strand. The second imager strand was subsequently introduced and imaging resumed. Sequential two-colour imaging and strand exchange typically required roughly 4 h.

NPCs were analysed using custom MATLAB routines adapted from the published MINFLUX_NPC_Tracking workflow14. Candidate NPCs were selected from the NUP96 channel and filtered using geometry-based quality-control criteria to exclude incomplete or poorly resolved pores.

For each NPC, the pore centre was determined from NUP96 localizations and used for spatial registration. The eightfold rotational phase was estimated from the angular distribution of NUP96 localizations using the complex order parameter \({z}_{8}=\langle {e}^{i8\theta }\rangle \). Individual NPCs were rotated into a common eightfold reference frame, and the same rigid-body transformation was applied to the corresponding importin-β localizations. Aligned NUP96 coordinates were rendered directly to preserve the native octagonal architecture of the NPC scaffold.

Because importin-β localizations did not exhibit a robust eightfold angular organization, their spatial distribution was quantified using radial density analysis relative to the NUP96-defined pore centre. Localizations were binned by radial distance, corrected for annular area, normalized in each NPC and averaged across pores. Individual radial profiles were smoothed before calculation of the population mean and s.e.m. The resulting mean radial density profile was rotationally symmetrized to generate the final importin-β density map. To assess the contribution of radial geometry, a uniform random two-dimensional distribution was generated in the analysed pore radius and processed using the same radial binning, annular-area correction, normalization, smoothing and symmetrisation as the experimental localizations (Fig. 3g).

We adapted a previously established coarse-grained model of the NPC26 to incorporate importin-β proteins. In this model, each amino acid (p) of NPC and importin-β proteins is represented by a single bead, the nuclear envelope is modelled using fixed membrane particles (m), and the solvent is treated implicitly. Protein residues are divided into three sub-categories: scaffold residues (sc) and FG residues (FG) of NPC proteins and importin-β residues. The potential energy of the system is given by

Non-bonded interactions between particles i and j are described by Lennard–Jones potentials, whose strength \({\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{ij}}\), length σij and cutoff values \({r}_{{\rm{c}}}^{{\rm{\alpha }}}\) are provided in Supplementary Table 2. The Lennard–Jones potentials were shifted by their values at the corresponding cutoff radii: that is, \({U}_{{\rm{LJ}}}({r}_{c}^{\alpha })\). The bond potential between adjacent beads of the FG-protein was modelled using the finitely extensible nonlinear elastic potential67 with kFE = 30kBT and RFE = 1.5σ. The radiall positions of importin-β were confined by a half-harmonic potential with stiffness kc = 100kBT/σ2, limiting their radial distance to r ≲ Rc = 81σ ≡ 48.6 nm.

Simulations were performed in LAMMPS (Release Sept. 2021)68,69. Time is reported in units of \(\tau =\sqrt{m{\sigma }^{2}/{k}_{{\rm{B}}}T}\), where m is the bead mass (identical for all bead types). Following earlier work26, we determined the reduced length scale of Lennard–Jones potential obtained as σ ≡ 0.6 nm by matching the root-mean-square inter-residue distance (RE) of a single NUP98 FG chain (amino acids 1–499) in both the homopolymer model and the corresponding Martini representation in the weakly interacting regime70. We found that \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5 reproduces the RE of a single NUP98 FG chain measured by single-molecule FRET, whereas \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.42 best matches in situ FLIM–FRET for the NUP98 FG domain in the NPC26, reflecting in particular the effects of PTMs.

The membrane particles representing the nuclear envelope were constructed from a 100 × 100 nm2 coarse-grained POPC bilayer using the Python script insane.py71,72, with a reduced area per lipid (0.3 nm2) to prevent solvent permeation (command: insane.py -l POPC -x 100 -y 100 -z 100 -a 0.3 -o bilayer.gro). A half-toroidal pore was then generated using BUMPy71 (command: bumpy.py -s double_bilayer_cylinder -f bilayer.gro -z 10 -g l_cylinder:10 r_cylinder:430 r_junction:120 l_flat:1920). To reduce computational cost, only phosphate beads were retained. NPC scaffold and membrane particles were fixed throughout the simulations. To prevent FG domains and importin-β molecules from crossing the membrane, a Lennard–Jones potential with a large repulsive range was applied (Supplementary Table 2).

We used the constricted NPC model II26 including the following FG-NUPs: NUP54, NUP58, NUP62, NUP98, POM121, NUP214, NUP153 and NUP358. Importin-β was modelled using PDB ID 3W5K (ligand Snail1 removed)73. Importin-β molecules were treated as rigid bodies using a rigid-body integrator with a Langevin thermostat and a damping coefficient 10τ (LAMMPS command: fix rigid langevin molecule). FG beads were integrated using the Verlet algorithm74. NUP98 FG chains were thermalized using Langevin thermostats with damping coefficient 10τ (ref. 75).

Importin-β molecules were added to systems of size 320σ × 320σ × 400σ. FG-NUPs were first equilibrated at \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5 for 106τ, during which they formed a surface condensate on the NPC scaffold. These compact conformations allowed us to efficiently introduce NImp-β = 100 importin-β molecules76 with random initial positions and orientations around the NPC. With FG-NUPs frozen and weak interactions (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.1), importin-β molecules were allowed to diffuse for 3.4 × 104τ with thermostat damping coefficient 1,000τ. Subsequently, the full system was equilibrated with \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.42 and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.1 for 105τ using a time step δt = 10−3τ and thermostat damping coefficient 10τ. Production conditions were then applied by setting \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β to their target values, followed by simulations of at least 106τ. Three independent configurations from the equilibration phase were selected as starting points for independent production runs. Structural visualization was performed using VMD77.

To examine how O-GlcNAcylation affects FG-NUP dynamics, we performed molecular-dynamics simulations of the human NPC using the Martini 2.2 coarse-graining scheme. We used the constricted NPC structure (PDB ID: 7R5K, ref. 39). NUPs were grouped into scaffold proteins and disordered FG-NUPs and converted to Martini CG models using the martinize.py script50,78. FG-NUPs included NUP54, NUP58, NUP62, NUP98, POM121, NUP214 and NUP358 (Supplementary Table 3). All scaffold proteins and grafting-anchored ordered domains of FG-NUPs were restrained with a harmonic spring (1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−2).

We generated O-GlcNAcylated NPC models at three modification levels (fgly = 0.18, 0.3 and 0.6), where fgly denotes the fraction of O-GlcNAcylated Ser/Thr sites (Supplementary Fig. 11). Potential O-GlcNAcylation sites were predicted using YinOYang79, which assigns each residue a probability p ∈ [0,1]. Residues with p ≥ pth were considered glycosylated. The resulting number of modified sites Ngly determined fgly = Ngly/Ntotal, where Ntotal = 58,768 is the total number of Ser/Thr residues across all FG-NUPs.

Simulations were performed using GROMACS (v.2020.6 and v.2025.2)80,81. Interaction strengths for protein–protein, protein–sugar and sugar–sugar interactions were rescaled by parameters α, λ and γ, respectively70,82. The optimal α = 0.78 was determined by matching RE of an untreated NUP98 FG chain to single-molecule FRET measurements (Supplementary Fig. 12) and the dense-phase density of FG condensates (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). For O-glycosylated FG-NUPs, interactions involving sugars used λ = 0.15 and γ = 0.5, consistent with experimental osmotic second virial coefficients of aqueous sugars and protein–sugar mixtures83,84.

A cubic box (170 nm per side) was constructed to accommodate the NPC. Secondary-structure restraints were assigned using DSSP85. Elastic networks in ordered domains were generated using Elastic Network in Dynamics86 (default parameters; a distance range of 0.9 nm; force constant 500 kJ mol−1 nm−2). All FG domains were modelled as coils except for locally ordered regions in NUP358 (Supplementary Table 3). The system was solvated with Martini water containing 10% antifreeze beads87 and neutralized with NaCl to 150 mM. The total number of solvent particles was about 4 × 107.

Initial energy minimization used steepest descent with maximum step size 0.01 nm and force tolerance 1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−1. During this step, position restraints (1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−2) were temporarily removed to allow global relaxation. Lennard–Jones and Coulomb potentials were first softened using the GROMACS free-energy framework (parameters: couple-lambda0=vdw-q; sc-alpha = 0.1; sc-coul= yes; sc-power = 2; sc-sigma = 0.3), followed by a second minimization using full potentials.

Equilibration proceeded as follows. First, NVT simulations at 310 K were performed for 100 ns (velocity-rescaling thermostat88, time constant 1 ps, time step δt = 0.015 ps) using reduced interaction scaling (α = γ = λ = 0.3) to relax chains into coil-like conformations. Next, NPT equilibration at 310 K and 1 bar was performed for 100 ns (velocity-rescaling thermostat88, semi-isotropic Berendsen barostat89, time constant 12 ps, compressibility 3 × 10−4 bar−1). Interaction parameters were then gradually increased. For untreated NPCs, α was raised from 0.3 to 0.5 and then 0.6. For O-glycosylated NPCs, α was increased from 0.3 to 0.6 and then 0.7, with γ = 0.5 and λ = 0.15. This stage lasted 1.5 μs. Production simulations were conducted for at least 2 μs at target α values, using the same thermostat and barostat parameters as in the final equilibration step and a time step δt = 0.02 ps.

Sample sizes were not determined by formal statistical power calculations but were based on previous experience with the respective imaging and biophysical assays26, practical considerations and the requirements for robust and reproducible measurements. For molecular-dynamics simulations, replicate numbers and trajectory blocks were selected on the basis of convergence and reproducibility criteria. Exact sample sizes, numbers of independent experiments and independent sample preparations are reported in the corresponding figure legends.

For experiments in which representative images are shown, including those in Figs. 1b, 2a, 3e and 4b, Extended Data Figs. 1a,b, 2a and 8e and Supplementary Figs. 18–20, experiments were independently repeated at least three times and yielded similar results. Representative images were selected from these independent experiments. Randomization was not applicable because treatments were applied to entire cell cultures or biochemical samples. Experimental variability was minimized by using matched culture, sample-preparation and acquisition conditions.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Uncropped images of immunoblots are provided in Supplementary Fig. 20. O-GlcNAc modification-site annotations were obtained from the O-GlcNAc Database v.2.0 (https://www.oglcnac.mcw.edu/). The human NPC scaffold and the importin-β structure used for the simulations were obtained from the PDB, enteries 7R5K and 3W5K, respectively. Box plots display the median (centre line), mean (central square), interquartile range (box), and whiskers extending to data points within 1.5×IQR. Importin-β remained detectable up to 100 µM dye but became obscured at 1 mM, suggesting that the effective local concentration at the NPC approaches the millimolar range. b-e, TRFA parameters of purified NUP98 FG domains co-phase-separated with increasing molar ratios of importin-β: (b) fitted slow-component timescale ρslow, (c) fundamental anisotropy r0, (d) residual anisotropy rp, (e) fitted local dye motion ρfast. f-j, Apparent segmental motion, quantified by the fitted slow-component timescale, across multiple labelled sites in NUP98 FG domains in the absence and presence of importin-β (1:1 molar ratio). Data represent mean ± s.d. from n = 3 independent replicates.

a, Snapshots from the end of coarse-grained MD simulations showing co-condensation of NUP98 FG domains with importin-β at varying molar ratios (NImp-β/NFG) and different FG–importin-β interaction strengths (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β). Importin-β is shown in red and NUP98 FG chains in grey. b, Concentration profiles of FG chains along the simulation box. The ratio of importin-β to FG chains (NImp-β/NNUP98) is indicated in each panel. The symbols and error bars represent the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The solid lines represent double error function fits to the concentration profiles26. c, d, Experimentally measured FG-domain concentrations in freshly formed NUP98 FG condensates co-phase-separated with different molar ratios of importin-β: (c) FG concentration in the dense phase and (d) in the dilute phase from fluorescence experiments. Data represent mean ± s.d. from n = 5 independent replicates. Notably, in the absence of importin-β, FG chains form nanoscale assemblies that persist in solution, leading to a slightly elevated apparent concentration in the dilute phase. e, MD-simulated FG-chain concentrations in the dense phase of co-condensates of NUP98 FG domains and importin-β as a function of molar ratio NImp-β/NNUP98, comparing different FG–importin-β interaction strengths. Symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The grey shading indicates the experimentally measured dense-phase concentrations from (c) (mean ± s.d.), narrowing the range of possible FG–importin-β interactions in the model to 0.4 <\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β < 0.5.

a, Concentration profiles of importin-β beads along the simulation box for different molar ratios of importin-β to NUP98 FG chains (NImp-β /NNUP98). The solid lines are double-error-function fits26. b, Phase diagram summarizing the concentrations of importin-β in the dilute (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dilute}}}\)) and dense phases (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dense}}}\)) as a function of FG–importin-β interaction strength \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β, obtained from the profiles in (a). c, The partition coefficient of importin-β (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dense}}}/{c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dilute}}}\)) plotted as a function of molar ratio NImp-β/NNUP98 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.4 and 0.42. The dashed lines are fits of \(a{e}^{\frac{b{N}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}}{{N}_{{\rm{NUP}}98}}}\) to the data points within the range 0.5 ≤ NImp-β/NNUP98 ≤ 1. Extrapolation to the infinitely dilute limit (i.e., NImp-β/NNUP98 → 0) yields partition coefficients of 16.5 ± 6 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.4 and 1120 ± 364 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42. Proteomics data estimate the partition coefficient of importin β1 inside NPCs to lie between 400 and 1300 (dark grey rectangle; see Supplementary Text). To account for possible strong crowding effects in the NPC, compared to the cytosol/nucleus, the uncertainty band is extended downward by an additional factor of ten (light grey rectangle). For simulations with very low importin-β copy numbers, larger numerical uncertainties are expected, accounting for the observed outlier. FG–importin-β interactions of \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42 capture the proteomics-derived partition coefficient and are consistent with the measured FG concentration (Extended Data Fig. 3e). For \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β ≥ 0.44, nearly all importin-β molecules in the system are absorbed into the condensate (Extended Data Fig. 4a), consistent with an extrapolated partition coefficient far above 1000 and thus outside the expected range. In a-c, the symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ.

a, Snapshot of a simulation containing a single importin-β molecule (red) embedded in an NUP98 FG condensate (grey) uniformly filling a cubic box of width 38σ. b, Simulation for multiple importin-β molecules partitioned into an FG condensate confined to a slab geometry (360σ × 90σ × 90σ). For mean-squared-displacement (MSD) analysis, the box was divided into nine bins of width 40σ along the x-axis (vertical black lines). c, MSD of the centre of mass of a single importin-β molecule, ⟨ΔR2(t)⟩, for different FG–importin-β interaction strengths \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β. d, Averaged MSD of multiple importin-β molecules located near the centre of the condensate slab (bin range −20σ < x < 20σ), measured at 4.8 × 105τ. The interaction strengths were \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42 and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5. MSD components along the x-axis (left), y-axis (middle) and z-axis (right) are shown. The black dashed lines in (c) and (d) indicate linear fits to the MSD curves: in (c), fits were applied for t > 6 × 103τ; in (d), fits were applied for t > 15 × 103τ.

a, Concentration of importin-β in the dense phase of NUP98 FG condensates. Symbols represent the importin-β concentration at the centre of the condensate slab, cImp-β (x = 0); the symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ (see Extended Data Fig. 4a). The solid lines show fits of the function \(a{e}^{b{\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\beta }}}\) to data points within the range 0.42 ≤ \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β ≤ 0.5. b, Translational diffusion coefficients (D) of importin-β inside FG condensates, rescaled by the diffusion coefficient of a single importin-β in solution, D0 (see Supplementary Fig. 3). For molar ratios NImp-β/NNUP98 = 0.2 to 2, the symbols represent diffusion coefficients of importin-β molecules located in the centre bin of the condensate slab (see Extended Data Fig. 5b). Diffusion was averaged over the y- and z-directions, D = (Dy + Dz)/2, i.e., directions parallel to the condensate interfaces. The mean was calculated from n = 90 simulation snapshots (sampled every 5000 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The error bars indicate s.e.m. across all importin-β molecules within the central bin. The solid lines show fits of \({a}^{{\prime} }{e}^{{b}^{{\prime} }{\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\beta }}}\) to the data points within 0.42 ≤ \({\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}-{\rm{\beta }}}\le 0.5\). c, Estimated diffusion flux of importin-β across the NPC \({J}_{{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}}=A{c}_{{\rm{Imp}}}^{{\rm{dense}}}\times {D}_{{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}}\). The symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. For reference, we used D0 = 51 μm2/s as the translational diffusion coefficient of free importin-β in solution (see Supplementary Text). The NPC was approximated as a cylinder of radius RNPC = 0.05 μm, height HNPC = 0.1 μm and volume \({V}_{{\rm{NPC}}}=\pi {R}_{{\rm{NPC}}}^{2}{H}_{{\rm{NPC}}}\). A geometric prefactor \({V}_{{\rm{NPC}}}/{H}_{{\rm{NPC}}}^{2}\) rescales the condensate-derived flux to the NPC geometry, neglecting effects from non-uniform spatial distributions.

#1354. From crying kid to Ballon d'Or hopeful: How fearless Rio Ngumoha toughened up, via quitting Chelsea for Liverpool at just 15 and being shielded from 'crime and stuff' in East London

Published: 14:00 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EST, 10 November 2026

Rio Ngumoha is back in with the older boys, only this time there are no tears.

It is hard to believe the Liverpool and England winger could ever feel intimidated on a football pitch, given his talent was so apparent at the age of six that his older brother, James, gave up school to coach him.

Ngumoha can smile about the tears now, for sitting here at 18 years old as a full international on the verge of his first Three Lions start is a happy ending.

'I was six, maybe only five, playing for a local team,' he recalls, holding court with journalists at England's base of the Tottenham Hotspur training ground. 'I got an assist and I could hear my mum on the side saying, "Well done". Then I heard them saying that I was playing with older boys, and I just panicked. I started crying and walked off the pitch. I was so scared because everyone was older than me.'

Ngumoha is the youngest player in Thomas Tuchel's 26-man squad for this week's Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain. Harry Kane is 15 years his senior.

'After that game, I realised I could have definitely competed with them,' he adds. 'So yeah, I've toughened up a bit.'

Rio Ngumoha is the youngest player in the England squad after years of 'toughening up'

Ngumoha quit Chelsea for Liverpool because he says: 'I felt like I needed a new challenge'

Tougher, wiser and, what becomes clear when talk turns to Kane's Ballon d'Or, is that Ngumoha has grown in confidence, too. So confident, in fact, that not only does he want one of his own, he believes the game's ultimate individual honour is not beyond his reach.

The question was put to him, admittedly, but he took it and ran with it, much like he does the football.

'Harry Kane winning the Ballon d'Or is a big, big thing,' says Ngumoha, in keeping with his generation's fascination with the prize. 'Being known as the best player in the world… I would like to achieve it, and I think I can do it.'

A misplaced belief after less than 20 senior starts? You would ordinarily argue so, but Ngumoha's talent appears so rare that it's better to imagine where it could go, not where it cannot. I was there in Tampa in the summer when, then 17, he played the second half of England's 1-0 World Cup warm-up win over New Zealand. Come the end, he had been the best winger on the pitch. We wondered then if there was still a way into the squad for a player only in the States to train at the Florida pre-camp.

'I knew before going to the camp that I couldn't go to the World Cup anyway,' - it turns out he was not on the provisional 55-man list - says Ngumoha. 'So I just chose the pre-camp to prove myself, to be free, to play with some expression. I did that and I made a good impression.'

He achieved that on his debut in Tampa by beating his man, and the man after that, too. I put it to him that dribbling is a lost art.

'I feel like I'm quite fearless,' he says, after nodding in agreement. 'If there's an opportunity to beat my man, I'll always do it. It was the way I grew up, really, playing in cages near my house. Even at Chelsea, sometimes, they just let me play free. Then when I moved to Liverpool, I've never really been told to stop. I like exciting people. I like getting people off their seat.'

Ngumoha shows a quiet maturity and has been starring in the Premier League for Liverpool

To recap, Ngumoha was raised in East London by his mother and brother. He reveals that, through football, they shielded him from 'crime and stuff'. Football was 'an escape route'. He played for Chelsea's academy from the age of eight but left at 15 to join Liverpool. Why?

'I felt like I needed a new challenge,' he says. 'Like if I had stayed at Chelsea... I'm not saying that I wouldn't have got to the first-team as quick, because I believe in my ability, but I feel like Liverpool just gave me a new pathway.

'The plan they set for me was straightforward. For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool. They just said, if I prove myself, because they knew how much ability I had, they knew that I would definitely be a first-team player and a star-in-the-making for them. It has been the right choice so far.'

For one so young, there is quiet maturity to Ngumoha, one that means FA staff have permitted this interview. Often, the fledglings are kept closer to the nest. But then, there is a reminder of his youthful innocence.

'Nando's is still my fantasy meal,' he says. 'I get sweet potatoes, four boneless thighs, peri-tamer, some garlic bread. They need to give me a little sponsorship, the Nando's Black Card!'

The exclusive card he mentions gives the holder and up to four guests complimentary food for one year. The career that awaits Ngumoha means free chicken should be the least of his rewards. #1353. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1352. Man United chiefs set for Monaco summit TOMORROW to decide Michael Carrick's fate... as Ineos face taking their compensation for sacked managers and executives over £30m

Published: 02:40 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 15:11 EST, 10 November 2026

Michael Carrick's fate as Manchester United head coach will be decided on Wednesday when chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox meet with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco.

If United decide to sack Carrick, it would push the compensation paid out to coaching staff and executives over the last three years under minority owner Ratcliffe and Ineos close to £30million.

Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as the favourite to take over, and buying the Argentine out of his contract with the US national team would cost another £7million.

Berrada and Wilcox flew to the south of France on Tuesday to attend a scheduled summit of Ineos executives.

Berrada and Wilcox will make their recommendation to Ratcliffe on Wednesday, with all the indications pointing to Carrick paying the price for his team’s alarming descent into the Premier League relegation zone.

United sources are maintaining that no final decision has been reached. Co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer would still need to give their approval for the sacking.

Michael Carrick is pictured arriving at Manchester United's training ground at 7.15am

Mauricio Pochettino is the frontrunner to replace Carrick - leaving his role as US head coach

Who do you think is truly to blame for United¿s disastrous season - the manager or the club¿s leadership?

It’s understood that the Old Trafford hierarchy would want to inform Carrick of their decision face to face, so there may not be any official confirmation from the club until Thursday.

The 45-year-old turned up for work at Carrington at 7.15am on Tuesday morning to oversee training with the players who are not away on international duty amid increasing uncertainty over his position after ten months in charge.

Sacking Carrick would leave United searching for their third permanent head coach this year after he replaced Ruben Amorim in January.

It’s unclear what would happen to his backroom staff. Goalkeeper coach Craig Mawson was already at the club when Carrick arrived and would be likely to stay, along with Travis Binnion who moved up to first-team coach after working with United’s age-group teams.

Jonny Evans had just left his role as loans manager, but returned to work alongside his old United teammate as part of a new coaching team that includes Steve Holland and Jonathan Woodgate.

Carrick was only handed a two-year contract in May and would be due a pay-off from United who have already spent £22.7million in compensation since 2024 under Ineos.

It includes £10.4million to Erik ten Hag and his staff when the Dutchman was sacked four months after being given a contract extension, £4.1million to Dan Ashworth who lasted just 159 days as sporting director, and £8.2million to Amorim and his backroom team when they left after 14 months.

It would have been as high as £16.7million but United saved half of that figure when the Portuguese coach returned to work at AC Milan.

Avram Glazer and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, co-owners, are pictured at Old Trafford in September

Pochettino was strongly linked with the United job before the club appointed Ten Hag in 2022 and again when he was under pressure two years later.

The 54-year-old is currently busy at the US national team base south of Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double-header against Haiti.

However, it’s known that Pochettino would be interested in a return to the Premier League where he previously worked at Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton.
