(a) Representative immunoblots of Xenopus egg extracts used in this study: High Speed Supernatant (HSS) and Nucleo-Plasmic Extract (NPE). Untagged Xenopus PRIMPOL expressed via wheat-germ IVTT (In Vitro Transcription/Translation) was used as a positive control. Two polyclonal antibodies raised against non-overlapping antigens from Xenopus PRIMPOL were used for immunoblotting. Although the predicted molecular weight of Xenopus PRIMPOL is ~77 kDa, IVTT-expressed Xenopus PRIMPOL migrated closer to ~95 kDa. No band of that molecular weight was detected in either HSS or NPE. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (b) A representative immunoblots of egg extracts (HSS and NPE) compared to lysates from adult frog tissues (heart, liver, spleen, and lung) known to express PRIMPOL (according to XenBase). The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (c) Coomassie-stained gel of purified human PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, and PRIMPOLΔRPA (quadruple point mutant D519R, F522A, D551R, I554A). (d) Diagram of in vitro primase-polymerase assay for PRIMPOL. SYBR Green I was used to detect DNA synthesis by recombinant PRIMPOL on a linear ssDNA template. This assay does not contain RPA or any other replication factors. The plot shows the enzymatic activity of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, and PRIMPOLΔRPA measured using this assay, error-bars represent the standard deviation from three independent experiments. Note that 15 μM of aphidicolin (APH) does not impair PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity. (e) Three representative kymograms showing GINSLD655 (orange) and FEN1kikG (blue) dynamics in mock-depleted extract supplemented with 10 µM aphidicolin and 30 nM PRIMPOLWT. No fork restart events were observed under these conditions, likely because aphidicolin inhibited DNA synthesis by replicative polymerases. (f) Biological replicates of fork restart efficiency measured with two different extract preparations. Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of replication forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05 and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (g) Two representative kymograms showing RPAmCherryXL (green), PCNALD655 (red), and wild-type FEN1KikG (blue) binding to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLWT. (h) Two representative kymograms showing RPAmCherryXL (green), PCNALD655 (red), and FFAA-FEN1KikG (blue) binding to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLWT. FFAA is a FEN1 mutant (F343A/F344A) whose interaction with PCNA has been disrupted. (i) Fork restart efficiency calculated from the experiments shown in panels (g) and (h). RPAmCherryXL signal was used to identify fork restart events, defined by a transition in the RPA growth rate from slow to fast. Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test.

(a) Diagram of single-molecule experiments with site-specific leading-strand DNA lesions. Top: a 30-kb DNA molecule containing DNA-Protein Crosslinks (DPCs) positioned ~10 kb away from each end was digested with ProteinaseK, leaving behind small (~4 aa) peptide adducts. If a replication origin fires in the middle of this DNA substrate, both replication forks will encounter the peptide adduct on the leading-strand template, resulting in CMG uncoupling. Bottom: a representative kymogram illustrating CMG uncoupling from both peptide adducts. This experiment was performed in extract supplemented with 30 nM PRIMPOLWT, which promoted fork restart at ~50% of uncoupled CMGs. (b) Biological replicates of CMG speed distributions measured with two different extract preparations. Blue lines indicate median values; shaded boxes represent 95% CI estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of replication forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05 and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (c) A representative immunoblots of samples from the experiment in Fig. 1j. Reaction mixture samples were collected at the 45-min timepoint. A trace amount of endogenous PolA1 (<1% of the total amount) evaded the immunodepletion. (d) A representative immunoblots of chromatin-bound proteins from a chromatin fractionation experiment with mock-depleted and Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with buffer or 30 nM of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, or PRIMPOLΔRPA. (e) A representative immunoblots of chromatin-bound proteins from a chromatin fractionation experiment in undepleted extract supplemented with DMSO or 100 μM of aphidicolin. Reactions were also supplemented with buffer or 30 nM of PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLAxA, or PRIMPOLΔRPA as indicated. In (d) and (e) chromatin was first licensed in HSS for 30 min, then NPE was added to the reaction, samples were collected at 60 min after NPE addition, and chromatin was fractionated by centrifugation and washed 2 times to remove any unbound proteins. For (c-e), the experiments were repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data.

(a) A representative fluorescence image of recombinant PRIMPOL labelled with increasing amounts of SNAP-Surface® Alexa Fluor® 647 (SNAPAF647) compared to a serial titration of a known standard (GINSAF647, where the PSF3 subunit is fluorescently labelled). A 1.5x molar ratio of SNAPAF647 to PRIMPOL was used to label all protein preps employed in this study. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (b) A representative gel image showing the results of the plasmid replication assay comparing DNA synthesis in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled PRIMPOLWT or 30 nM fluorescently labelled PRIMPOLWT-AF647. Time points were collected at 15,30, 60, and 90 min for Mock-depleted extract, and 30, 60, 90, and 120 for Pol α-depleted extract. The gel images from the two additional independent repeats are provided in the Supplementary Data. (c) Quantification of the plasmid replication assay depicted in panel (b) from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey bars) and supercoiled plasmid signal (light grey bars) were measured at the 90-min time point and normalized to the total DNA synthesis signal of the PRIMPOLWT control. Data represent mean ± SD from three independent experiments. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05. p-values were determined using a two-tailed two-sided student’s t-test. (d) Representative kymogram from an experiment imaging 30 nM of PRIMPOLWT-AF647 (magenta), FEN1KikG (blue), and RPAmCherryXL (green) in Pol α-depleted extract. Note that PRIMPOLWT-AF647 binding events are so numerous that it is impossible to resolve individual PRIMPOL molecules. (e) The distribution of fork speed before and after PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart corresponding to experiments shown in Fig. 2a, b (fork speeds were extracts from the growth rate of RPA tracts). Results from two experimental replicates are shown. ‘N’ indicates the number of forks analysed; blue horizontal bars denote median values; grey boxes indicate the 95% CI estimated via bootstrapping. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, ‘**’ denotes p < 0.01, and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (f) Example kymogram showing the binding of PRIMPOLΔRPA (3 nM) to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract. (g) Example kymogram showing the binding of PRIMPOLAxA (3 nM) to DNA in Pol α-depleted extract. (h) Example kymogram showing the binding of PRIMPOLWT (3 nM) to DNA in mock-depleted extract. (i) Fork restart efficiency measured from experiments conducted in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with buffer, 4.5 nM of SNAP-Surface® Alexa Fluor® 647 (AF647), 3 nM of PRIMPOLWT-AF647, 3 nM of PRIMPOLAxA-AF647, or 3 nM of PRIMPOLΔRPA -AF647 (results of two independent replicates are shown). Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (j) Distribution of time delays Δt1 and Δt2 measured for productive PRIMPOLWT-AF647 binding preceding fork restart. Δt1 denotes the time delay between PRIMPOL recruitment and dissociation, Δt2 denotes the time delay between PRIMPOL dissociation and fork restart. ‘N’ indicates the number of forks analysed; blue horizontal bars denote median values; grey boxes indicate the 95% CI estimated via bootstrapping. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, and ‘*’ denotes p < 0.05. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test.

(a) AlphaFold3 prediction of interactions between PRIMPOL (human) and MCM4 (human and frog proteins). (b) Multiple sequence alignment highlighting the conservation of PRIMPOL residues predicted to interact with MCM4 and MCM7. (c) Coomassie-stained gel of purified full-length PRIMPOL constructs: PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOL3A, PRIMPOLDED, and PRIMPOL29-35:Linker. (d) Enzymatic activity for different full-length PRIMPOL mutants measured using the in vitro primase-polymerase assay. Data represent mean ± SD from three independent experiments. (e) Two representative kymograms showing RPAmKikGR (green) and PRIMPOLWT-AF647 (magenta) binding to DNA being unwound by uncoupled CMG helicases in undepleted extract treated with 15 µM aphidicolin (imaged at 15 sec/frame). (f) Coomassie-stained gel of purified FLAG-SNAP-PRIMPOL1-60 bait constructs harbouring mutations in the MCM4-interacting region. (g) Immunoblots assessing PRIMPOL expression after plasmid transfection into PRIMPOL-deficient HCT116 cells (related to Fig. 3f, g). (h) Representative images of DNA fibres used to measure fork restart efficiency in HCT116 cells (related to Fig. 3h,i). Forks were labelled with CldU (red) before UV-C irradiation and with IdU (green) after irradiation. Yellow arrows indicate forks that did not restart, white arrows indicate restarted forks. The scale bar denotes 25 μm.

(a) Representative kymogram from an experiment imaging RPAmCherryXL (green) and FEN1kikG (blue) in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLDED. PRIMPOLDED did not facilitate CMG-dependent restart, but retained the ability to support CMG-independent restart (white asterisk). (b) Fork restart efficiency measured in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with buffer, or various concentrations of PRIMPOLWT or PRIMPOLDED (related to Fig. 4b, results from two experimental replicates are shown). Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. Fluorescently labelled PRIMPOL was used for the 3 nM experiment, and unlabelled PRIMPOL was used for the rest. (c) Fork speed distributions measured in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM unlabelled PRIMPOLWT or PRIMPOLDED (related to Fig. 4c, results from two experimental replicates are shown). Fork speed before restart and after CMG-dependent restart were extracted from the growth rate of RPA tracts. The rate of DNA synthesis during CMG-independent restart was extracted from the growth rate of the internal FEN1 tracts. Blue horizontal lines indicate median values; shaded boxes represent 95% CI estimated via bootstrapping. In panels (b) and (c), ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, ‘*’ denotes p < 0.05, ‘**’ denotes p < 0.01, and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test.

(a) Fork restart efficiency measured in (Pol α and Mock)-depleted extract, (Pol α and Pol δ)-depleted extract, and (Pol α and Pol ε)-depleted extract (results from two experimental replicates are shown, related to Fig. 4d). Data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘*’ denotes p < 0.05, ‘**’ denotes p < 0.01, and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test. (b) Representative kymogram of RPAmCherryXL (green) and FEN1KikG (blue) from an experiment in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol δ, which was supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled PRIMPOLWT (related to Fig. 4d). White arrows indicate CMG-dependent fork restart events. Interestingly, in this experiment FEN1KikG accumulated behind the restarted fork during leading strand synthesis, even though canonically FEN1 is an Okazaki fragment maturation factor and lagging-strand synthesis in this experiment was blocked by depleting both Pol α and Pol δ. Most likely, here FEN1KikG is binding to PCNA deposited on the nascent leading strand by CTF18-RFC (see cartoons in Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). (c) Representative kymogram of RPAmCherryXL (green) and FEN1KikG (blue) from an experiment in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol ε, which was supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled PRIMPOLWT (related to Fig. 4d). White asterisk indicates CMG-independent restart event. (d) Coomassie-stained gel of purified recombinant Xenopus Pol ε used for experiments shown in Fig. 4d. (e) Coomassie-stained gel of purified recombinant Xenopus Pol δ used for experiments shown in Fig. 4d. (f) Immunoblots of samples corresponding to experiments from Fig. 4d. Samples were collected directly from the single-molecule flow-cells at the end of each 90-min experiment. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data.

(a) Immunoblots of samples from the plasmid replication assay shown in Extended Data Fig. 7b. Reaction mixture samples were collected at the 45-min timepoint. The sample from the single-molecule flow-cell was collected at the end of the 90-min experiment. The experiment was repeated independently twice, and data from an additional independent replicate are provided in the Supplementary Data. (b) A representative gel image showing ensemble plasmid replication assay in mock-depleted or Pol α-depleted extract, supplemented with buffer or 30 nM PRIMPOLWT. DMSO or 3 μM of ATR inhibitor (AZD6738) was also added to each reaction as indicated. Time points were collected at 30, 60, and 90 min. Gel images from the two additional independent repeats are provided in the Supplementary Data. (c) Quantification (mean ± SD) of the ensemble plasmid replication assay shown in Extended Data Fig. 7b from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey bars) or supercoiled DNA signal (light grey bars) was measured at the 90-min time point and normalized to the total DNA synthesis signal of the Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with PRIMPOLWT control in the absence of ATR inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 7b, section v). ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, ‘*’ denotes p < 0.05, ‘**’ denotes p < 0.01, ‘***’ denotes p < 0.001, ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were determined using a two-tailed student’s t-test. (d) Coomassie-stained gel of purified PRIMPOL phospho-mutants: PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLΔ201-260, PRIMPOLS255E, PRIMPOLS255D, and PRIMPOLS255A. (e) Enzymatic activity for PRIMPOL phospho-mutants measured using the in vitro primase-polymerase assay. Error-bars represent the standard deviation from three independent experiments. Data represent mean ± SD from three independent experiments. (f) Fork restart efficiency measured in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM of unlabelled PRIMPOLWT, PRIMPOLΔ201-260, PRIMPOLS255E, PRIMPOLS255D, or PRIMPOLS255A (related to Fig. 4e, results from two independent replicates are shown). The CMG-independent restart activity of PRIMPOLWT is similar to that of PRIMPOLS255A because the DNA damage checkpoint is not active in the microfluidic flow-cell used for single-molecule experiments (see pCHK1 signal in Extended Data Fig. 7a). (g) Fork restart efficiency measured in Pol α-depleted extract supplemented with increasing concentrations of PRIMPOLWT or PRIMPOLΔ201-260 (related to Fig. 4f, results from two independent experimental replicates are shown). Fluorescently labelled PRIMPOL was used for the 3 nM experiment, and unlabelled PRIMPOL was used for the rest. For panels (f) and (g), data represent mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated via bootstrapping. ‘N’ denotes the number of forks analysed. ‘ns’ denotes p > 0.05, ‘**’ denotes p < 0.01, and ‘****’ denotes p < 0.0001. p-values were computed using the two-sample two-sided KS test.

#1342. Fans Can Own Piece Of Iconic Tifo With New Limited-Edition Range

Evertonians have the chance to own a genuine piece of supporter history, with material from the spectacular first fan-created tifo at Hill Dickinson Stadium transformed into a unique range of limited-edition accessories.

The original ‘On the Banks of the Royal Blue Mersey’ display, organised by supporters’ group The 1878s ahead of Everton’s Premier League fixture against Arsenal in December 2025, has been repurposed into a collection of tote bags, belt bags and bucket hats, giving supporters the opportunity to own a physical piece of one of the most memorable moments from the Club’s first season at its new waterfront home.

Created by Fanatics, the exclusive collection also includes royal blue and black T-shirts and a black hoodie featuring the distinctive design of the original display, complete with Everton’s iconic tower.

The striking tifo, which transformed the South Stand into a sea of royal blue, white and yellow, was a powerful demonstration of the passion and creativity of Evertonians and one of the standout moments of the Club’s historic first season at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

With only a limited amount of original material available, the tote bags, belt bags and bucket hats have been produced in strictly limited quantities, making each a special keepsake from a landmark moment in Everton’s history.

The collection also recognises the dedication and hard work of The 1878s, whose volunteers give their time to create spectacular displays, bring colour to the stands and help build the atmosphere at Everton’s new waterfront home.

In recognition of their contribution, a proportion of proceeds from the range will be donated to The 1878s, helping support the group’s continued efforts to create memorable displays and special moments for Evertonians.

The collection is a celebration of supporter culture and the important role fans continue to play in shaping the identity and atmosphere of Hill Dickinson Stadium, carrying forward the traditions and spirit of Goodison Park into a new era on the Liverpool waterfront.

With Christmas approaching, the range also offers a distinctive gift for Evertonians, whether it’s a T-shirt or hoodie bearing the tower design, or one of the exclusive tote bags, belt bags or bucket hats made from the original tifo. The T-shirts also make an ideal stocking filler for Blues looking for something a little different this festive season.

The limited-edition Tifo Collection is available now from official Everton stores and online

Supporters hoping to secure one of the exclusive tote bags, belt bags or bucket hats are encouraged to shop early, with only limited numbers available.

#1341. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

There may be some truth in that, but Carrick’s response felt the most accurate assessment of the lot and will certainly chime with supporters who have long questioned how and why so many United sides, regardless of the manager, reach a point where running, intensity and urgency seem optional. “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” Carrick said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

Having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Nico Paz scores a stunner to get Como ahead against Manchester United within 2 minutes! 😱 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/ikH9MVg6cB

You looked at Como and it was clear every player knew their job and role and went about it with relish. There were patterns of play, they ran, there was intensity and movement and they were quicker to everything.

Paz scored the first and third goals and set up a wondrous second for Tasos Douvikas that showcased Como’s talent at the same time as underlining United’s myriad fault lines. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. Jacobo Ramón completed the rout before Joshua Zirkzee scored the most hollow of goals for United late on.

Como extend their lead to 2-0 against Manchester United early in the second half! Anastasios Douvikas gets the goal 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/2O9qRG75tG

United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

Nico Paz capitalises on a mistake from Carlos Baleba to extend Como's lead against Manchester United to 3-0 😱 He's been involved in each goal 👏 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/D7kD8PGtcY

As for that second shortly after the restart? First the impressive Lucas Da Cunha rolled Baleba too easily. United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

#1340. Mauricio Pochettino is adored by his players, big on culture and good vibes, not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools - exactly what dysfunctional Man United are crying out for

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 17:59 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 10 November 2026

After one press conference during Mauricio Pochettino’s ill-fated spell at Chelsea, he hosted an Argentinian-style BBQ for approximately 130 people, including his players and their families, under a marquee set up in the first-team car park at their training ground.

Returning to the room and the assembled throng of journalists still working, Pochettino popped a large plate of sausages and steaks down on the desk. He insisted it did not constitute bribery for better coverage of him. Just thought we might like to join.

This was Pochettino personified. Big on togetherness. Insisted on creating a homely environment for everyone. Believed a harmonious culture at Cobham would help performances on the pitch. Even kept a big box of lemons in his office because he reckoned they harnessed ‘energia universal’. He emphasised the importance of a good mood.

Goodness knows that’s what Manchester United need right now. And if they do decide to dismiss Michael Carrick, the prospect of managing possibly the biggest club in world football would not faze Pochettino – now the bookies’ favourite to take over.

Indeed, the 54-year-old would relish the challenge.

A few days before USA’s World Cup victory against Bosnia and Herzegovina to reach the last 16 at this summer’s tournament, coach Pochettino invited a small group of journalists to interview him at the team hotel – the Ritz-Carlton in Laguna Niguel, overlooking the Pacific Ocean 50 miles south of Los Angeles.

Manchester United could do with a dose of Mauricio Pochettino - and he would relish the challenge

The United States manager - who would cost around £7.5million to release - has openly admitted he wants to lead them in the future

Towards the end of the interview the Manchester United job came up in conversation. Pochettino turned to his long-time assistant coach Jesus Perez and said: ‘One day, your dream comes true... you go to Manchester United!’.

The Argentine clarified somewhat by explaining that Perez, while living in London, would often visit Manchester on days off to visit the National Football Museum. Perez responded with a smile: ‘United should have got you’.

One thing about Pochettino that Manchester United players will soon figure out if he takes the reins at Old Trafford is that he is not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools. At the World Cup, he appeared to criticise the intervention of FIFA - and President Trump – in suspending Folarin Balogun’s ban to make the striker available for a knockout clash with Belgium.

‘I feel disappointed with too many people. They put politics and manipulation, talk about ethics and integrity [first]. If we talk about the history of this game, I am disappointed in a personal way.’

With Pochettino, you’re either all in or you’re out. Look back to his time at Tottenham for evidence of that: the decision to exile stars such as Younes Kaboul, Etienne Capoue and Paulinho into a ‘bomb squad’ - and give chances to stars such as Harry Kane - was the start of his success there.

He’s a builder of teams, works with the tools he has and makes players better. Again, that sounds like the sort of thing United are crying out for.

Pochettino is big on culture – he adopted the mantra ‘culture eats strategy for breakfast’ after a meeting with the chairman of U.S. fast food chain Chick-fil-A – and worked hard to change the holiday camp feel at the USA team. Senior stars believed they did not need to put in the extra work to keep their places. The most notable example saw national team poster-boy Christian Pulisic, once of Chelsea, attempt to skip key games after a long season for AC Milan. Pochettino put a stop to that.

The Argentine does not suffer fools, is big on culture, and can deal with big club executives - his time at Tottenham taught us that

He can manage upwards, too. He handled chairman Daniel Levy well, and credited open dialogue as being key to the partnership with the chairman which yielded a runners-up finish in the Premier League and a run to the Champions League final.

‘I speak to him a lot, we talk a lot, we have very good communication,’ Pochettino said in 2018.

‘That means sometimes we agree and sometimes we don't agree. But after, when the decision is made, we are so strong in the delivery of it which shows it is best for the club’.

His cordial relationship with Levy meant Spurs were unconcerned when he met Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016 at Scott’s in Mayfair towards the end of Louis van Gaal’s troubled reign at Old Trafford.

There was nothing untoward in that - after the restaurant meeting Pochettino returned to Spurs training, and United appointed Jose Mourinho that summer.

But he was again touted as a contender when Mourinho was dismissed two years later.

Levy sacked him in 2019, but Pochettino has remained respectful and has since praised Levy’s impact.

On the field, his time at Spurs became famous for relentless intensity - a high energy approach with a high press. Think flying full-backs Danny Rose and Kyle Walker, and all-action midfielder Mousa Dembele. For another example of him getting the best from players look at Cole Palmer. The Englishman has never since replicated his numbers from 2023-24, Pochettino’s only season at Stamford Bridge.

The football, admittedly, was a little chaotic at Chelsea. It lacked control, and not even a mountain of meat could prevent him from being quizzed about his style of play in press conferences.

Chelsea’s fans never took to Pochettino. He was the face of Spurs, after all. Pochettino might be walking his dog – a Rhodesian Ridgeback called Sansa, named after the Game of Thrones character Sansa Stark – and the odd supporter would happily stop him to have a cosy chat. But he was always going to struggle to win over the supporters in their entirety.

He once said the first time he felt a connection with Chelsea’s supporters was in April 2024 after defeating Erik Ten Hag’s United 4-3, when Cole Palmer scored twice in the 10th and 11th minutes of stoppage time. That was 11 months after he joined.

He never quite won over the fanbase of Chelsea, where his football was chaotic and his high-intensity values led to accusations that he had worsened their injury crisis

One source at the time said Pochettino wanted ‘machines’ who had the physicality to play the high-energy philosophy he craved, and like at Spurs there was indeed a great deal of high-intensity running involved in training.

However, this talk of his sessions being fitness-focused led to accusations that his methods were contributing to their crippling injury list. Pochettino disputed that, telling us he did not come ‘from Mars’ and that he knew how to manage footballers better than those on social media. He was extremely defensive whenever asked if his training was primitive.

It would be fair to debate whether United have the players to play this way – and indeed how Pochettino himself would respond to the changing landscape of the Premier League.

Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi noted recently that upon his return to the Premier League after two years away that almost all clubs now play a more physical game than when he was at Brighton. With more teams doing the same thing that once made a Pochettino side different, how would he adapt?

We are told leaving his job in charge of the USA is more contractually feasible now than it was before the 2026 World Cup when Spurs made checks last season. He has a buyout clause, apparently worth around £7million, though that does not include the compensation required to recruit Perez and Co.

Should United require any character references, they need only ask their own Luke Shaw. He wrote the epilogue of Guillem Balague’s book Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs, having played under him at Southampton. Shaw admitted in those pages that he would love to work with his old coach again someday. Pochettino was there for him when Shaw broke his leg – still a man-manager even when they were no longer working together.

But United could also ask any number of Chelsea players who worked with Pochettino. They largely loved him. At the time of his dismissal in May 2024, one agent of a senior figure in the changing room told us that their client was ‘devastated’. Nicolas Jackson, formerly of Chelsea and now of Aston Villa, responded to Pochettino leaving by posting two face-palm emojis on Instagram.

Pochettino had his favourites. Conor Gallagher was one of them, and the Cobham graduate's contractual situation seemed to be a source of angst between the coach and Chelsea’s hierarchy.

Players tend to love Pochettino - Luke Shaw (right), one of Manchester United's veterans, had a strong relationship with him at Southampton

His power waned at Chelsea - the club hired a set-piece coach after he insisted he didn't want one, and he was gone before the specialist arrived

As noted, Pochettino was a builder hired to work with one of the Premier League’s youngest squads but did not get the time he wanted to mould Chelsea and never hid his desire for more power at Stamford Bridge. It is said they once had the chance to sign Ansu Fati from Barcelona on favourable financial terms, but did not go through with the transfer after the manager decided he was not for him.

We did get a glimpse of Pochettino’s waning power when Daily Mail Sport asked him once whether he would like a set-piece specialist adding to his staff. He dismissed the idea, suggesting he did not need one. Chelsea then lost the Carabao Cup final when Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk headed in the winner in extra time from a corner, with Gary Neville coining the ‘blue billion-pound bottlejobs’ jibe.

A month later, Chelsea agreed a deal to hire Bernardo Cueva from Brentford to lead a new department dedicated to set-pieces. Pochettino responded by reminding us: ‘I am the head coach and I am going to decide if some people are going to be with me or not, or if I’m going to add more people or not to the touchline.’ He was gone before Cueva arrived in the summer.

An end-of-season review was held in May 2024, and Pochettino, along with Chelsea’s hierarchy, decided after a single season that it was not working. Not for him, and not for them.

Now those at the helm of United need to determine whether he is the man to bring the good vibes back, perhaps also with a little meat.

#1339. Moyes Reflects On 592 Games & Looks To Future

In the spring of 2002, Everton was a club in the doldrums.

Knocked out of the FA Cup at Middlesbrough, lying a stressful 16th in the Premier League, in 10 of the previous 11 seasons the Toffees had finished in the bottom half of the table.

Cue the appointment as manager of a flame-haired, driven young firebrand who swept into the Club like a force of nature. In the 11 seasons which followed, Everton finished outside the top half only once.

There were four seasons of European football, an FA Cup final and three seasons lording it over Liverpool in the table.

When he returned for a second spell as manager in January 2025, with Everton one point above the relegation zone, having endured 16th, 17th and 15th-place finishes in the previous three seasons… his first full season back saw the Club challenging for a place in Europe.

Now David Moyes is about to join the 592 Club, the same number of matches the legendary Harry Catterick oversaw.

No other Everton manager has taken charge of more.

Is David Moyes proud of reaching that landmark? Do things stay the same once Everton has touched you?

“Yes I am proud,” he tells the Official Matchday Programme at the Finch Farm training complex he helped design. “The thought of being the Everton manager who has managed the most games is something I’m very proud of.

“I’d dearly love to have added trophies to that statistic. But during the times we’re talking about we didn’t have the kind of financial backing Harry had.

“When I became the manager, Bill Kenwright said, ‘We don’t have much money, David. I’ll be able to give you five million a year to spend and if you generate anything else then it’s yours. But I’ll only be able to give you five million a year’.

“I told him, ‘That’s great, Bill, as long as I can do what I want with the players, as long as I can take them away and give them the best facilities’, and he shook my hand on it. He made good on that promise.

“That was that and it was how we worked. By the way, I pushed him hard for more! But I understood how it was.

“But that first time at Everton, when I look back, I hope we don’t take it for granted how good it was, really. How close we came. When you look back now and people tell me how many times we finished above Liverpool, how many times we got into Europe, we were in the middle of it and it felt quite disappointing at the time because I was trying to break the ceiling on the top clubs.

“At the time I was thinking, ‘My goodness, this is driving me mad that I can’t catch the top teams’.

“We didn’t have a big budget but we qualified for the Champions League. Duncan’s goal against Manchester United that night was magical. There were other things which stay with me.

“From my first day, Unsy’s goal against Fulham sticks with me. The FA Cup semi-final against Man United also stands out.

“After that semi-final, which we won on penalties on the Sunday, we were due to play Chelsea the following Wednesday night. So we were staying down and the atmosphere amongst the players was great. We went to Chelsea a few days later and we drew that, too. So we were really competitive with all the teams.

“Then I remember when we went and lost 2-0 at Fiorentina in Europe, but came back and won 2-0 in one of the great Goodison atmospheres. I get emotional talking about it now! I had a picture in my mind that night of Andy Gray’s goal against Bayern, and I was thinking the atmosphere was so like that.

“We came so close and went out on penalties. Sometimes I remember actually how good a team that was.

“But I probably take more pride from bringing in players who went on to become England internationals because I saw that as them getting better as a result of what we did with them.

“For that to happen we needed the team to do well also, to become more attractive so players wanted to come to us.

“And people were interested in coming to Everton at the time. That was an era when only four or five teams were getting into Europe every season. And it wasn’t an easy job to be in the top five in England.”

Two of Moyes’ managerial rivals in that era were Arsene Wenger and Sir Alex Ferguson. They remain the only bosses to have managed more Premier League matches than him, but Moyes’ managerial journey was initially born of a desire to become a better player.

A centre-half, Moyes was a Scottish league title-winner with Celtic in 1981/82 and a Scotland youth international, but the ambition and drive which would later characterise his management was clearly evident even in his early 20s.

“I did my coaching badges at a very early age,” he explains. “I think my leadership was one of my qualities as a player; I was captain of most of the clubs I was at – and I thought doing my coaching badges would probably give me an advantage. I became a qualified coach when I was about 21 – purely to try to become a better player.”

So driven was the young Moyes he actually took his coaching badges twice!

“I did my badges in Scotland,” he smiles. “At that time it was the ‘C’ licence, the ‘B’ licence and then the ‘A’ licence, after which you became a coach. But when I left Celtic and I moved to my first club down in England, which was Cambridge United, I thought, ‘I don’t know if this badge is going to be recognised down here’.

“So I then started to do the English courses!I actually went and completed all the work again.

“I only needed to do it once but I actually did it twice. I thought that maybe in England the Scottish licence wouldn’t be quite as well respected, but as it is, the Scotch coaching badge is highly respected worldwide. It still is.

“So I went and did it again at Lilleshall and I became a qualified coach twice over. It’s a bit like going to university and doing the same degree in different universities!

“I was from a family where my dad had run boys’ teams in Glasgow. I was brought up that way and I was always really interested in that side of it.

“I was always thinking what I would do when I finish? I didn’t really think I’d have enough qualifications to do anything else so I maybe hoped I would get a job with my badges.

“But ultimately I was doing it mainly because I wanted to become a better player.”

Moyes added: “I was a Scottish youth international, a Scottish schoolboy international and when I looked at the players who I had to try and be better than... it was really difficult as a centre-half at that time and those badges helped me an awful lot.

“I had a good career. I think I had more than 600 games and the clubs I worked at really helped me because they gave me an understanding of how things worked at the lower levels, not having all the mod cons.

“I’ll always go back to my early days at Celtic where I believe that I learned all my traits of what a good club really looks like, what winning means. At Celtic, I learned all about the pressures of being at a big club, what it’s like playing for a club like that and also having a chance to work with Scottish internationals. At the time, when I was a young player at Celtic, they were as good as any team in England. Celtic would have played any team in England and given them a run for their money.

“The level of players I was working with, training with and playing with, gave me a great insight into what a big club really looked like.”

Moyes’ manager at Celtic was Billy McNeill, the legendary European Cup-winning captain who as a manager won four Scottish league championships, including a league and cup double in the club’s centenary season.

“He was my first real managerial inspiration,” adds Moyes. “He gave me my debut and he was also a centre-half who wanted me to do well.

“He was probably the first one, but there were others on the journey who were so valuable.

“At the time, being a coach wasn’t probably the biggest thing for me, I was trying to become a better player.

“I always took things from so many coaches, people who would stand out for different reasons. Terry Cooper was my manager at Bristol City and he was a brilliant man-manager and treated us all brilliantly well. He was also a great player.

“Then there was Iain Munro with Dunfermline and John Beck at Cambridge United. He might have had a certain reputation but he had some brilliant ideas.

“Some of his ideas might have been extreme, but there were also so many good things which he did.

“I also had managers who you’d think, ‘Well, I won’t do that!’

“Obviously, my dad was a big inspiration because he ran boys’ teams and I watched from a distance how he did it.

“But probably the most inspiration I took was from three Scots: Andy Roxburgh, Walter Smith and Sir Alex Ferguson.

“They were probably the people who inspired me most. They were Scottish so I would go to the coaching courses, even when I’d qualified, nearly every year just to be around them.

“They were the people who were probably my biggest inspirations.”

One of that inspiring Tartan trio was a factor in Moyes becoming Everton manager for the first time in 2002.

Guided by their driven young manager, Preston had just been denied a second successive promotion, this time to the Premier League, in a Play-Off final at Wembley.

Everton were hovering dangerously close to the relegation zone and had just been knocked out of the FA Cup on Teesside when the decision was taken to part company with manager Walter Smith.

“I spoke to Walter,” reveals Moyes. “I went to his house in Lymm.

“Walter was a really good friend. When I was a player in the Scottish youth team, Walter was the assistant manager to Andy Roxburgh. They were great people and I had huge respect for what they’d done in management. So, I phoned him up and I said, ‘Can I come and see you?’ I went round and I said, ‘They’re offering me the Everton job’, and he already knew because Bill had mentioned me to him.

“He was great. He said, ‘Well, you have to take the job, it’s a great job’.

“But what I really remember about that day was he said to me, ‘You’re really lucky, you know? We have a really good player in the youth team’. It wasn’t what I was most focused on because I was thinking more about the job – but that boy was Wayne Rooney.”

Typical of his drive and his work ethic, Moyes left that meeting to go and meet Everton chairman Bill Kenwright in London – via Bristol!

“I actually drove to Bristol Rovers first because I wanted to watch the centre-forward they had as a potential signing for Preston. I had my scout Clive Middlemass in the car with me,” Moyes recalls.

“We went down in the car to Bristol Rovers to watch the centre-forward, then went on to meet Bill in London.

“As a result it was really late at night when I got to London. I had been given opportunities to manage other clubs in the Premier League, Sheffield Wednesday and Nottingham Forest, jobs like that.

“But there was an old director at Blackpool who I used to see now and again. And he used to say to me, ‘The club for you is Everton’, and that stuck with me.”

Hours later, he was offered the job and so began a love affair which, 24 years later, still burns brightly.

David Unsworth scored the first goal of the David Moyes era after 32 seconds against Fulham, Duncan Ferguson added another 13 minutes later and, despite the wobble of a Thomas Gravesen red card before the match was even half-an-hour old, Moyes guided his new team to the first of their 246 wins under his leadership.

“I don’t think anything surprised me about the Club,” he says today. “I was well versed in football, in watching football so I knew exactly what I was coming to.

“But probably the big thing which struck me was when I was driving in, and I’ve told this story before, but it’s absolutely true.

“I was coming in on a nice spring evening. I can remember it was quite bright and looking out the windows all I could see was Everton strips everywhere.

“That was my over-riding memory. I was relatively young and inexperienced in some ways, but I’d been around the leagues and I just remember thinking, ‘My goodness, everybody in the streets in Liverpool are Everton supporters.’

“That was where I came up with ‘the People’s Club’ line. I think in a way that might have helped me be accepted.

“A lot of people said, ‘Ah, you must have thought that up beforehand’ but I didn’t. It was genuinely just driving in when I thought it.

“Did I think I’d still be there 10 years later? Probably not, but when I think back about myself then compared to now, I was a real fighter then, I was going to challenge everything and I wasn’t going to roll over. I believed in my coaching, I believed in what I could do if I had a chance to do it, partly because of the success we’d had at Preston without a great amount of money, up against Graeme Souness’ Blackburn, or Jean Tigana’s Fulham or Big Sam’s Bolton.

“When I came in I had a good knowledge of the lower leagues, I’d seen a lot of the players first hand and I knew people who had passed on good information to me. I thought if I could tell Bill about the good young ones maybe we could sign them?”

Cue a procession of some of the most inspired budget signings in Premier League history.

Phil Jagielka, John Stones, Tim Cahill and Joleon Lescott were all snapped up from Championship clubs, Leighton Baines was in only his second season as a Premier League player at Wigan, while Seamus Coleman was snapped up from Sligo Rovers in Ireland.

Jagielka, Stones, Lescott and Baines went on to play many times for England, Cahill became an Australian World Cup legend while Coleman is currently on 81 Ireland caps, many as captain.

Then there was the goalkeeper who Moyes considers his best-ever signing.

“Nigel Martyn was probably our best signing but there were so many others,” he reflects. “But you can’t take all the credit for them.

“For example, with Bainsey, Alan Irvine went to watch England Under-21s in a European tournament. He came back and told me, ‘We’ve got to sign him’.

“I remember going to watch Jags at Burnley playing for England Under-21s, at right-back. We were always out trying to pick up players. I took Bill Kenwright with me in my car to Millwall, where our car was getting beaten up on the way in! We actually went to see Lucas Neill but we came back raving about Tim Cahill. So we were always out trying to find the players who we thought could make a difference for us.

“I think football has changed dramatically since then. So many games are on television now and you can see any game you want. But back then we were always out, my staff as well.

“I used to say to my staff, ‘If you want to work for me then you need to understand that there’s no days off. You’ll get days off somewhere. But not now’.

“If you wanted to work for me, then that’s the way it was, because I felt that the only way I was going to try to be as good as some of the managers in the Premier League was to try to work harder than them, gain more knowledge than them, or find out about more things which could help me.”

It was a quest which worked. Three times David Moyes was voted the League Managers’ Association Manager of the Year, and at West Ham he secured the club’s first major silverware in 43 years when he celebrated victory over Fiorentina to win the UEFA Europa Conference League.

Eighteen months later he was back at Goodison Park, guiding Everton to our first win in six matches in the Premier League and winning his latest Manager of the Month award after remaining unbeaten throughout the entire month of February.

“Coming back wasn’t difficult, but it was frightening!” he admits. “I had left and obviously a lot of people were disappointed I’d gone, but I also do think it was probably the right time to leave for different reasons as well.

“Everton has never left me, so getting the chance to come back was a great opportunity. But could I keep them up? I wasn’t sure.

“But the move from Goodison Park meant so much to me.

“The new stadium wasn’t as big a thrill as leaving Goodison, because Goodison was where I had worked for 11 years.

“I told a couple of my close friends that I’d been offered the Everton job and they were saying, ‘Oh, you’ve got to go’. But I was saying, ‘What if they go down? I’m done! I’ll have to move back up to Scotland’.”

An unbeaten nine match run, including three successive wins and a famous 2-2 draw with Liverpool, ensured the spectre of relegation was quickly banished.

Then in his first full season Everton constantly knocked on the door of European qualification, only falling away in the final fortnight.

“Coming in, I knew it wasn’t going to be all singing and all dancing and there were going to be big changes,” says Moyes.

“But in those circumstances I actually thought last year was a fabulous year, considering where we were, with players out of contract, new people coming into the Club, me trying to get used to Everton again.

“I thought last year was a great season. This year, with a smaller squad and with the situation at the top of the Club changing again, my idea was for the progression to continue.

“I did believe we could build year on year. I hoped it wasn’t going to take 10 or 11 years to get to the level we were at. But when you look back at what we’d done before, it didn’t take 10 or 11 years, it took two or three years. So my hope was that we could do it even quicker here.

“I had done it at West Ham. They were in relegation trouble and we made Europe. I dreamed that I could do it with Everton too and I’ve got to say the dream came so close.

“This year feels as if we’ve got a more difficult situation. It’s probably harder than last year in some ways, because of our squad size. It will be hard to maybe reach some of the things we targeted last year, but I’ve got to hope that we’ve got enough in the bag to do something special.”

Taking charge of his 592nd match tonight, David Moyes has already achieved something special.

“I’m incredibly proud to be the Everton manager,” he reflects. “I’m sure Harry Catterick, Howard Kendall and Joe Royle were also incredibly proud. The Club gets you, and if you get the Club – then it’s so big.

“I’ve got huge respect for any managers in the game who have been at clubs for long periods, people like Brian Clough, Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsene Wenger and Bobby Robson. Managers who have had longevity at their clubs.

“Everton has been huge for me and my family. My son David has gone everywhere and has got to sing with the players, while my father has lived with, and watched it all.

“That’s why it’s so important. What is also important is that I’ll always try to do the right thing for Everton Football Club.”

That will always be the case for David Moyes as manager of Everton Football Club.

#1338. Sarina Wiegman receives honorary damehood from Prince William at Windsor Castle - after leading Lionesses to back-to-back European titles

Published: 14:28 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 10 November 2026

Lionesses manager Sarina Wiegman has been awarded an honorary damehood by Prince William after leading England to back-to-back Euro wins.

Wiegman is Dutch and therefore cannot be made a substantive dame. Instead she has picked up the honorary title, because the Netherlands does not have a British monarch as its head of state.

She said upon being awarded the title at Windsor Castle on Tuesday: 'I feel very privileged to receive my honorary Damehood from His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle today.

'It is a day I will never forget and made even more special by sharing it with members of my family.

'I would like to again express my sincere gratitude for this honour and for the continued respect and warmth I experience from the English people. I thank everyone for their support.'

Wiegman was named in the King's New Year's Honours list at the end of 2025, alongside several members of her England team.

England manager Sarina Wiegman (left) has been awarded an honourary damehood by Prince William (right)

Captain Leah Williamson was awarded a CBE, with Alex Greenwood, Keira Walsh, Georgia Stanway and Ella Toone all being honoured with MBEs.

Wiegman said at the time: 'I would like to express my sincere gratitude for this honour. When I first arrived in England, I could never have imagined the respect and warmth I've experienced from the English people. I deeply thank the fans for their support.

'This title is a reflection of my exceptional team of players and staff. My congratulations go to Alex, Ella, Georgia, Keira, Leah and also Dr Ritan Mehta who have all been celebrated for their brilliant contributions.

'Our team values mean that when there is recognition for one, then there is recognition for all. I want to pay tribute to every member of our EURO squad. They should all be celebrated for everything they brought to the pitch and for the positive role they play in society. I'm proud to work alongside such a dedicated group of people.'

The former Netherlands coach took over the England team in 2021 and led them to success at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025.

She also reached the World Cup final in 2023, and signed a new two-year contract extension earlier this year, which will take her to the end of the 2029 Euros.

#1337. Everton Remembrance Service Held At Goodison Park

Representatives from the Armed Forces, Everton Football Club and Everton fan groups gathered together at Goodison Park on Wednesday morning for the annual Everton Remembrance Day Service.

Organised by the Football Club and the Everton FC Heritage Society, the ceremony was led by Reverend Henry Corbett, the Chaplain to Finch Farm, and Father Paul Harris.

Club Ambassadors Ian Snodin and Graham Stuart laid wreaths on behalf of the Football Club and the Everton Former Players' Foundation, who were also represented by former Blues winger Ronny Goodlass.

The British Army, Royal Air Force, Royal Navy and Merchant Navy also laid floral tributes, as did the Everton Shareholders' Association, the Everton Former Players’ Foundation, Everton in Community and Everton Free School.

Everton in the Community’s veterans programme, the Everton Fan Advisory Board, the Tri-Service Toffees, the Everton Collection, Everton Football College and the Ruleteros Society were also represented.

Heritage Society member, Paul Kelly, delivered a short address, while a representative from Everton in the Community's veterans programme read the names of the fallen from the Everton Football Clubs of Merseyside, Chile and New Zealand. Bugler Sam Lovatt played the Last Post at 11am, preceding a two-minute period of silence.

Remembrance Day is commemorated every year on 11 November to mark the armistice signed between the Allies of the First World War and Germany at Compiègne, France, for the cessation of hostilities which took effect at 11am – the ‘11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month’ – in 1918.

Those remembered from the three football clubs were:

First World War: Edward Atkinson, Frank Boundy, Harold Boyne, William Braidwood, James Brannick, Thomas Brewer, David Campbell, Arnold Cantell, Jeffrey Carmichael, Henry Churchill, Frederick Collinson, Alfred Corlett, Malcolm Fraser, Thomas Gracie, David Murray, Harry Norris, Thomas Norse, Leigh Richmond Roose, James Roy, Donald Sloan, Wilfred Toman, Richard Wynne.

Second World War: Brian Atkins, Alfred Pennington, William Reid, Thomas Robson, William Sumner.
