#1331. Scott McTominay reveals hospital dash and heart shock treatment days before Scotland's World Cup opener

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:25 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Scott McTominay has revealed he needed a procedure to reset the beat of his heart just two days before Scotland’s World Cup campaign kicked off back in June.

Heading into the opening game against Haiti in Boston, the explanation given from the Scottish Football Association was that McTominay had been carrying a sickness bug.

But, after the squad had flown from their training base in Charlotte, McTominay had actually been whisked away to hospital straight from the airport via a police escort.

The 29-year-old had shock treatment on his heart before then going on to play all three games as Steve Clarke’s side were knocked out at the group stage.

The Napoli midfielder subsequently underwent corrective surgery back at the start of the season and missed Scotland’s opening four fixtures in the Nations League.

Now back in the squad ahead of the upcoming double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland, McTominay has opened up for the first time on his health issues.

Scott McTominay had a heart procedure two days before playing against Haiti

Scott McTominay in action during Scotland's 1-0 World Cup win over Haiti

Asked about what happened, he replied: ‘The sickness bug? You’re not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup. It’s not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before — well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup.

‘But you have to take the cards you’re dealt on the chin. It’s part of the game. There’s nothing I could do about it and the shock went well, I was back in normal rhythm then 24 hours later you’re playing a World Cup game.

‘The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game.

‘You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking: “How has this happened to me?” But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football.

‘Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say: “Well, it’s part of the process”.

McTominay was given full reassurance from the doctors and medical staff that the procedure had gone well, insisting it was never in his thoughts to pull out of the squad.

Asked whether it was playing on his mind across the three games against Haiti, Morocco and Brazil, he said: ‘No. I put it to bed. I tried my best to put it to bed anyway. Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and sleep and stuff like that.

‘You have to get back round to doing it again. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you’re dealt, there’s nothing you can do about it.’

Some fans had questioned McTominay’s form throughout the World Cup, oblivious to the fact that he was effectively playing through an ongoing heart issue.

Asked whether the criticism bothered him at the time, he continued: ‘It’s tough. It’s never easy, things like that, but you can’t use things like that as an excuse because that’s just not in my nature.

‘I take whole responsibility for a lot of the things that we didn’t create or didn’t score the goals in the World Cup.

‘I can put my face out there and say that that was nowhere near good enough. But that’s part of football. You have to get away and think about it and reflect and come back a better player.

‘I didn’t know that’s what people were saying. I probably had an idea.

‘I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it. You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be.

‘For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.’

#1330. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Is there anything Harry Kane can't do? 🧐 His goal kick very nearly led to a Bayern Munich goal 😲 https://t.co/fqbsN7KOjw

And then Bayern did score. The ball was played inside to Kane, in centre field and afforded too much space. He delivered a perfectly weighted through ball for Alphonse Davies to run on to. The pace was perfect, allowing the Canadian not to break stride and stroke it past Raya. Kane did not fire the ball in, he did not make Davies work to reach it and he did not give Jurrien Timber any chance of cutting it out. It was perfect. Few players could do that. “Harry Kane puts the ball in a space from 30 metres that doesn’t exist,” Arteta said. True.

Harry Kane with an OUTRAGEOUS assist, and Alphonso Davies equalises 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/6cGXrUloHW

It was Saka’s replacement who gave Arsenal the lead, Eberechi Eze profiting from Martin Odegaard’s perceptive, lofted pass and taking advantage of Bayern’s ragged defending and some suspect goalkeeping from 40-year-old Neuer to score from an angle. Initially it was ruled out for offside, but that was overturned after a VAR check to provide Eze with a bit of redemption after being hooked against Nottingham Forest at the weekend.

VAR has given it, and Eze strikes Arsenal into the lead at the Allianz 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/i1LjrZVnbI

Neuer had his own slice of redemption as he saved well from Bruno Guimarães’ close-range header, pushing it against a post with Raya also excelling to beat out another header, this time from Dayot Upamecano.

When Timber was punished for handball, as he blocked Kane’s shot, the penalty was given. Up stepped Kane and we knew the rest. At that point it felt like Bayern would win, but Arsenal continued to play courageously and pushed on, as they had done throughout, risking conceding further goals.

Harry Kane, what a penalty 🥶 He scores in his TENTH consecutive Champions League game to give Bayern the lead 😳 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/4k4jPCQEWF

They were rewarded as Rice started the move, playing the ball in quickly to Noni Madueke with substitute Viktor Gyokeres laying it back into the midfielder’s path. He strode on and Neuer was again beaten from an angle. It was certainly warranted, even if it did not detract from Kane’s night. But will he have a greater one on Monday?

It had similarities [with last year’s league phase game]. I think we managed to create more chances but I think that Arsenal – and it’s something that has been mentioned by them before the game – they’ve worked a lot on retaining the ball and making it difficult to get the ball back. We did feel that.

It was a game in chunks. They had moments, we had moments. In our moments, I think we exploited the spaces in behind a little bit better maybe but we played against a top team and the result is a result between two big teams.

Last year they reaped the benefits of a top-two finish: home ties all the way to the final and a guarantee of avoiding the other club in the top two.

They have a chance to pick off Real Madrid at the Emirates, and will anticipate Aston Villa (who still have to play Barcelona and PSG) and Real Betis dropping points.

Given PSG have already dispatched Manchester City and Barcelona, it is hard to envisage them dropping a point, though they do have the odd off night.

Arsenal’s chances of grabbing second could come down to winning their remaining games and Liverpool slipping up. But with five games to go, these permutations are probably premature.

Wow, what a game. That is one of the highest levels that we have played. The level of opposition, what the game required, and our level as well. Two teams who wanted to press each other and wanted to attack and wanted to play. It was a fascinating game.

I think we started the game incredibly well, we were so dominant, we did everything to deserve the first goal. We didn’t score the goal and lost Bukayo and had to adapt to it.

We gave a terrible chance away after our corner which could have cost us, then we scored the goal. In the second half, the game was even,  they started probably a little bit better before they scored and they you have to react and we certainly did.

The spirit of the team, the quality we have showed on the second goal as well.

They are a bit concerned. A player having to come off with a sharp pain is never good news but we have to wait and see.

For me he’s the clear winner, his numbers speak for themselves. He’s obviously up against some other world class players. When you play with him you see how good it is, and when you play against him you see how much of a pain he is! As a striker to play that pass for the goal... he’s ridiculous. Lucky I can play with him, not so lucky when I have to play against him.

I thought it was a good performance. Probably the draw was a fair result overall. We probably just didn’t get quite enough right tonight to get the win.

Nice to get the assist to get back into the game and then I thought we had some good moments but not enough over the 90 minutes.

When you play against teams like Bayern who are man to man all over the pitch you have to apply certain principles, and I just kept running and managed to get away from my man. When they are following you all over, I just kept running and I was in on the goal.

He’s been making such a good impact from the bench [Gyokeres]. He’s made some great runs tonight and set me up for the goal. When you play against man to man, who follow you everywhere over the whole pitch, it’s such a tough game. You have to apply certain principles and concepts, and you’re constantly thinking about where the space is. For the goal, Noni one-touch set, Viktor’s one-touch set, those little movements put you through on goal.

In periods of the game, it felt like Arsenal were trying to play in the manner of Bayern or PSG by leaving themselves so light at the back with acres of green grass to cover.

Would they play like that in a quarter-final? Probably not, and they were emboldened by Bayern missing some key players. But it helped them create danger and have some strong spells, even if there were some scary moments going the other way.

Somewhere between that display and Arsenal’s rearguard in the Champions League final is probably the sweet spot.

A high-quality game between two of the most plausible winners of this season’s Champions League finishes level.

It was a helter-skelter contest at times. For all the talk of Arteta being a conservative coach, Arsenal committed numbers forward in their press and when they attacked, and that left them vulnerable to Bayern’s fast transitions and Kane’s passes from deep.

Perhaps it is a missed opportunity to beat Bayern in the Allianz, given the German side started without Olise, Kimmich, Musiala and Diaz, but a point from the hardest fixture of the league phase is more than acceptable.

The fly in the ointment is the injury suffered by Saka in the first half, but Eze and Madueke performed well in his absence.

Just one minute to play and Bayern have the ball in Arsenal’s half, but Calafiori gets his foot in. Madueke does well to keep it and Lewis-Skelly finds Eze.

Timber with dig from outside the box after a poor defensive header from Bayern, and Neuer tips it over. Rice to take the corner, and Arsenal’s set-pieces have caused problems throughout. This might just be Arsenal’s chance to win it.

Swung to the back post, but Tah did enough.

Bayern had an injury worry of their own now: Luis Diaz, not judged fit to start, has pulled up and will have to come off. Bayern were in a promising position in the Arsenal half.

Harry Kane looking for another of those arced passes forward, but Eze read it and retrieved. Arsenal finishing the stronger when it comes to possession and territory. Perhaps that Premier League intensity bearing fruit as the game progresses.

A couple of fouls given away by both teams, it has been a bitty few minutes. But Arsenal do well to find Lewis-Skelly free in the middle of the pitch, and he finds Rice who drives the away team forward.

Neither team appears inclined to settle for the draw, but Arsenal have the wind in their sails. Mikel Merino is on for Martin Odegaard, who has probably been Arsenal’s best player on the night.

Arsenal back level again, and it is an emphatic finish across Neuer from Rice, after a deft touch from Gyokeres around the corner at the edge of the box. Bright football around the box from Arsenal. Still 10 minutes or so to play.

Arsenal have been scoring gorgeous team goals all season. They have done so in all three of their Champions League games this season. They were labelled as “boring” after the Forest victory but that game was the exception, rather than the rule, on the evidence of this campaign.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

Arsenal deep in Bayern territory after Rice’s cross towards Eze glanced off the head of a defender. Bayern are keeping a good defensive shape though, Arsenal finding it difficult to penetrate. Arteta is preparing another pair of changes.

Luis Diaz with a snap shot that brings a sharp save from David Raya. On the balance of chances and threat created, Bayern have earned their lead. But still plenty of football to play. Arsenal have not scored from a set-piece this season, but they have looked dangerous tonight. They need another couple.

Neuer has just smashed into Stanisic, sweeping up a long ball Timber was chasing.

With Tzolis out and Saka now likely to be joining him on the sidelines, at what point does Arteta turn to Dowman in the league and Champions League? Obviously there are so many physical and defensive demands that are very difficult for a 16-year-old to meet... but the talent is there.

Arsenal enjoying plenty of territory and possession now, but you’d say Bayern look more likely to score on the counter-attack. Arsenal content to keep the ball and set themselves for a late assault.

Lewis-Skelly with a no-touch turn in midfield but then he takes too long and Bischof wins the ball cleanly. Davies nutmegs Rice on the counter, but Madueke tracked back diligently to snuff out the danger. At the other end, Karl fouls Eze who has enjoyed a strong game, aside from his goal.

Karl and Diaz are on for Bayern, replacing Gnarby and Saibari. If anything that shifts Bayern up a gear. Arteta has also made a double change: Lewis-Skelly on for Guimaraes, and Gyokeres on for Havertz.

The more open and transitional this game has become, the less comfortable Arsenal have looked. I’m not surprised Arteta has taken off Guimarães, as they have been struggling in that midfield battle for much of this second half. It feels like Bayern have taken this game to a place that Arsenal did not quite want to go: lots of space, lots of running, lots of interchanging positions.

Laimer with a foul on Eze near the left-corner of the penalty area, so Arsenal have a free-kick in a promising position for a cross. Havertz, Konsa, Gabriel and Timber the targets.

Brilliant deliver from Odeegard, somehow Arsenal fail to apply the finishing touch from a few yards out.

Bayern then escape and stream forward on the break, and Laimer snaps a shot wide.

Arsenal looking a little shaken at the back after conceding the goal, but Raya is fouled from the corner which helps them clear their lines. Luis Diaz is about to come on for the home team.

Bayern Munich lead for the first time on the night. Kane with a short stutter, before sending Raya the wrong way and wrapping the shot into the back of the net with power.

Harry Kane, what a penalty 🥶 He scores in his TENTH consecutive Champions League game to give Bayern the lead 😳 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/4k4jPCQEWF

Laimer’s pull back deflected into the path of Harry Kane, and Timber had his arm raised as he slid in to make the block. The referee wasted no time to give the penalty, and there are few complaints. Kane with the chance to score a ninth penalty against Arsenal. Raya up against him.

Bruno Guimaraes and Odegaard with some silky touches to help Arsenal win a free-kick in midfield. Arteta has some of his subs warming up, though he has already used one with Saka going off early on.

Arsenal close to a second goal again, after neat football involving Guimaraes and Havertz to release Eze on the left, and Neuer stuck out a leg to help Bayern scramble the ball away. It would be a surprise if this finished 1-1.

That’s a few times in this game that Arsenal have been ripped open after all going forward for a corner. It’s very uncharacteristic for Arteta’s side, who are usually so solid in their defensive shape.

The game continues to be very open, but some of that is the quality on show from both teams. Will Arteta call off the dogs at some point and tell his players to sit off in a defensive shape, or will they keep swinging punches?

Now Raya makes a world-class save at the other end! Upamecano skipped through the Arsenal press and there was acres of space to exploit again. Gnabry stood up a cross to the back post and Raya made a point-black save from Saibari’s header. It looked like he had to score from six yards.

What a save from Neuer! Down low to keep out a Guimaraes header from the corner. He was reaching back to the goal-line and he plucked the ball up on to the bar.

Arsenal were then stretched on the counter, but Saibari was offside.

Kane almost produced another great through ball within 30 seconds of the restart, but Gabriel made an interception. Arsenal need Bruno Guimaraes to be on the ball, on a couple of occasions he has been caught in space when Bayern come forward.

Arsenal respond though, and Arsenal win a corner through Eze.

Tah replaces Kim at centre-back, so a like for like change.

Arteta will be very disappointed by how Bayern were able to find Kane free in the middle from a throw-in. Whether Konsa should have been higher or Madueke further across, it was too simple.

A high-wire act from both teams, who are pushing numbers forward with and without the ball. Lots of man-to-man duels all over the pitch, and when one is lost there is loads of space to exploit. It has made for an entertaining half, and 1-1 is a fair scoreline. Arsenal controlled the first 25 to 30 minutes, but Bayern have looked dangerous.

The bigger story for Arsenal is the thigh injury suffered by Saka. It would be very surprising to see him before the November international break, at best. He pulled up abruptly.

Lovely Bayern move, whenever they reach three or four passes against Arsenal’s man-to-man pressure they have runners flying forward. Gnabry takes on a shot from a tight angle, and it deflects behind for a corner. Raya does well to claim.

Alphonso Davies’ pace is causing Arsenal some problems, and now it is Bayern’s turn to have a corner. Arsenal have lost some of their control of the first 30 minutes, but still look dangerous themselves. Timber is fouled from the corner, Arsenal free-kick.

Odegaard with a poor pass in the middle of the park, but Konsa produced a tremendous block to stop Kane’s left-footed shot across Raya.

Within 10 seconds, Arsenal are at the edge of the Bayern box through Rice and they win a corner after Eze’s shot was blocked.

The corner is flicked to the back post, where Calafiori was inches away from scoring from six inches out. Close to Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

The game is stretched now and quite entertaining, a very different feel to Arsenal’s Premier League assignments. Konsa realised Arsenal were short of numbers and lunged in against Harry Kane, hacking him down at the expense of a booking. Rice and his team-mates recovered well against the counter in any case.

Kane with another superb pass, perfectly curled around Timber into the path of Alphonso Davies who finishes beyond Raya. Kane had too much space in the middle of the pitch, Madueke perhaps guilty of not narrowing in.

Arsenal winning most of the aerial battles and duels for second balls at the moment, Bayern not building any pressure or fluency. There has been the odd flash of danger when Kane flips a pass in behind but Arteta’s team are comfortable at the moment.

Odegaard almost finds Eze with a lovely disguised through ball.

Odegaard has enjoyed the extra space on offer all game. Arsenal’s captain whips the corner to the back post where Guimaraes was free, but he shins a volley wide.

That makes two goals in three games for Eze. Although he got hooked at half-time in one of them (against Forest on Sunday). It feels like that’s probably how it’s always going to be with a player like him, to be honest. Highs and lows.

Kane’s range of passing in evidence again, with a driven diagonal over Gabriel’s head towards Saibari but he could not control the ball that was fizzed towards him. Kane is drifting towards the left to open up the pitch for those crossfield passes.

Arsenal caught out on the break by Harry Kane taking a goal kick, from which he picked out Davies with a raking pass down the left. Saibari helped the ball on for Gnabry who was free on the right, but Raya was down quickly to save and Rice cleared.

Arsenal have a corner, after a nice Madueke backheel released Timber. They have the upper hand in this game, but they have lost a major attacking reference with Saka going off. Arsenal enjoying the lion’s share of possession so far, which is perhaps a reflection of Bayern’s absentees. Kane has just dropped into his own box to receive a pass, and Konsa followed him all the way.

Alphonso Davies runs beyond the Arsenal defence for the first time in the game after Gnabry dribbles past Madueke, but Gabriel made a good challenge from the wrong side.

Havertz has been booked for a foul on Stanisic. Bayern have not been able to build a head of steam as an attacking force so far, but their pressing has forced Arsenal into longer balls forward. No serious chance so far.

So it is now Madueke on the right and Eze on the left for Arsenal. A shame for the spectacle that neither Saka nor Olise are on the pitch, and the Arsenal man had started the game quite brightly.

Saka had a quick chat with Arteta before going down the tunnel. He gestured towards his left quad.

Big problem here for Arsenal: Bukayo Saka has collapsed to the turf after playing a pass, and he looks to have pulled a muscle in his thigh. That is surely his race run tonight, and it looks like he could be out for a few months based on how he went down. Eze is coming on.

Arsenal get the game under way, playing in their navy away kit.

It seems like Vincent Kompany may have taken a leaf out of Thomas Tuchel’s tactical book. Kompany appears to have done the same here with Davies, usually a left-back, starting as a winger.

We are going to have to play I expect three or four different games at different stages throughout the game, so we need to have everybody ready to adapt throughout.

Kane has already played against Arsenal since leaving Spurs, so some of the vinegar has gone out of that sub-plot but it is still worth noting that he has scored 15 goals in 22 appearances against them. Several of those goals have been penalties, but Kane is so much more than a goalscorer these days, especially at Bayern where at times he appears to have a free role.

A fascinating aspect of tonight’s game is how Konsa and Gabriel decide to deal with him. Will Arsenal commit to a man-to-man press, with the centre-backs following Kane well beyond the halfway line, or preserve a more zonal approach?

Manchester United are now 4-0 down against a Como team managed by Cesc Fabregas. There is still 15 minutes or more to play. You can follow the rest of the game here to see if they can stem the bleeding.

Will the substitutes again make the difference for Arsenal tonight? In each of their last three league victories, they have won because of goals scored by substitutes. This speaks to the quality of Arteta’s squad, obviously, but also to the Arsenal manager’s ability to pick the right players for the right moments. Over the last year or so, this has become a real strength.

Karl had been expected to replace Olise on the right, but Kompany looks to have stiffened up his midfield by starting Pavlovic, Laimer and Bischof. It will be interesting to see how Saibari and Kane dovetail, two stick-on strikers. It is not Bayern’s strongest team, with Luis Diaz also on the bench.

Bayern Munich starting XI: Neuer, Stanisic, Kim Minjae, Upamecano, Davies, Pavlovic, Laimer, Bischof, Gnabry, Saibari, Kane

There was little doubt that Arteta would view this game as one that suits Jurrien Timber rather than Ben White. Arsenal’s manager has changed tack by starting Calafiori, who was rested for Arsenal’s first two Champions League games, but Bayern at the Allianz is a significant step up in grade. Madueke rewarded for his showing at Forest.

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Two changes for tonight's test ✊

Vincent Kompany is in the building. It wasn’t clear whether the Bayern head coach would be able to attend tonight’s game because he’s been battling a nasty virus over the last few days. He did not do the usual pre-match press conference yesterday but clearly feels well enough to be here tonight.

In an extract from Sam Dean’s new book on Arsenal’s resurgence under the Spaniard, he reveals that Mike Ashley was keen to bring Arteta to Newcastle United in 2019.

Sam writes: “Arteta also did not have a coaching staff assembled. It is believed that he tried to bring some key individuals on board, such was his interest in accepting Newcastle’s offer, but that the timing was not right for the people he truly wanted. In the end, much to the frustration of Newcastle and Ashley, he said no.”

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Arsenal won 3-1 at the Emirates in November in a performance of real class. It was arguably their most complete showing of the entire campaign.

Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1329. Momiki Hat-Trick Sees Blues Thrash Durham

Yuka Momiki’s second-half hat-trick helped Everton make it four wins from four in the Subway Players Cup with an impressive 6-0 win against Durham.

The 30-year-old came on at half-time and netted a fine trio of goals, with a brace from Noemie Mouchon and a first goal for Everton for Jutta Rantala completing the scoring for the dominant Toffees.

The Blues set the tone for the evening as Mouchon rifled an effort in to the palms of Cat Sheppard within the opening minute.

Rantala then followed that up with a venomous strike of her own two minutes later as the keeper was called in to action once more.

The Finland international, who celebrated her birthday on Tuesday, came even closer on 9 minutes as her rising shot rattled the crossbar.

It was Rantala who then opened the scoring on 20 minutes as her persistence paid off. Hannah Cain pulled an enticing ball across the face of goal. Fellow forward Rantala brought it down before unleashing an unstoppable effort in to the top right corner to net her first goal in royal blue.

The hosts continued to control the tempo throughout the opening 45 – probing their opponents and boasting the clear majority of possession and chances.

At the break, Phelan made a double change as Rosa van Gool, Maz Pacheco and Momiki replaced Wheeler, Kitagawa and Vignola.

Those substitutes immediately paid off as Momiki fired home at the Gwladys Street End five minutes after the interval. Upon reaching the penalty spot, Everton’s number 29 elegantly placed the ball in to the bottom right corner.

That corner was found by the ball again on 64 minutes as Mouchon finished past the diving keeper. The French forward brought the ball down excellently – it almost sticking to her right foot. She then pulled the trigger early, slotting past the outrushed Sheppard.

One minute later, Plano came on for her Everton debut to mark another memorable evening for the Club’s Academy.

Momiki then doubled her tally in the 70th minute with the best of her three strikes. From the edge of the box, she curled in to the far corner. The Gwladys rose, with Momiki’s appreciation for the iconic stand reciprocated by the Evertonians’ cheers.

With five minutes remaining, Mouchon secured a brace of her own. The forward saw an initial strike saved, but prodded home the rebound to cap off a rapid break.

The loudest cheer of the night occurred only a single minute later as Momiki secured the match ball to conclude a brilliant evening to be a Blue.

#1328. Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4,5,6,7,8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

#1327. Police 'are trawling through dodgy Fire Stick sellers' bank accounts to contact illegal viewers' of Premier League football and films

Published: 11:08 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:40 EST, 11 November 2026

A former detective has revealed the lengths authorities are going to in order to crack down on the use and sale of 'dodgy Fire Sticks'.

Law enforcement organisations across the UK are taking a tougher stance on these devices – and how they are used and distributed – with multiple people having been convicted and jailed in recent years for selling and supplying them.

The devices, which often cost anywhere between £30 and £100 – in comparison with around £30 a month for a Sky Sports subscription – give customers access to a range of premium TV services without paying, most notably in a football sense with access to live matches.

But Rav Wilding, a former detective who recently appeared on the BBC Morning Live show, has sent a fresh warning to individuals that use them.

Wilding said: 'People are buying them online usually on the black market and then they're getting all these services for free essentially.

'But it's a crime. It's not allowed. Owning the stick itself is not a crime, but using it for this purpose is.'

A former detective has revealed the lengths authorities are going to in order to crack down on the use and sale of 'dodgy Fire Sticks'

Wilding went on to say that along with a crackdown on sellers through house raids, authorities are now looking through their accounts to find out in further detail who is using the devices.

They then often contact those users in a new step, with it estimated that around four million people or households have got these Fire Sticks at the moment.

Wilding added: 'All of them are using them illegally. They're going for the distributors. They're going for the sellers. They are having a lot of success. But actually, once they've got the seller, they're going through their accounts.

'They're seeing who has been paying the money for these illegal things, and if they've been paying them for these sticks then people should possibly expect a conversation or two if the police want to know why they've been paying them money for this.'

Wilding revealed that this included checking bank statements to find out the information of individuals who have been paying for such a service, and authorities have been joined by subscription service providers in their clampdown attempts too.

'They (subscription service providers) are losing money to this, so they have been reaching out and are taking action against those people using them illegally as well,' he explained.

'So I wouldn't say it's something you should do. It is actually a crime and it can have a nasty fine, a huge fine and also a custodial sentence for users and sellers of these things.'

Rav Wilding appeared on BBC Morning Live and sent a fresh warning to users of the devices

Daily Mail Sport has previously reported FACT is playing a leading role in the crackdown on the devices, with the anti-piracy organisation liaising with police forces across the country.

And Kieron Sharp, chairman of FACT, added: 'We have a wide range of enforcement options - from issuing cease and desist notices to "knock and talk" visits - through to full criminal prosecutions where appropriate.

'We will take robust action against those involved - not only targeting sellers and distributors, but also those facilitating and profiting from the illegal activity.'

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1325. A Yeboah back in the Premier League? Leeds legend Tony's nephew Kelvin wanted by several clubs in January transfer window after scoring 18 goals in MLS for Minnesota United this term

Published: 04:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 04:36 EST, 11 November 2026

Another goal-packed season for Kelvin Yeboah in Major League Soccer (MLS) is expected to spark interest among Premier League and Championship clubs in January.

Yeboah has ended the campaign with 18 goals and made five assists for Minnesota United who finished 10th of 15 teams in the Western Conference, just one point outside and one place outside the play-offs.

It means the season is over for the 26-year-old nephew of Leeds legend Tony Yeboah.

Yeboah describes himself as 'more of a modern nine' than his uncle Tony, who was famed for his muscular physique and his ability to strike with ferocious volleys from distance. He is sharp and mobile with a goal instinct.

Premier League and Championship clubs have been monitoring his progress this season.

Everton and Crystal Palace, both in search of firepower and options up front, are among those who have been linked to a move. Free-spending Ipswich are another.

Kelvin Yeboah is wanted by many Premier League goals after a fine goalscoring season in MLS

Yeboah scored 18 goals for Minnesota United - with Everton, Crystal Palace and Ipswich keen

The striker is the 26-year-old nephew of Tony Yeboah, a Leeds United legend of the mid-1990s

There is interest also from Europe. Hoffenheim boss Christian Ilzer signed Yeboah when in charge of Sturm Graz, after the young forward had scored four goals against his Austria Vienna team in a cup tie in the previous season.

Yeboah has been in Minnesota since the summer of 2024. There is another season on his contract and the option of one more after that.

But he remains keen to test himself at the top of the European game and there is a growing feeling that he could be on the move in the next window.

'As a footballer, you want to play on the biggest stages and express who you are as a person,' he told Daily Mail Sport in an interview on the eve of the MLS season. 'I just want to keep scoring goals and give myself the best chance of that happening.'

He grew up in Italy from the age of three to 15 and represented the Azzurri at Under-21 level. He is also eligible for Ghana where he was born.

At 15, he moved to London where he played non-league football for AC London and had trials at several clubs including West Ham before joining WSG Tirol in Austria at the age of 18.

Yeboah scored 20 goals in a year at Sturm Graz before returning to Italy. He was 21 when Genoa signed him for £6million. It should have been the perfect homecoming but the club then owned by 777 Partners plunged into financial chaos.

Relegated from Serie A they were unable to pay wages and Yeboah was loaned to three different clubs in three different countries before finding stability in Minnesota. He has 36 MLS goals in 79 appearances.

#1324. Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1,2,3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

The physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions. Fragile or misshapen nuclei are hallmarks of cancer, cardiomyopathy and premature ageing4,5. Nuclei in stem cells gradually stiffen during differentiation4,5,6,7. While these changes are widely recognized as consequences of altered nuclear composition and chromatin dynamics, they also influence genome organization and transcription8,9,10. Despite the importance, the physical state of the nucleus at the earliest stages of mammalian development, when life begins, remains unclear.

During the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program. In mice, this transition occurs within the first approximately 48 h after fertilization and is associated with a surge in new transcript production, known as major zygotic gene activation (ZGA)11,12,13. Major ZGA occurs during the mid-to-late two-cell stage, and embryos that impair ZGA fail in subsequent development. Around the time of ZGA, chromatin exhibits distinct structural and biochemical changes accompanied by histone modifiers and transcription factors14,15. By contrast, whether the nucleus organizing chromatin undergoes any crucial changes that drive ZGA is not known. In somatic cells, nuclear shape and mechanics depend on lamins, which line the inner nuclear membrane16,17. Lamins are long-lived, enriched in eggs and are crucial for mammalian development18,19,20. Previous studies have documented that, of the two major types, A-type lamins exhibit cell-lineage-specific differential expression patterns, whereas B-type lamins are constitutively expressed throughout development16. However, their dynamics and transiency, as well as the underlying core regulatory mechanism, during the earliest embryonic stages are poorly understood. Likewise, how the nuclear lamina, which forms a structural meshwork, controls nuclear mechanics and genome dynamics during this critical transition is unknown. Investigating physical nuclear characteristics necessitates direct quantification and manipulation of their mechanical properties. However, achieving this without compromising cell viability poses a challenge.

To investigate physical nuclear properties, we first performed high-resolution confocal scanning of fertilized mouse eggs during early cleavages (Fig. 1a). Our three-dimensional (3D) images of nuclei with H2B–mCherry, expressed without perturbing development (Extended Data Fig. 1a), revealed their distinct shape features, showing uneven local deformation at the two-cell stage in contrast to their predominantly spherical appearance at the one-cell and four-cell stages (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Timelapse imaging revealed that one-cell nuclei remained spherical during the cell cycle (Fig. 1d). Two-cell nuclei underwent slow, incremental deformation, which started at around 21 h post-insemination (h.p.i.), peaked at 24–26 h.p.i. and then gradually regressed by 32–36 h.p.i. (Fig. 1e). At the four-cell stage, nuclei were again spherical (Fig. 1f) (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Videos 1−3). Before the onset of deformation, two-cell nuclei had fully swollen and reached steady sizes; once deformed, the altered nuclear shapes persisted for hours (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Similar deformation was observed using emerin–eGFP for the nuclear envelope (Fig. 1g) or mCherry–NLS for the nuclear interior (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

This finding prompted us to develop a biophysical setup that quantitatively characterizes the mechanical properties of early embryonic nuclei in situ (Fig. 1h). The setup equipped a pressure-controlled nanocapillary, of which the tip was inserted into a fertilized embryo to capture the nuclear surface. A weak, constant suction pressure (2.1 × 101 kPa) pinched the surface, which was then stretched through axial translocation of the nanocapillary. The nuclei could be gradually strained, resulting in tension, and the strain reached a maximum just before the detachment (Fig. 1i). The analysis could be performed from the one-cell to four-cell stages, over which the predominantly fluid-like cytoplasm minimally influenced the measured mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f). Measurements were also insensitive to nuclear markers and were comparable to label-free imaging results (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h).

Our analysis revealed that two-cell nuclei were significantly more deformable than one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1j). The deformable nature persisted throughout the cell cycle (from 21 to 32 h.p.i.) even as DNA doubled at about 24 h.p.i. Nuclear stiffness, as estimated based on the nanocapillary pressure and the extent of nuclear deformation, transiently lowered at the two-cell stage (one-cell, 5.0 ± 1.3 nN µm−1; two-cell, 2.0 ± 0.5 nN µm−1; four-cell, 4.6 ± 1.9 nN µm−1; n = 18, 38 and 13 embryos, respectively) (Fig. 1k). The stiffness values varied between male and female pronuclei (30.7 ± 21.3%, n = 8 pairs) and between blastomeres of each two-cell embryo (23.5 ± 14.5%, n = 16 pairs), while the differences were pronounced among the developmental stages (Extended Data Fig. 2i). Two-cell nuclei also exhibited significant plasticity, in contrast to more elastic one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1l) (shape recovery, 91.0 ± 4.3% for one-cell; 66.9 ± 8.0% for two-cell; and 87.9 ± 4.6% for four-cell). The deformable two-cell nuclear stiffness was consistent when embryos were examined using lower nanocapillary pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). An alternative capillary-based approach, using an incremental suction pressure that aspirated nuclei, yielded consistent results (n ≥ 12 embryos per stage) (Extended Data Fig. 2l–n). These corroborate the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus.

Our nanocapillary-based assay at 1.2 × 101 kPa minimally perturbed development, enabling us to relate two-cell nuclear stiffness with embryos’ developmental competence (Fig. 2a). We found that all fertilized embryos that timely reached the blastocyst stage had soft nuclei (2.0 ± 0.6 nN µm−1; n = 66 of 66 embryos), while nearly half of the embryos that impaired development had stiff nuclei (n = 7 of 15 embryos; defined as more than twice the mean nuclear stiffness of the normal development) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Detecting embryos with stiff nuclei was infrequent (8.6%; n = 7 out of 81 embryos). The outcome was regardless of the fluorescent tag type and marker expression levels (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). A similar mechanical feature was observed for cloned embryos created through somatic cell nuclear transfer (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,d,e) (n = 46 embryos). Thus, deformable two-cell nuclei are a signature of normal preimplantation development.

a, Schematic of the assay. Embryos prepared through in vitro fertilization or through somatic cell nuclear transfer were subjected to the nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement during the two-cell stage using a pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k), after which the embryos resumed standard culture. b, The relationship between two-cell nuclear stiffness and the frequency of development to the blastocyst stage at 96 h.p.i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For b, statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney U-tests (two-sided); the thick horizontal bars (red) represent the mean values.

We next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus. Using immunofluorescence, we first examined four major lamins, A/C, B1 and B2, and found that lamin B1 transiently cleared from the two-cell nuclear envelope, nearly paralleling nuclear softening (Fig. 3a,b). The clearance was rapid and substantial, with an approximately 70% decrease in peripheral signal during the early-to-mid two-cell stage (21 to 24 h.p.i.; Fig. 3b). Lamin A/C and B2 levels also changed, but their trends were gradual and monotonic, with only a minor decline, if any, during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Another nuclear envelope protein, Lap2β, also changed little (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Live-embryo imaging confirmed the clearance of lamin B1 from the two-cell nuclear envelope with a decay time constant of 86 ± 44 min (n = 5 embryos; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). An immunoblotting assay revealed a reduction in lamin B1 during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3d), suggesting degradation.

Our pilot assay using wortmannin implicated that autophagy promotes lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Autophagy is active in early embryos and is essential for preimplantation development21. In live-embryo imaging, the autophagy factor LC322 was diffusive at the one-cell stage and accumulated in the two-cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Our antibody microinjection targeting LC3 suppressed lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Cell cycle progression as monitored by EdU was normal (Extended Data Fig. 4g). We therefore designed a construct that interferes with the endogenous interaction between lamin B1 and LC3, using a short fragment of lamin B1 carrying LC3-binding domains and an intrinsic nuclear localization signal23 (hereafter, sfLB1; Fig. 3e). When expressed in embryos, this fragment was predominantly nucleoplasmic (Extended Data Fig. 4h), while a major autophagy substrate p62 maintained stable protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Our analysis revealed that the clearance of lamin B1 was suppressed by sfLB1, whereas lamin A/C and B2 remained largely unperturbed (Fig. 3f,g). An accumulation of lamin B1 was detectable in western blot analysis of lysates (Extended Data Fig. 4j). A sfLB1 variant (sfLB1Δ), which was nucleoplasmic but with abrogated LC3 binding23 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,k), had little influence on lamin B1 clearance (Fig. 3f,g). The development of embryos was impaired by sfLB1, but not by sfLB1Δ (Fig. 3h).

To understand the mechanistic basis of lamin B1 clearance, we constructed fluorescent reporters based on full-length lamin B1 fused to mCherry. Consistent with the results shown in Fig. 3a–c, the wild-type (WT) construct (flLB1wt; Fig. 3e) localized to the nuclear envelope and exhibited rapid lamin B1 clearance (T1/2 = 83 ± 44 min, n = 18) (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). The other three constructs carried mutations near or at an LC3-interacting region core motif (flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A)) or at the major N-terminal CDK1 phosphorylation site for nuclear-envelope breakdown24 (flLB1(S24A)) (Fig. 3e). These constructs also localized to the two-cell nuclear envelope (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Notably, the mutations that abrogated LC3 interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5b) suppressed the lamin B1 clearance, whereas the mutation at the CDK1 site did not prevent the clearance (Fig. 3i). The mutations in flLB1(5A) were at the site targeted for autophagic degradation of lamin B1 during oncogene-induced cell senescence23. The selectivity of lamin B1 over lamin A/C and B2 was also consistent with the phenomenon reported in senescent cells23.

Our assay further suggested that lamin B1 is degraded through an autophagy–lysosome pathway. This was confirmed by tracking the fate of flLB1wt and identifying its predominant lysosomal localization and formation of foci (n = 18 embryos; Fig. 3j,k). flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) localized much less to lysosomes (n = 12 and 14 embryos; Fig. 3j,k), while the numbers of lysosomes remained comparable (Fig. 3l). We did not observe prominent lamin-B1-positive structures bulging from the outer nuclear membrane23 nor an accumulation of lysosomes on the nuclear surface25 within the timescale examined. Collectively, our mechanistic view of lamin B1 clearance is shown in Fig. 3m.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 on two-cell nuclear stiffness. Nanocapillaries indicated that two-cell nuclei of which the envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1 were stiffer and less plastic than controls (4.2 ± 1.3 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (sfLB1; Fig. 4a–d). These nuclei were as stiff as normal one-cell and four-cell nuclei (~5 nN µm−1, Fig. 1k). We next overexpressed lamin B1. As WT lamin B1 rapidly dissociated from the nuclear envelope, we used flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) to compensate for the clearance. Whereas excess loading of these lamins resulted in collapsed nuclei, titrating expression levels preserved the overall nuclear shape, with lamin B1 loaded to the nuclear envelope at a level comparable to that using sfLB1 (Fig. 4a,b). We found that flLB1(F454A/L457A) profoundly increased nuclear elasticity and stiffness (4.0 ± 1.1 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (Fig. 4c,d), while overall autophagic activity as assessed by LC3 signal26 was maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5c). The phenotype quantitatively mirrored the embryos perturbed through sfLB1. By contrast, flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, which lacked the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif for farnesylation16 and remained nucleoplasmic, did not significantly alter nuclear shape and mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 5d). These data indicate that two-cell nuclear stiffness depends on the nuclear envelope localization of lamin B1.

Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) showed nuclei of which the shape remained largely deformed as in normal two-cell embryos (Fig. 4a). These nuclei were soft and plastic (1.6 ± 0.4 nN µm−1, n = 10 embryos), despite their comparable level of nuclear envelope loading to sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4b–d). The minimal mechanical impact of flLB1(5A) was probably due to its poor assembly competency at the nuclear envelope for the following reasons: first, our nuclear isolation assay indicated that flLB1(5A) was more soluble than flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4e). Second, sfLB1(5A) showed comparably slightly higher affinity for LC3 than sfLB1(F454A/L457A) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, our expansion microscopy (ExM) analysis revealed a less-uniform peripheral localization of flLB1(5A) in comparison to endogenous lamin B1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A)27 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–g). The difference in peripheral DNA signals appeared less pronounced between perturbed embryo groups (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Our nanocapillary-based assay further suggested an early reduction in nuclear stiffness before lamin B1 clearance (Figs. 1k and 3a,b). Collectively, our data suggest that lamin B1 controls two-cell nuclear stiffness depending on their assembly stability at the nuclear envelope and that the stability depends on the site to which LC3 binds.

We next examined whether the observed nuclear changes impact the two-cell transcriptional reprogramming. We analysed the above embryos using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 1). The first cleavage and following cell cycle progression were normal in those embryos; the overexpressed protein levels were stable and comparable among conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Our analysis indicated that the transcriptomes of flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos were distinct from those of the flLB1(5A) and non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified more than 3,000 downregulated genes in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos compared with the non-injected controls (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). The downregulation was evident even when compared with flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4g), whereas very few DEGs were detected between flLB1(5A) embryos and the non-injected controls (Fig. 4h). Importantly, the genes downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) overlapped more with major ZGA and two-cell-activated genes than with minor ZGA and one-cell-activated genes28 (972 out of 3,763 (25.8%) versus 251 out of 3,763 (6.7%); P < 0.01, Fisher’s exact test) (Fig. 4i). The overlap was even greater when compared with another major ZGA gene list29 (1,338 out of 2,508, 53.3%) (Fig. 4i,j). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC embryos did not show an appreciably altered transcriptome at comparable expression levels (Extended Data Figs. 5g and 7e). Our analysis also indicated perturbed expression of key transcriptional regulators Obox15 in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos but it was not prominent in flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4k). The profiles of maternal and zygotic Obox genes suggested a failure in minor-to-major ZGA transition15.

We next analysed how ZGA is altered when the nuclear envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1. Analysing embryos overexpressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, along with the non-injected controls, we found that thousands of genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated through sfLB1 (Extended Data Fig. 7f–l and Supplementary Table 3). Many downregulated genes identified as DEGs were shared between sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos (71.1%; Fig. 4i (bottom right)). Developmentally essential genes were enriched among the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7m). Analysing published chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) datasets further indicated sharp H3K4me3 signals around the transcription start sites of the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7n). We therefore performed genome-wide profiling of H3K4me3 through an optimized cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis. By establishing a condition that maintained the nuclear structure, reproducible signals were obtained that agreed with previously published ChIP–seq data14,30 (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e). Our analysis indicated that H3K4me3 is more abundant at transcription start sites in sfLB1 embryos than in the non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 8f). It has been demonstrated that broadly spread noncanonical H3K4me3 is removed by histone demethylation for major ZGA14. Indeed, H3K4me3 remained accumulated in broad-domain H3K4me3 (bdH3K4me3) in sfLB1 embryos, whereas H3K4me3 enrichment in lamina-associated domains unchanged (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Analysing the expression levels of histone methylation-related enzymes, key lysine demethylase (KDM) genes, which are needed to eliminate bdH3K4me314, were downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) and sfLB1, but the changes were not significant through flLB1(5A) and sfLB1Δ (Fig. 4m). These data suggest that the establishment of histone methylation status2 failed in embryos when lamin B1 stiffened the two-cell nuclear envelope.

There was a marked difference in nuclear stiffness between the embryo groups that failed in major ZGA and those that were transcriptionally less perturbed. To test whether nuclear stiffness per se was inhibitory to ZGA, we developed a molecular tether–anchor system that targets the nuclear envelope and stiffens nuclei (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The tether comprised an elastic I27 module of titin31 of which the ends were fused to a pair of GFP nanobodies. The anchor was made based on a minimal KASH domain fused to mEGFP for outer-nuclear-envelope localization32. When co-expressed, the tether was recruited to the anchor-coated nuclear envelope and increased nuclear stiffness by around twofold (4.3 ± 1.5 nN µm−1, n = 20 embryos; Fig. 4n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Nuclear plasticity and deformation decreased accordingly (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Importantly, in the tether-stiffened nuclei, lamin B1 levels were as low as in normal mid two-cell embryos (Fig. 4p). Lamin A/C and B2 also remained largely unperturbed (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Our mRNA microinjection into late zygotes minimally affected pronuclear stiffness, first cleavage and cell cycle progression (Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Moreover, our two mutant tether derivatives, one that weakened its affinity to the anchor (tether LaG16(5A)) and one that impaired its elastic force-generating property (tether titin(W34E)), showed no appreciable impact on nuclear shape and mechanics (Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d,j). In contrast to the WT, neither of the two mutants significantly impaired development (Extended Data Fig. 9k). Thus, our tether–anchor system increases two-cell nuclear stiffness and perturbs embryonic development when it binds to the nuclear envelope and exerts force.

Our RNA-seq analysis revealed that embryos in which the nuclei were stiffened by the tether WT (tWT) exhibited distinct transcriptomes compared with those expressing the LaG16(5A) tether mutant and the non-injected controls (Extended Data Fig. 10a). A total of 634 genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated in the tWT embryos, while much fewer DEGs were identified in tether-mutant embryos (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e; versus the non-injected controls). Furthermore, the expression of the Obox cluster and other major ZGA genes was dampened (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Downregulation of key ZGA genes and transcriptional repression were detectable in quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) and 5-ethynyl-uridine (EU) incorporation analyses (Extended Data Fig. 10g,h). Whereas the impact on ZGA was broader and less variable for flLB1(F454A/L457A) than for tWT (972 versus 168 genes; Fig. 4i versus Extended Data Fig. 10e; Fig. 4j versus Fig. 4q), 82.2% of the downregulated genes in tWT embryos were shared with those perturbed through sfLB1 or flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4r). Together, we conclude that deformable two-cell nuclei are integral to the execution of proper ZGA.

We next examined the effect of lamin B1 persistence on early development. As a result, approximately 50% of the embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) did not progress beyond the two-cell stage (Extended Data Fig. 5h), comparable to those perturbed through sfLB1 (Fig. 3h). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC did not significantly affect development, indicating that the effective site of lamin B1 is at the nuclear envelope. Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) also showed impaired development, despite their nearly normal transcriptome (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Our analysis indicated that those embryos accumulated DNA damage as detected through phosphorylated H2A.X (γH2A.X) foci (Extended Data Fig. 5i), a developmental impediment33. By contrast, DNA damage levels in embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) were as low as those of non-injection control. Our results do not exclude the possibility that the suppressed ZGA and basal DNA damage combinatorially impaired development. Nonetheless, our data indicate that embryos with stiff two-cell nuclei are unable to facilitate proper ZGA and early development. Embryos with tether-stiffened nuclei also exhibited a two-cell arrest (Extended Data Fig. 9k), supporting the necessity of nuclear softness for development.

Given the impact of nuclear stiffness on ZGA, we examined chromatin dynamics in deformable and non-deformable nuclei. Our ExM images at 24 h.p.i. showed peripheral layers of DNA and lamins, with the overlap comparable to those analysed using electron microscopy34 (~150 nm; Extended Data Fig. 6i). Our imaging further revealed a preferential localization of DNA near concave regions of the two-cell nuclear envelope (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Lamin B1 signals also exhibited a weak negative correlation with nuclear deformation35 (Fig. 5b,c). However, the biased DNA localization was shared among deformable nuclei regardless of lamin B1 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), suggesting that nuclear deformation is associated with peripheral DNA organization.

We next examined how deformable nuclei are linked to gene expression regulation during ZGA. In 3D images, large fluorescent foci positive for elongating RNA polymerase II (Pol II Ser2P) shifted their distribution towards the nuclear periphery, as nuclear deformation increased from 21 to 24 h.p.i. (Fig. 5d,e). Notably, the majority of the Pol II foci became more frequently associated with nuclear concavity (Fig. 5f). The focus sizes increased over time, and their growth was suppressed by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5g). Concomitantly, DNA mass volume decreased by 14.7 ± 6.5% (Fig. 5h). We next performed sequential 3D fluorescence in situ hybridization (3D FISH) analysis36 to examine the link between peripheral transcriptional activity and ZGA (Fig. 5i–l). We analysed the genomic loci of Kdm5b and Obox6, along with Gabarapl1 as a non-ZGA control and found that their distributions were broad and changed from the early to the mid-to-late two-cell stage, but the average distance remained 2–3 µm from the nuclear periphery around the time of major ZGA (2.7 ± 2.0, 2.0 ± 1.6 and 2.1 ± 1.3 µm, respectively; 28 h.p.i.) (Fig. 5i–k). Pol II Ser2P intensities were greater when the Obox6 and Kdm5b loci were positioned >1 µm from the nuclear periphery, while DAPI signals remained unchanged, suggesting that the increased local transcriptional activity was not merely a consequence of higher chromatin density (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j). This trend was not observed in Gabarapl1 (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Our sequential FISH further enabled us to determine the locations of multiple gene loci within the same nucleus (Fig. 5l). Our data indicated a widespread positioning of Obox6 and Kdm5b loci at 21 h.p.i. and a change in the localization of gene loci at 28 h.p.i., with a frequent incidence of their concomitant presence near the nuclear periphery. This locus distribution was disrupted by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5l). Notably, Pol II Ser2P intensities at Obox6 loci depended on the nuclear stiffening, while their changes at Kdm5b loci appeared less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We therefore performed sequential 3D DNA–RNA FISH analysis to detect nascent Kdm5b transcripts and found a surge in the production around 2–4 µm from the nuclear envelope, and it depended on peripheral nuclear stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 10l–n). In summary, our data suggest that soft and plastic two-cell nuclei ensure the formation of active transcription sites a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope and enable the coordinated positioning of key ZGA gene loci around the sites for expression.

Our study reveals physical characteristics of early embryonic nuclei and their distinct changes that facilitate ZGA. Our data show that the autophagy factor LC3 and lamin B1 clearance confer nuclear plasticity and softness, and that deformable nuclei are key to robust zygotic transcription. Extensive studies have profiled epigenetic states of chromatin and provided a genome-centred view of this critical developmental transition. Our study highlights the importance of physical nuclear state for this transition and underscores the need for integration of diverse embryonic parameters, including their subcellular material properties.

Our work identifies a transient phase of nuclear deformability that manifests as cells transition through a totipotent state (Fig. 1). Notably, this nuclear change marks normal preimplantation development and contributes to transcription and gene locus movement (Figs. 2, 4 and 5). Notably, the sites of active DNA transactions appear a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope, often associated with local negative curvature, suggesting the generation of inward forces around these sites (Fig. 5d–h). During ZGA, chromatin undergoes dynamic remodelling and compaction37,38,39, while maintaining contact with the nuclear lamina40. A flexible nuclear envelope may accommodate these internal and peripheral chromatin activities, mediating a mechanical conflict for the consolidation of functional genome architectures. Our analysis also suggests that intense transcriptional activity near the deformable nuclear envelope enables the full activation of key ZGA genes that shape the two-cell epigenome14 (Fig. 4l,m). Such mechanical control may also operate in naive embryonic stem cells, in which soft nuclei are linked to pluripotency and priming for differentiation41.

We find that the embryonic mechanism governing lamin B1 clearance shares similarities with nuclear autophagy activated during oncogene-induced cell senescence23 (Fig. 3). As autophagy is accompanied by an increase in intracellular calcium levels and is independent of mTORC1 in early embryos21,42, the clearance is most likely developmentally programmed. Our data suggest a role of nuclear translocation of LC3 and its distinct effect on nuclear shape and mechanics. Further analysis of its regulated nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling43 should reveal the mechanistic basis behind the physiological and pathological nuclear remodelling.

Our findings also raise several interesting questions for future studies. First, our imaging assay detected diluted lamin B1 at convex regions of the nuclear envelope35 (Fig. 5b,c). It remains to be explored whether the clearance of lamin B1 merely contributes to nuclear softening or controls DNA organization by sensing local nuclear curvature. Second, as lamins influence transcription44,45 and the chromatin–lamina contacts change during development40, understanding the interplay between mechanical cues and biochemical factors that ensures robust transcriptional control will be an essential next step. Third, soft and transcriptionally active nuclei, yet enriched with lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope, were prone to DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). As excess lamin B1 can cause persistent DNA damage46, autophagic clearance of lamin B1 may be necessary to protect against such damage. It would be interesting to dissect nuclear actin in two-cell nuclei47, as per its involvement in DNA damage repair48.

Physical nuclear stability is likely important for early embryos, given the potential mechanical challenges they face during passage through the uterine tube49. Yet this period coincides with a transient state in which nuclei become less mechanically resilient. Early mammalian embryos are also prone to DNA lesions and chromosome missegregation50,51,52. Understanding how embryos navigate the vulnerable state may reveal principles underlying developmental robustness.

Mice (ICR and B6C3F1/Jc1 or slc (BCF1)) aged 5–15 weeks53 were purchased from CLEA Japan, Japan SLC or Kiwa Laboratory Animals, maintained in light-controlled (light: 08:00 to 20:00; dark: 20:00 to 08:00), air-conditioned rooms (ambient temperature: 23 °C ± 1.5 °C, humidity: 50 ± 10%) at each facility and used for experiments. All mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and all efforts were made to minimize suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

To obtain oocytes, female mice were superovulated by intraperitoneal injections of 7.5 IU of pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG; ASKA Animal Health), followed by 7.5 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; ASKA Animal Health) at 48 h after PMSG injection.
