(a) Tumors 4 and 7 analyzed as in Fig. 1h. Cells are colored by classification or the indicated feature levels. (b) Heatmap of mean feature levels in each subpopulation across all HR+ tumors analyzed by CyTOF (n = 14, including 3 anchor repeats, see Table S3). Rows present standardized values. (c) Two luminal PDX models analyzed by CyTOF after removal of mouse cells (human CD298-positive; mouse MHC class 1-negative), and classification into three subpopulations (Fig. 1j). PDX-1 comprised of six tumors, with equal cell sampling per tumor; PDX-2 comprised of one tumor. Heatmaps show the mean feature levels within each subpopulation for each model. (d) UMAP of MCF7 CyTOF data using all measured markers. Points are colored by cluster (left) or the indicated feature or signature (right).

(a) Distribution of DBSACN-defined cell subpopulations across independent MCF7 CyTOF experiments of MCF7 cells, showing consistent proportions of the different cell states. (b) UMAP representation and DBSCAN clustering of two different MCF7 parental cells or single-cell derived clones analyzed by CyTOF, using only epigenetic features. Points are colored by the classification of different subpopulations or the expression levels of the indicated feature or signature (PermCell). (c) The distribution of cells among the populations defined by DBSCAN clustering in the MCF7 parental (p) or single-cell derived clones (c). The single-cell derived clones recapitulate the entire spectrum of heterogeneity observed in the parental population. (d) UMAP representation of CyTOF analysis of six independently grown tumors from the PDX-1 model (n = 6 tumors, each grown in a different mouse), colored by subpopulations. Cells from each individual tumor are mapped onto the joint UMAP, and the distribution of cells among the three subpopulations for each tumor is shown.

(a) Confusion matrix of XGBoost model predictions for all 3 subpopulations across HR+ tumors (n = 14) using only epigenetic features, excluding cell identity markers. Rows were normalized to show predictions as percentages of cells within each true class. (b) Representative examples of XGBoost-based noise prediction procedure. UMAPs of individual tumors are shown before (left) and after (right) prediction. Points are colored by classification; non-clustered cells before prediction, or cells in which prediction confidence <95% are marked in gray. (c-d) XGBoost models distinguishing Cycling cells from all other tumor cells (c) or specifically the basal-like cells (d) within the HR+ CyTOF cohort. SHAP scores show feature contributions to classification, ranked in descending order. (e) Percentage of proliferating cells (assessed by the levels of pRb, as in Fig. S3) in each epigenetic sub-populations (Cycling, luminal and basal-like). #1284. Italian Media Cast Verdict on England Ace John Stones at Inter

There can be little doubting the quality of John Stones, one of the greatest defenders in Premier League history. After all, the Englishman lifted six top-flight titles with Manchester City before moving to Inter Milan this summer.

The 32-year-old arrived in Italy with a wealth of experience, having played 94 international matches for England. Add to that his Champions League final win in 2023 – coincidentally against Inter – and it looked like a great signing for the Serie A side.

However, only months into his spell abroad, it doesn't seem as though things are going so well for Stones.

Making £120,552 per week, Stones is the eighth-best-paid overseas Englishman right now, and there was much anticipation for his debut at Inter. The centre-back made his first appearance in pre-season against Real Betis, coming on for 20 minutes. That first showing had new fans excited, as they hyped up his ball-playing skills.

He actually scored the winner in that 1-0 victory, earning praise from Italian media outlet Gazzetta dello Sport, who handed the debutant a 7/10 rating for his short cameo, noting: "The timing and punctuality are English—a goal on his debut, without wasting a second—but what's most striking is the coordination of a seasoned striker."

When the season proper started, Stones made his official debut in Serie A, coming off the bench again for the 4-1 opening round win over Monza. Since then, though, he's played just three more times in all competitions – including in the loss against Real Madrid in the Champions League – starting just once.

The issue is familiar to anyone who has followed Stones in the past few years of his career. Indeed, injuries are to blame for his lack of game time.

An increasing number of footballers are playing with holes cut in their socks - here's why.

Stones has been sidelined with a hamstring strain since September, only just returning to the bench last weekend, as he was an unused sub in the 2-0 win over Como. Amid the fitness concerns, the Italian press are starting to express their doubts.

In an eye-opening update, it's now been suggested that the Englishman could be replaced at Inter in the January transfer market. Gazzetta dello Sport ask the damning question: 'What has happened to Stones?'

The article then claims he's 'under scrutiny' and states that if his fitness doesn't improve, his position in the team could be at risk when the winter window opens. The report adds:

"Various physical issues hang over him. In the last five years he has never managed more than 25 appearances in the Premier League: 14, 23, 16, 11 and just 9 last season. For now, he is stuck on three [in Serie A]."

Stones has not been called into Thomas Tuchel's squad for the November international break to face Croatia and Spain. As such, he can use the next few weeks to get himself up to full fitness, with Inter facing Atalanta on 22 November in their next match.

There are nine games in total for the Italian club until the January transfer market opens. It appears as though Stones has until then to cement his status in the team as a reliable option for Cristian Chivu.

#1283. Henry jokes Juventus spell is ‘when I started losing my hair’ before legendary Arsenal status

France and Arsenal legend Thierry Henry jokes about his time at Juventus when played out of position on the left wing. ‘That is when I started losing my hair!’

The 49-year-old wrote his name in the history books for the Premier League club and his country, including the World Cup, the European Championship, and two Golden Boot awards as top European scorer in 2003/04 and 2004/05.

Yet it was hard to predict that would’ve been the outcome when he had a brief spell at Juventus in 1999.

Henry scored just three goals with two assists in 20 appearances for the Bianconeri, most of them playing on the left wing.

He sat down with a French podcast and described the unusual and ill-fated experience with Italian football.

“I played on the left wing at Juventus,” said Henry on Kampo.

“As a winger, you need to move depending on where the ball goes. So basically, you’re the third attacker when you need to get to the back post, in the middle when you’re needed there, but then also have to track back and get into position with the five behind you when losing the ball.

“That is when I started losing my hair, by the way!”

Henry was sold to Arsenal that summer and the rest is history, going on to score 228 goals with 107 assists in 377 competitive games for the Gunners as a centre-forward.

It wasn’t Juventus, it was that chewing gum buffoon Ancelotti who failed at utilising Henry properly.

Ultimately it did not matter, as we sold even Zidane (whose wife wished to leave) and gained the world’s greatest GK, a Ballon d’Or winner in Nedved, Zambrotta, Thuram etc. in return.

@Pinturicchio then Ancelotti went to Milan. And won Scudetto, Coppa Italia also 2 (TWO) CL trophies. Btw, who did Milan beat in CL 2003 Final ? I forgot, could you remind us ?

#1282. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another important save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo

Had the former Newcastle United player scored so late in the game, the home crowd’s frustration may have boiled over. The point means Le Bris’ side have still not won a league game since August and remain bottom of the table. This is proving to be a tougher second season in the top flight for Sunderland, but if they keep playing like this, they will not remain in the bottom three for much longer.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

“It’s still a long journey, we know with this busy schedule playing in Europe, playing in the Carabao Cup, it’s a new challenge for us and we need to embrace it. I think we showed this afternoon that we are in this challenge, we want to embrace it and be ourselves and we probably deserved a bit more today.”

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

“It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some big saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1281. Top Sports Ranked By Average Daily Calorie Intake

Every sport requires a different level of maintenance in terms of nutrition; some are endurance sports, some are skill-based and others combine some combination of the two which ensures calorie intake varies widely.

At the top end of elite sport, the finest details can have the biggest impacts and what goes into an elite athlete's diet has developed into an extreme science the most demanding sports require an exceptional amount of calories per-day for maintenance and training and for match/tournament days.

However, there is a clear trend as to the higher forms on this list — it's centered around power and stamina, which should give away clues as to what will feature. Other factors come into play, such as refuelling mid-race/competition, sodium levels and much more.

Therefore, we've scouted and collated the top 10 calorific-heavy sports, ranked by daily calories consumed which, when compared to the calorie count of the average individual (2,500 kcal for men, 2,000 for women), goes to show what the body needs to perform at the elite level.

Six Premier League first-team players were tracked over a week of doubly labelled water by Liverpool John Moores researchers. They burned 3,566 calories a day and ate 3,186–3,789 on match days, 2,956 on training days.

It all hinges on match schedules, body makeup, position and load. Typically, footballers remain lean and light, boasting few bulging muscles in favour of agility, speed and constant running, which ensures they eat good carbohydrates, proteins and healthy fats — something which is attainable or even managed by healthy, regular gym-going individuals.

Lionel Messi is indisputably the GOAT when it comes to football, winning titles and breaking records wherever he goes, but how does he do it?

An Ironman race (a long-distance triathlon) is the most extreme mismatch in sport. A study of 18 Ironman athletes measured men burning 10,036 calories over the race and taking on 3,940 — finishing roughly 7,000 in the red on the day.

Since the gut cannot absorb anywhere near as much as the legs expend, it is an incredibly difficult task to manage especially since they also have to balance sodium intake too. Kristian Blummenfelt, the Olympic and Ironman champion, burns 7,000–8,500 a day in training and eats 4,900–6,400.

Thirty-one national-team skiers, weighed and recorded under supervision, ate 4,862 calories on a training day and 4,304 on a sprint competition day — the men's figures, from a 2019 study in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism.

Per hour really puts the sport into perspective, as skiers have to eat between 500 and 1,000+ calories per hour. It also varies across the type of flat terrain (500 – 650 calories per hour), hill/skate skiing (700 – 900 calories and racing (1,000–1,300).

Jordan Mazur, the 49ers' coordinator of nutrition, puts lineman requirements at 3,500 to 6,000 calories a day depending on whether a player is holding weight or building it. It varies due to a player's position, body size, and whether they need to build, lose, or maintain mass, with Joe Thomas revealing the amount of calories he had to eat as an offensive lineman.

Requirements are different for NFL skill players (wide receivers, defensive backs, quarterbacks), big skill players (linebackers, tight ends) and linemen (offensive and defensive linemen), with a high focus on carbohydrates and high protein.

This is the highest genuinely measured single-day intake on the list. During the 2025 Western States 100, a world-class runner finishing third in 14 hours 19 minutes took on 6,720 calories mid-race — while burning 16,104, confirmed by and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology.

He finished nearly 10,000 calories down. Whilst it is less dramatic than others on this list, the constant flow of movement over a long period of time drives up the calorie figures. Elite runners target 60g to 90g (and up to 120g with advanced gut training) of carbohydrates per hour using gels, chews, or sports drinks, as well as sodium-focused supplements and drinks to avoid hyponatremia, which leads to illness, passing out and long-term organ issues.

Heavyweight rowing has the highest routine training demand of any Olympic sport. A 2022 study of 14 elite open-class men put their requirement at 6,775 calories a day in a high-volume week, dropping to 4,626 in a taper.

Intake reportedly tracks it — around 6,970 a day for a national squad at peak volume, per two national-team dietitians writing in Current Sports Medicine Reports, though they label that data unpublished. Individual elite training sessions, roughly twice a day of intense on-water rowing, running, and heavy weightlifting, can burn up to 5,000 calories per session block alone.

The foundational study is still Wim Saris's 1989 work at Maastricht, which followed five riders through the Tour de France using doubly labelled water. They averaged 24.7 MJ eaten against 25.4 MJ burned — roughly 5,900 and 6,070 calories a day, sustained for three weeks. Mountain stages push the peak towards 9,000.

It also varies across different parts of races. There's flat/sprint stages (estimated 4,000 to 5,000 calories burned), mountain/hard stages (7,000 to 9,000+) and in-race fueling to consider as well, that amount to 400–500 calories/hour via gels, carb-mix drinks and rice cakes.

Professional sumo wrestlers are famously extremely powerful, and large. The amount of mass and force needed to succeed at the top level is remarkable, and the bulk comes from structure, not volume — and a consistent dose of the famous Japanese stew, chankonabe.

Reports describe them as being in a place of healthy obesity, with caloric intake ranging from approximately 5,000 to 8,000 kcal—and oftentimes exceeding 10,000. They burn incredible amounts due to their intense keiko (training), which can last up to six hours and begins early in the morning, and they typically skip breakfast, train in a fasted state, and then consuming a massive, nutrient-dense meal at midday—allowing for a metabolic cycle that promotes efficient weight gain while supporting muscle development.

Michael Phelps is the reason everyone thinks they know this number, and the number everyone knows is wrong. The 12,000-calorie breakfast that circulated during Beijing was never his figure. He corrected it himself in an interview with Olympics media: "It's just not true. Maybe eight to ten thousand calories per day."

Even corrected, it is enormous — the product of five to six hours in the water, six days a week, in a medium that strips body heat faster than air. Swimming's demand is relentless rather than explosive, and it runs year-round, ensuring that calories are high but the metabolic and muscular workrate ensure they are one of the most muscular-bound athletes out there.

Usain Bolt was in no doubt when naming the true Olympic GOAT between himself and legendary swimmer Michael Phelps.

The number at the top of this list is also the softest. Brian Shaw, four-time World's Strongest Man, walked Men's Journal through a seven-meal day totalling 12,019 calories — 705g of protein, 1,402g of carbohydrate — eaten across roughly 13 hours. "It's constant," he said. "All day long I have to eat, but it's part of the job."

Everything here is self-reported by men with an interest in the legend. Treat it as the ceiling of what's claimed, not what's proven. Eddie Hall, the former World's Strongest Man, claimed he would devour over '12,000 calories a day, sometimes up to 15,000', which perfectly rounds off this list.

England captain Harry Kane has praised Tottenham Hotspur academy graduate Will Lankshear and revealed that he has spoken to one of the striker’s former coaches about his goalscoring ability.

Speaking at England’s pre-match press conference ahead of Thursday’s UEFA Nations League encounter with Croatia, Kane was asked by GIVEMESPORT reporter Sam Cohen whether Lankshear could eventually succeed him as England’s first-choice centre-forward.

Lankshear has attracted attention following his goalscoring performances for Middlesbrough, with the former Tottenham youngster emerging as a potential candidate for future senior international recognition.

Kane, who also developed through Tottenham’s youth system before establishing himself as one of the world’s leading strikers, admitted he had been impressed by the youngster’s progress.

“I wouldn’t say I’ve followed his whole career. Obviously, this season it’s been hard not to hear about him, and he’s done extremely well at Middlesbrough,” Kane explained.

“I’ve spoken to a friend of mine who coached him here at the younger age groups and said that he’s a goalscorer. He knows how to score, he’s in the right place at the right time, he’s a great finisher.

We talk about a striker sometimes as having that goalscoring instinct, and I think he’s one of those players for sure.

Despite his praise, Kane was keen to stress the importance of allowing Lankshear to continue developing without unnecessary expectations.

“He’s still early in his development. I think what he’s doing right now is perfect for him, playing loads of games, scoring goals and getting confident.

“Whether he comes into the senior side, it’s down to Thomas. If he did, I’m sure he would learn loads here, surrounded by the attackers that we have.”

Will Lankshear for Middlesbrough this season

Kane, who was named the 2026 Ballon d’Or winner, also acknowledged the ongoing discussion surrounding who might eventually replace him as England’s number nine, but warned against placing that responsibility on a young player too early.

“It’s not a time to put too much pressure on him. I know there’s a lot of talk about who’s going to replace me when I’m not here anymore, but just let him do what he’s doing. I think it’s great for his development.”

The England captain revealed that he has crossed paths with Lankshear on a couple of occasions during their respective Tottenham careers, although the pair have not spent significant time together.

“I’ve come across him a couple of times, when he first signed here at Tottenham and then again when we played him in pre-season. I haven’t really spent much time with him.”

Kane concluded by expressing his willingness to help the youngster should he eventually receive an England call-up.

“As time goes on, if he continues, I’m sure he’ll be on the right path to get his chance.

“If he does make it into the senior team, it’ll be great to work with him and try and help him develop as a player.”

Kane’s comments provide an encouraging assessment of Lankshear’s potential, while making clear that the striker’s immediate priority should remain regular football and continued development at club level.

#1278. Defender David Bates recalled by Scotland after almost eight-year absence

Published: 13:34 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 13:45 EST, 11 November 2026

David Bates has been rewarded for a strong start to life in Turkey by earning a recall to the Scotland squad almost eight years after his last appearance for the national team.

The 30-year-old centre-back has been added to Sebastien Pocognoli’s group after Luis Binks withdrew ahead of the Nations League matches against North Macedonia on Friday and Switzerland on Monday.

Bates currently plays for Amedspor and has started all 11 matches this season as his club have soared to third in the Turkish Super Lig.

The defender won all four of his caps under Alex McLeish while playing for Hamburg in the 2018/19 campaign. His last appearance for the national team was in a 2-0 win over San Marino in a Euro 2020 qualifier in March 2019, in what also turned out to be McLeish’s last game in charge.

Former Rangers player Bates joined Amedspor in the summer after spending four years in Belgium with Mechelen and then Standard Liege following his Aberdeen exit in 2022.

Brondby captain Binks is the second centre-back to drop out of the squad initially named by Pocognoli last week, after Swansea’s Stephen Welsh sustained an injury and had to be replaced by Los Angeles FC’s Ryan Porteous last weekend.

David Bates playing for Scotland against Albania back in 2018

Sebastian Pocognoli is keen to create a winning culture in the Scotland squad

The head coach is viewing this month’s double-header as crucial to his preparations for the Euro 2028 qualification campaign, which could begin in March if Scotland are not involved in Nations League play-offs.

'I think that these two games are, if we start the qualification in March, the last package of games that we have to use to be ready for the March camp,' Pocognoli said.

'If it’s not the case (that the Euro campaign starts in March), we can play friendly games which can be useful for June, so we have more time to prepare. And maybe, if we are really strong in the next two games, maybe we have play-off games. That’s the ambition.

'These can be useful also for the process of the qualification. But if the qualification starts (in March), we need to be ready. That’s why this camp for me is crucial in terms of demanding to the players, try to impress me and do everything to improve.

'I believe if we want to go to the Euros and be successful, we need to build this qualification feeling by winning games and to build the best winning culture possible.'

#1277. Calafiori: ‘I feel older than I was’ in revamped Italy, Arsenal star ready for France

Riccardo Calafiori admits he is ‘starting to feel a little older than I was’ in an Italy squad that is skewing towards youth, as the Arsenal man sees ‘positive elements’ for facing France in the Nations League.

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

This is a head-to-head for the top of Group 1, as France are currently leading on 10 points, followed by Italy with seven and Belgium on six.

The top two both go into the quarter-finals of the Nations League, then hoping to make it into the Final Four, so Sunday’s trip to Brussels is the deciding factor.

“Having a packed stadium tomorrow will help us, but we know who we are up against, so I doubt it is possible for us to snub this test ahead of Sunday,” said Calafiori in his press conference.

“We’ll play our best tomorrow and then can think about the Belgium game.”

While initially Calafiori had been used as a central defender for Italy, the role he also had at Bologna, he has only recently begun to take the left-back spot for the Nazionale as well.

This is in the wake of his Premier League-winning performances in that position for the Arsenal defence.

“There are a lot of young players in this squad, so I am starting to feel a little older than I was,” added the 24-year-old.

“I have relatively little experience with the Nazionale, but in every match I try to inspire my team and be a leader, more through my actions on the field than any words I might use.”

Italy’s Nations League campaign had started with a disastrous 2-0 home defeat to Belgium, the debut on the return of Roberto Mancini to the bench, but it was followed by victories over Turkiye and an impressive 1-1 draw on French soil.

“I always said it was too early to see big changes and the work the coach was doing, but it certainly helps to get positive results,” noted Calafiori.

“It gives us some more confidence, and tomorrow is again an important test. It was tough for us in France, it was important that we come away with heads held high, and we achieved that.

“Tomorrow we are on home turf, the stadium is going to be packed, these are all positive elements that allow us to build more self-belief, albeit aware there is still a lot more work to do.”

There are reports Kylian Mbappé might miss this match through a muscular injury, only the latest setback after losing Marcus Thuram, Pierre Kalulu, Aurelien Tchaouameni, Manu Koné, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Ousmane Dembélé, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

“I think this is going to be a very complicated match. France have a lot of options available still, so it doesn’t change that much, and we must stay concentrated on ourselves,” assured Calafiori.

“There isn’t much time to prepare tactically and do things that are too different to at club level, so it’s more about determination and heart.”

The Arsenal defender had man-marked Michael Olise in the first meeting, so will he be doing the same again?

“I hope that I will have to do it tomorrow too. It’s always fascinating to face players of this level.”

#1276. Footage Shows  Moment Usman Nurmagomedov Jumped UFC’s Merab Dvalishvili

In a post which has now been deleted, UFC star Ilia Topuria has shared footage of the shocking moment Usman Nurmagomedov jumped Merab Dvalishvili. He also slammed the incident, calling out the cowardly behaviour.

Dvalishvili revealed today (11 November) that he had been jumped by the Russian fighter while in a hotel lobby ahead of his upcoming RAF Abu Dhabi match. He is scheduled to take on Marlon Moraes this Saturday, but the fight is now in doubt. Indeed, the 35-year-old has been left bruised and bloodied after his unexpected clash with Nurmagomedov, which comes weeks after his UFC 333 title fight with Petr Yan.

Dvalishvili has spoken out on the incident.

Topuria has now shared footage of the shocking moment Nurmagomedov jumped Dvalishvili. He also added his own comment as he called out the incident before later deleting his post on X, which had read:

"You’re a bunch of cowards, and you’ll be held accountable for what you’ve done. You’re anything but real men."

The wild footage has emerged elsewhere online, as it shows Nurmagomedov, one of the greatest Russian MMA fighters in history, approaching Dvalishvili from behind before swinging at the Georgian. A mass brawl ensues – watch the full clip below:

Revealing what had happened, Dvalishvili took to social media to show the aftermath of the incident. First, a caption read: "Was doing an interview for RAF in hotel lobby and Usman and his buddies came up from behind and started punching me and my young friend. Security was holding me - They kept kicking us when we were down like losers."

But in the clip, the 35-year-old spoke with pure emotion, as blood dripped down his face. He called out Nurmagomedov, explaining what went down:

“What a sneaky way, guys, just two of us came here in Abu Dhabi, and Usman Nurmagomedov and his friends came like snakes from behind, what kind of fighters are you? What kind of men are you? You came from behind, there is just two of us and you guys were prepared, what the f***?”

While still receiving medical care, he continued: “We bleed, we fight, we work, you guys are just sneaky guys, you are not real men, what the f***, if you want to fight let’s fight, we are fighters, bro. You guys came from behind, all of your friends waiting for us in a sneaky way. I knew what kind of guys you are… We were fighting like real men, 20 guys vs just two guys, we are warriors, you are p******."

#1275. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. The captain took exception to that, suggesting it was Carrick’s decision to play that way.

“It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence,” he said.

“That’s on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.”

Sam Dean has a prescription for Manchester United, based on Mikel Arteta’s turnaround at Arsenal.

He writes: “Once a football club is in a doom spiral, it is extremely difficult to get out of it. Manchester United have proved that for many years, with their collapse under Michael Carrick the latest sorry episode in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era.

“It is possible, though, for a big Premier League side to rebuild and return to the top. For inspiration, United need only look towards north London, where their old rivals Arsenal pulled themselves out of a similar, if not even more perilous, situation a few seasons ago.”

Read here to find out his specific suggestions, including to “be brutal” with overpaid stars. Carrick may have started today.

Eli Junior Kroupi is back on the bench for Bournemouth.

The forward was linked with a host of big clubs over the summer after his 13 league goals for his side last season.

A fractured metatarsal, coupled with Bournemouth’s reluctance to sell, mean he is still with the club, and he may get minutes today.

Bournemouth XI: Petrovic, Truffert, Cook, Hill, Evanilson, Adams, Silva, Smith, Tavernier, Kluivert, Rayan.

Subs: Di Gregorio, Soler, Brooks, Christie, Gannon-Doak, Diakite, Adli, Kroupi, Rodriguez.

Harry Maguire will captain United in Fernandes’ absence. Carrick has gone for a midfield of Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans ahead.

Matheus Cunha and Noussair Mazraoui have also been dropped after their shambolic performances against Como.

Matthijs de Ligt is back on the back although Como was his first start for 11 months after a chronic back injury.

Manchester United XI: Lammens, Dalot, Maguire, Yoro, Heaven, Baleba, Mount, Andrey Santos, Tielemans, Amad, Mbuemo.

Subs: Darlow, De Ligt, Martinez, Mazraoui, Fernandes, T. Fletcher, Cunha, Lacey, Zirkzee.

Today's United starting XI! 💪🇾🇪 https://t.co/i1amM2Zeih

Now the pressure is on, the conversation has already moved onto what next.

Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Antonio Conte, Julian Nagelsmann and Kieran McKenna are all in the frame to succeed Carrick if things go south soon.

What is striking is that none of the options are convincingly capable of such a vast, difficult task. That’s not their fault - it’s the owners’.

That’s the opinion of at least one managerial candidate linked with the United gig, should Carrick be given a healthy sum to walk away and take up an interest in koi carp.

With Fernandes dropped, that moment has probably got closer.

He writes: “A source close to one of United’s managerial candidates said: ‘It’s clear they need order and discipline. The dressing room is out of control and that is the first thing to fix.’

“That view was echoed by a friend of another candidate, who said: ‘The players talk too much. United is one of the biggest clubs in the world and that has to be respected.’”

Carrick had hinted as much in his pre-weekend press conference.

Fernandes’ zesty outburst, where he said United’s tactical failings against Como were “on the manager and staff” has understandably seen his position as United captain questioned.

Carrick did not rule it out, saying: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1274. Liverpool Confidential: Why Will Wright is the breakout star of Reds academy - LEWIS STEELE reveals club's plans for 6ft 3in hat-trick hero, his rise from Euxton Villa to Anfield and why coaches believe he's Andoni Iraola's next big thing

Published: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 16:17 EST, 11 November 2026

On Will Wright’s last two trips abroad, he has needed to check in some extra baggage on the return flight.

Two UEFA Youth League away games, two hat-tricks and a pair of match balls to go with them. It’s now 13 goals for the season for 18-year-old Wright after his treble in a 5-3 win at Fenerbahce last week, and he has earned a first England youth call-up to boot.

Another hat-trick in one of those three games for the Young Lions? You wouldn’t bet against it – but Wright is used to these rapid rises.

Eighteen months ago, the 6ft 3in striker signed for Liverpool on a Friday, passed his driving test at 8am the next morning and then played for the first team the day after in a friendly at Anfield.

Now, the former Salford City striker is the name on everyone’s lips around Kirkby – with many thinking he could be the next cab off the rank from Liverpool’s famed academy.

Will Wright has lit up the academy goal charts this season for Liverpool, scoring a pair of hat-tricks in the UEFA Youth League

The Under 19s captain struck a brilliant treble against Fenerbahce last week to take his season tally to 13

Wright was first spotted by Salford scouts when playing for local side Euxton Villa, a ninth-tier club who have two England internationals among their alumni in David Unsworth and Sam Johnstone. Wright’s father, Mark, coached at Euxton and is an ex-professional for Preston North End.

It was an unusual path as most future stars are normally signed up by their mid-teens but Wright had injury issues amid a growth spurt that took him to the lanky frame that now bullies defenders. He had heel issues and has worked with a specialist on fascia problems.

Wright made his Salford debut in an 8-0 FA Cup defeat by Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City in January 2025 but scouts had already been alerted by his 50-goal haul at youth level. Arsenal, led by then-academy chief Per Mertesacker, launched an aggressive approach to sign him.

At one point, Liverpool signalled to Wright and Salford that they were pulling out of the deal, given Arsenal’s interest was so advanced. But the Reds soon returned to prevent the Gunners signing their next ‘Wrighty’.

The deal was worth peanuts in the grand scheme of things, around £300,000. It is good money for League Two Salford, though, and they will be set for additional payments for first-team appearances, honours and future national team caps.

Wright, who has a younger brother and is a Nike athlete, is a throwback No9. It is easy to reach for comparisons to current players but the way he combines pace, power and prolific finishing is not too dissimilar to Erling Haaland.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September, receiving possession on the touchline around halfway, tricking his way past two defenders and curling a sumptuous effort into the top corner.

He is the captain of the Under 19s team and I have watched him play live several times, including one game last season where he was clearly targeted by Atletico Madrid defenders. The striker was clattered, suffered a medial ligament injury and was sidelined for several months.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up

He has returned with a vengeance, with a hat-trick against LASK last month and then last week's effort against Fenerbahce. What impressed more in the latter was not his goals – one a penalty, the other two both true poachers’ finishes – but his assist.

Wright was on a hat-trick at the time but, instead of shooting, he played a ball to Finn Inglethorpe – son of academy director Alex – to score. Earlier, Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie had argued over who was to take a penalty. Wright won the row and scored.

Under 21s boss Rob Page told the pair later that he would rather them show hunger to score and passion rather than shy away. Page is a huge fan of Wright and said: ‘There was a real maturity about his performance. One of the parts of the development for all the forwards is being unselfish in their actions.

‘As much as he wants to see the headlines and be successful himself, it is all about sharing that. Will has done that really well today with a hat-trick, a complete performance.’

Pressed on how far away Wright is from the first team, Page replied: ‘He doesn’t have to worry about that. Just bring the best version of yourself every day in training, give absolutely everything in games as he does. The rest will take care of itself.

‘He’s got a great support around him. His family are very supportive. Alex (Inglethorpe) is there to lean on, he’s got myself and Jay (Spearing, academy coach). He never gets carried away.’

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up. They have also worked on his off-the-ball runs to the back post.

So, what next? It is understood a January loan is being considered. Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons. His agent was at the AXA Training Centre on Tuesday and there will be no shortage of clubs willing to take him on.

Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons

Wright got six minutes off the bench against Como in a friendly at Anfield in August, coming on for Alexander Isak up front

Andoni Iraola will be consulted, too. He has called up the likes of Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and Luke Chambers this season and is eager to use young stars.

Iraola is in frequent dialogue with youth staff such as Page, Inglethorpe, plus Luiz Fernando Iubel who is often cited as the ‘link’ between the academy and first team.

The Brazilian has been spotted at several academy games this term, including for Wright’s hat-trick in Turkey where Iubel sat alongside sporting director Julian Ward and loans manager Gary Probert.

Whether a first-team breakthrough comes now or in the future, the future for Wright looks bright.

Dominik Szoboszlai’s participation with Hungary this week remains in the balance with the national team doing all they can to get their captain fit for crunch games.

The Hungarians take on Georgia and Northern Ireland in must-win Nations League matches – and may have to go without their star man. Szoboszlai hurt his knee in the win at Crystal Palace and, after an injury-hit six weeks, could do with a rest.

But he will try his best to be fit for national team duty and a decision will not be made until the 11th hour.

It comes after Virgil van Dijk pulled out of Dutch duty with a minor muscle issue. It is believed he has been managing the problem for at least a month and was surprised to be substituted on to the field against LASK — which might explain the team conceding three after he came on!

Virgil van Dijk (left) has pulled out of international duty and Dominik Szoboszlai (right) could be set to follow him

Confidential readers will recall our musings on Harvey Elliott a fortnight ago, with Valencia sources telling us that the La Liga outfit might consider cancelling his loan in January.

The English midfielder had struggled in Spain for fitness and form. He was then sent off against Villarreal but, as we reported, Valencia would give him another chance to prove his worth.

He has started well, scoring a free-kick in what was his first start for any club in 285 days. It was part of a notable 6-0 win in the Copa del Rey.

Elliott ran over to fans and put his arms aloft appearing to apologise, which adds to his comments a week ago about the red card where he said: ‘I made a mistake and I’m truly sorry. It won’t happen again.’

#1273. Pochettino Already Has His Own Harry Kane Waiting at Man Utd in Fernandes

Mauricio Pochettino is closing in on the Manchester United job after GIVEMESPORT revealed that the two parties have reached an agreement in principle on personal terms.

Now, Man United must pay the Argentine's $10m release clause to prise him away from the USMNT, with an extra fee needed on top to take his coaching staff to Old Trafford too.

While all of this is going on, the Red Devils' hierarchy are still yet to sack Michael Carrick, but the 45-year-old is expected to be dismissed following talks between Omar Berrada, Jason Wilcox and Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week.

Berrada and Wilcox have recommended the appointment of Pochettino, who has been out of club football for two-and-a-half years after being sacked by Chelsea in the summer of 2024.

Should Pochettino's appointment be confirmed, there is no doubt that the 54-year-old is taking on a big job at Old Trafford, given how poor the club has been this term.

Expectations were high that the team would continue to build under the leadership of Carrick after they were so impressive in the first half of 2026, but instead they are in the Premier League relegation zone having won just one of their 10 matches this season.

Elsewhere, they were also knocked out of the EFL Cup after losing a 2-0 lead to be beaten 3-2 by Brighton and Hove Albion at the Theatre of Dreams, while they have also lost two of their four fixtures in the Champions League too.

United produced fantastic comebacks in their previous two games against AS Roma and Aston Villa, but it wasn't enough to convince Wilcox or Berrada that Carrick should remain in the dugout for the trip to Liverpool after the international break.

United will hope that Pochettino is at Anfield, and work will immediately begin on how he is going to turn their fortunes around, with seven weeks to go until the January transfer window opens.

Pochettino had great success with the likes of Harry Kane at Tottenham previously, and he actually has his own version of the England captain waiting for him at Old Trafford, and it's not Benjamin Sesko.

Kane was Pochettino's talisman during his time in charge at Spurs, with the England captain scoring more than 30 goals in a season on three occasions under the Argentine's leadership.

Kane has made no secret of the fact that the 54-year-old has had a big influence on his career, which has led to him winning the Ballon d'Or award in recent weeks.

Pochettino may not have someone on Kane's level when it comes strikers waiting for him at Old Trafford, but he does have Bruno Fernandes.

The Portugal international's decline this season has been one of the biggest mysteries of United's drop-off in recent months, but there is no doubting the quality and influence he has on this team, just like Kane had at Tottenham.

United scored 69 Premier League goals last season, and Fernandes either scored or assisted 30 of those, also registering the Premier League record for most assists in a single season.

The 32-year-old has been a shadow of the player he was last term this time around, but he still has six goals and four assists in 14 appearances.

United's record this season when Fernandes didn't score or assist

All of those goals and assists have come in four of those 14 appearances, with the Red Devils failing to win any of the 10 games where he has provided zero.

If Pochettino is going to get United back up the standings in the coming weeks, he needs to build his team around Fernandes and get the Portuguese star back to his best.

If he does, he has proven before that he can be as influential as Kane was in a Tottenham shirt for him.

Manchester United are attempting to finalise an agreement for him to replace Michael Carrick

#1272. Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive new patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

The heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

We generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs showed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

a,b, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice (aged 10 weeks) were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 1 week at 24 °C. Representative images of BAT IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) (a), and quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both (b). n = 6 per group. c,d, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 3 days or 1 week at 6 °C. c, Representative images of IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red) and DAPI (blue) in iWAT. d, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 4 per group. e, Representative IF staining for UCP1 (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) in human supraclavicular BAT. f, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs that are positive for UCP1+ only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 5 per group. g, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs from WT mice were reverse-transfected with H6pd Dicer-substrate small interfering RNAs (dsiRNAs) or control dsiRNAs and collected after 2 days. RT–qPCR analysis of H6pd, Rgs2, Hsd11b1 and Ucp1 mRNA levels. n = 3 per group. h–j, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice were injected with lentivirus overexpressing H6PD or mCherry as a control into BAT. h, After 2 weeks, H6PD and β-actin protein levels were analysed using western blotting (WB). i, Representative IF staining of BAT for GFP (green), perilipin (red) and DAPI (blue). j, Quantification of the BA-H cell percentage. For j, n = 5 (mCherry) and n = 4 (H6PD). Statistics were computed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (b, d and f), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (g (H6pd and Hsd11b1)) or unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (g (Rgs2 and Ucp1) and j); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. For b, d, f, g and j, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 25 μm (a (right), c (bottom)), 50 μm (a (left), c (top) and e) and 100 μm (i).

To enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes showed selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

We next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further showed TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently showed that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

We next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.
