#1267. Ryan Porteous reckons people are still reading too much into THAT red card against Germany that made him a pariah with Tartan Army

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 17:47 EST, 11 November 2026

From a distance, it was difficult not to look at the fall-out from Ryan Porteous’ rash challenge on Ilkay Gundogan in the opening match of Euro 2024 and draw sweeping conclusions.

Coming on the cusp of half-time in the Allianz Arena, the defender’s two-footed lunge on the German midfielder earned him a straight red card with a two-game suspension soon following.

The moment of madness led to Kai Havertz giving the host nation a three-goal lead from the penalty spot at the interval. By time-up, Steve Clarke’s depleted side had lost 5-1. The self-belief which they’d brought into the tournament was fast evaporating, too.

While no one doubted the scale of the task Scotland faced before a ball was kicked that evening, Porteous’ actions made the mission impossible. As a consequence, the former Hibernian defender found forgiveness hard to come by.

Those irate Scotland supporters who demanded that he suffered for his folly were granted their wish.

A player who’d featured in seven of the eight qualifiers disappeared from view thereafter, briefly emerging from international exile as a sub against Greece in March of last year, yet posted missing again throughout the World Cup qualifiers and from the tournament itself.

Ryan Porteous' red card gave Scotland a mountain to climb in Euro 2024 defeat to Germany

It seemed only logical to deduce that Clarke had also shared the anger of the Tartan Army and that the player’s status as a pariah was down to his simmering fury at the humiliation that woeful tackle caused.

Porteous always believed the matter wasn’t quite as clear cut as most imagine it to be.

‘I think people maybe read too much into that,’ said the 27-year-old.

‘In the conversations I had with Steve after the Euros and in the next qualifying campaign, the red card against Germany never came up.

‘We had loads of conversations, both when I was in and out of the squad.

‘Those are the things that people obviously don’t see.

‘They maybe think Steve Clarke is the type of person who wouldn’t phone you or text you. But he did. We spoke loads to be honest. He was really honest with me.

‘I texted him when he left the role and he messaged back eager to see me get back in the squad.

The Scotland defender was shown a straight red for this challenge on Ilkay Gundogan

‘Everyone knows Steve is a manager who, if he picks a squad and they do well for them and they get to a tournament, he’s loyal.

‘In terms of the conversations we had during those latter stages of qualification, he just told me to keep doing what I was doing.

‘He was honest and told me I would probably need some of those lads to drop off in form if I was going to make it. You have to respect that.

‘I went to a tournament in the Euros in 2024 and you had someone like John Souttar who missed out. So, I know what it feels like on both sides.’

Porteous, to his credit, doesn’t appear to be bitter about how matters unfolded post-Germany.

Regardless of the true importance of the red card in his status changing from mainstay to that of an outcast, he accepts that fairness and the game do not always walk hand-in-hand.

‘That happens in football, it’s just one of those things,’ he shrugged.

‘I’ve had a career where I’m up and down, I’m left and right, you just need to bounce back from it.

‘It was a fantastic experience for me to be part of that run we went on. It helped me grow massively. I don’t look at it as being unfair.’

Porteous has now returned from period in wilderness ahead of North Macedonia clash

By the time he’d moved from Watford to Los Angeles to sign for LAFC last August, he’d already reconciled himself with the fact that his Scotland career was in cold storage. The consolation was that this afforded him a different perspective on the November night when history was made.

‘It’s maybe tough when the squads were getting announced and then a couple of days after that,’ he reflected.

‘But then as soon as you’re watching the games, you just become a fan straight away again and want the team to do well.

‘I probably hadn’t experienced that for a while. It was actually good for me watching the World Cup qualifiers - because I was able to sit and watch them straight after training because of the time difference.

‘When Kenny McLean scored from the halfway line (against Denmark) I had half the team in LA shouting and screaming for Scotland! It was brilliant.’

While he’d clearly have preferred to still have been at the heart of things, his new life on the other side of the Atlantic allowed him to sample what it all meant to an invading army in the summer.

‘I had a few days off at one point and I went out to Boston,’ he explained.

‘I didn’t manage to go to the games, but I saw my friends and family who were over and we went to the baseball as well.

‘Being in that fan environment, it just gives you that extra little bit of hunger to get back.’

Porteous in action for Scots at training as they prepare for North Macedonia showdown

The profile of the MLS always offered him that possibility. Porteous’s club counts Gareth Bale and Olivier Giroud among its former players. Son Heung-min is the current star in Tinseltown. The Scot played against - and defeated - Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami in February. In such moments, one can feel a long way from Midlothian.

‘I think I could be the first guy ever to go from Dalkeith to LA! It’s very hot. They are actually choking for a bit of rain just now.

‘I used to blame the East Mains wind for losing my hair, but it’s still falling out over in LA even without the wind.

‘(John) McGinn has already peppered me after seeing a couple of my interviews over there.

‘I’ve had to change my accent so that people can understand me over there.

‘For the first couple of months, everyone was asking me to repeat myself. But it’s an incredible place and I’m enjoying every second.’

LAFC finished sixth in the Western Conference this year, good enough to book a slot in the forthcoming play-offs.

Porteous’ part in that meant he was firmly in Sebastien Pocognoli’s thoughts when Stephen Welsh suffered an untimely injury ahead of the two final Nations League matches.

Over two years on from that hideous night in Munich, this feels like a deserved opportunity to change the narrative which has surrounded him ever since.

‘People pay their money and they can have their opinions on me,’ he said.

‘I’ve got thick skin now. It’s never been an issue for me in terms of managers having to pull me aside and have a word or anything like that.

‘I’m in a good place now. Whatever criticism I get, it only makes me grow stronger as a person.

‘Hopefully, I can come back now a better player than what people saw before.

‘I have still got my strengths and I feel like I’ve added to my game as well from being in different leagues and different environments.’

#1266. Man Utd Could Target Antonee Robinson, He Says Pochettino is ‘Top-Class’

Mauricio Pochettino is in line to become the next Manchester United head coach. The Reds are preparing to appoint the Argentine with Michael Carrick facing the sack following a dismal start to the season, and they are ready to back him in the January transfer window too, according to GIVEMESPORT senior correspondent Ben Jacobs.

United have won just one of their opening 10 Premier League matches and sit inside the relegation zone going into the November international break. CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox recommended a change in the dugout to Sir Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS during a meeting in Monaco on Tuesday, with Carrick's time at Old Trafford coming to an end.

Pochettino has since been identified as Carrick's replacement with United in the process of triggering his £7.5million release clause at the United States national team. The Argentine has been with the USMNT for the last two years and was in charge for the home 2026 World Cup, a tournament in which his nation lost in the Round of 16, following a 4-1 defeat to Belgium.

Despite having three-and-a-half years left on his contract, Pochettino has now decided to leave and move to United, and he could bring one of his USMNT players with him to Old Trafford.

Antonee Robinson is the player in question, with United keen to strengthen at left-back and long admirers of the Fulham man.

Diogo Dalot has deputised in Luke Shaw's absence on the left side of the back four, but has struggled and was subject to strong criticism following Sunday's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa. Shaw suffered a muscle injury last month, and although he is nearing a return to full fitness, United are expected to look at adding a new left-back in January.

Speaking on the latest episode of GMS' Market Madness podcast on Tuesday, our senior football correspondent, Ben Jacobs, hinted that Robinson is someone United might look at in the January transfer window, having recaptured his form at Fulham this season.

However, the Whites might decide to cash in on the 29-year-old given their difficult start of the season and the fact he has just 18 months to run on his contract at Craven Cottage.

Jacobs said: 'There's still a chance that with Man United we see a left-back [targeted in January]. They've looked at David Raum in the past. Antonee Robinson might be a player that a few clubs look at in the winter market, especially if it looks like Fulham are struggling, and there may be some opportunism there.

"So we will get some winter movement, but there's just two bits of caution. The first is that this inflated market from the summer may bleed over into the winter and put a lot of clubs off spending mid-season. And the second broader point is that the winter market is always a seller's market, not a buyer's market."

Speaking in a press conference on Tuesday, USMNT left-back Robinson was asked about Pochettino amid speculation linking the ex-Tottenham and Chelsea boss about becoming the new man in the dugout at United.

“That news got sprung on all of us like the rest of the world,” Robinson said. “Similar things have happened in the past after the World Cup where huge teams lose a manager and they start looking at possible candidates.

For us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means, you know, we are very lucky and we know that we are working with a top-class manager.

“For us to have a manager who gets linked to those sorts of jobs means we’re very lucky we’re working with a top-level manager, he added. “But that never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it’s the World Cup or whether it’s this camp.”

USMNT face Haiti in a Concacaf Nations League fixture on Saturday and Robinson is preparing like business as usual despite talk around Pochettino moving to United. “As a soccer player, I’m pretty used to sort of fast-changing environments,” Robinson added. “So we’re all very good at just focusing on the next task at hand and the next game coming up.

“And for me personally, I don’t really look at him being in limbo with jobs. It’s just focusing on we’ve got a game for the weekend and I’m going to do everything I can to be ready to play for him.”

As well as Robinson, David Raum is another left-back United are looking at. The German, 28, has starred for RB Leipzig in recent years and has been capped 40 times by his national team.

#1265. Manna: ‘Napoli will be ready in January, did not spend wisely last season’

Napoli director Giovanni Manna assures they have ‘clear ideas’ on how to improve Max Allegri’s squad in January, but admits ‘perhaps we didn’t spend our money wisely’ last season.

The Partenopei are struggling badly both in Serie A and the Champions League, with calls for the coach to be sacked, perhaps rescued only by the injury crisis decimating his team.

President Aurelio De Laurentiis seems determined to stick with Allegri and that means giving him more alternatives in the January transfer window.

“We have clear ideas on how to improve, correct and complete the squad, and we will ensure that we are ready in January,” director of sport Manna told Radio Kiss Kiss.

It is very likely that several players will be moved on, above all Lorenzo Lucca and Noa Lang, who have failed to live up to expectations following big money moves.

“Last season we spent a lot, but perhaps we didn’t spend our money wisely, and I say that being fully aware of the criticism I deserve for that. The President and I never held back when it came to investments, but we did have to respect certain financial parameters, so over the summer opted for more of an austerity approach.

“Nobody banned us from making moves, but some situations were stalled and that blocked others in the transfer market. We’ll be ready in January.”

Manna was slightly reassured by the 1-1 draw with Lazio that saw Napoli go into the break for international duty.

“I saw an encouraging reaction in the second half, showing the kind of energy required to get out of the current situation, so we are hopeful things will be better once we get a few players recovered from injury.

“We are well aware of the situation, and we are not happy with how the season has started. Aside from injuries, if we did something wrong or made incorrect evaluations, we are here to work and fix it.

“It’s important to find a sense of calm and not try to experience every game as if it’s the last, as that doesn’t help.”

There have been reports that Napoli are pursuing Torino winger Alessio Cacciamani, who had already been targeted by Roma over the summer.

“He is certainly an interesting prospect who impressed at Juve Stabia and is showing his potential, but that’s a long way from saying he’ll come to Napoli,” replied Manna.

“There are many players we are keeping an eye on, and he is one of the most interesting young Italian players right now.”

Monza centre-forward Gustavo Varela is another name mentioned with regards to a potential January swoop from Napoli.

“He is a good player, but right now we have Lucca, who is young and can cover that role. Then we’ll see, based on who leaves, what will happen. He is certainly doing well, but I doubt Monza will want to sell a player like that in January, seeing as they are fighting for their Serie A safety.

“Napoli have not made any steps for Varela so far, we’ve done nothing.”

#1264. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1263. USMNT Want Pep Guardiola As Mauricio Pochettino Nears Man Utd Job

GIVEMESPORT understands that Michael Carrick will likely be informed tomorrow (Thursday, 12 November) that he has been sacked from his position as Manchester United head coach. It looks as though Mauricio Pochettino will take over at Old Trafford.

The Argentine has past Premier League experience, having coached London clubs Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur. Pochettino – who has been linked with the role since 2019 – wants the job, and it's understood that terms are now being finalised to bring him back to England.

However, he is currenlty in charge of the United States men's national team and will need to be replaced if a move to Man Utd is completed. With that in mind, it appears as though US soccer are now planning a highly ambitious move.

While Pochettino only signed a new long-term contract with the USMNT after the 2026 World Cup, GMS understands that the deal contains a $10m (£7.4m) release clause. That compensation will leave the US with a fair bit of cash splashing about as they look to hire their next manager.

Landing Pochettino in 2024, off the back of spells at European powerhouses Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain, was seen as highly ambitious at the time, but their next move could top even that.

A blunt verdict from Richard Keys spotlights a high-profile alternative to Mauricio Pochettino as Michael Carrick's replacement.

GMS understands US soccer want Pep Guardiola as their next men's national team coach. The Catalan is among the greatest managers of all time, but is currently out of work, having left Manchester City in the summer.

He spent a decade in England, from 2016 to 2026, winning six Premier League titles and the Champions League. It's worth noting that Guardiola's tenure partially overlapped with the period in which Man City were found to have breached Premier League financial rules (2009 to 2018), which may diminish some of his achievements.

Even so, the 55-year-old remains one of the best managers in world football, having also enjoyed considerable success at past clubs. His Barcelona side, with MLS star Lionel Messi, between 2009 and 2011 is widely regarded as the greatest football team of all time.

It probably bodes well for Man Utd that the USMNT are already weighing up options to replace Pochettino, with that sort of movement suggesting the Argentine's move to Old Trafford will be greenlit in the near future.

However, the US are likely to face one major issue in any pursuit of Guardiola. The iconic manager is currently on a break from football, and it's unclear when he wants to return to the dugout. Italy approached him to take over as their manager earlier in 2026, but were rejected.

At the time, Italian football federation president Giovanni Malago told La Repubblica (Via The Athletic): “Pep was honest. He took a sabbatical, partly for family reasons, but if he’d done anything, he would have done it with us.”

It remains to be seen if Guardiola's stance has softened in the time since.

#1262. Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 372–377 (2026) Cite this article

Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1. Aqueous metal–iodine batteries offer a promising platform for large-scale energy storage by combining earth-abundant electrode materials, aqueous electrolytes and conversion-type iodine chemistry2,3. Unlike intercalation-type positive electrodes, iodine positive electrodes store charge by reversible valence-state changes, offering access to multi-electron redox chemistry with increased capacity and redox potential4. Most studies have focused on the two-electron I−/I0 redox couple, with a theoretical capacity of 211 mAh g−1 at a redox potential of 0.54 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode10. Extending iodine conversion to the successive I−/I0/I+ redox couples doubles the theoretical capacity to 422 mAh g−1 while introducing the I0/I+ redox process at a higher redox potential of 1.07 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode11. However, despite this potential, achieving reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge3,7.

The crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways. Electron-deficient I+ is strongly electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water, resulting in hydrolysis and poor reversibility in aqueous environments9,12. Previous studies have achieved four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries by stabilizing reactive I+ through interhalogen complexes (for example, ICl2 or IBr2) in highly concentrated chloride- or bromide-containing electrolytes5,6,13. In these systems, electrophilic I+ coordinates with two nucleophilic halide ions (Cl− or Br−) through non-covalent interactions8,14. However, at water-enriched interfaces, hydration of nucleophilic species (Nuc) competes with these interactions and destabilizes I+ complexes (Fig. 1a). Highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes mitigate this competition by reducing water activity and increasing halide availability, but their high salt contents and corrosivity constrain broader implementation (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), necessitating new electrolyte chemistry and a mechanistic framework that move beyond reliance on halogen-containing electrolytes and conventional interhalogen stabilization5,8.

a, The mechanism of the competition between halogen bond and hydrogen bond. b, The conventional interhalogen stabilization mechanism in highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes. c, The KA–PA–Nuc framework levering anionic chemistry and halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free electrolytes. IHP, inner Helmholtz plane; OHP, outer Helmholtz plane.

Given the competition between I+ stabilization and hydration at water-enriched interfaces, overcoming this challenge requires simultaneous regulation of the interfacial environment and water–Nuc interactions. Anionic chemistry offers a powerful lever to coordinate these interfacial and molecular interactions15,16,17,18. Herein we establish a kosmotropic anion (KA)–polar anion (PA)–Nuc electrolyte framework for reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes (Fig. 1c). Systematic experiments and theoretical calculations reveal how the synergistic effects of PAs and KAs coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, thereby stabilizing interfacial electrochemical behaviour and promoting reversible four-electron iodine conversion. The applicability of this electrolyte framework is demonstrated across four halogen-free Nuc (urea, acetamide, pyridine and nicotinamide) and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Beyond establishing a halogen-free electrolyte chemistry, this work reveals how electrolyte chemistry governs iodine conversion across interfacial, molecular and electrochemical scales, providing a mechanistic basis for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

Stabilizing I+ against hydrolysis is essential for reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous electrolytes. Previous studies have relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes for interhalogen stabilization19,20, whereas more recent studies have explored specific additive-halogen nucleophilic substitution reactions21,22. These approaches primarily address I+ stabilization through specific molecular interactions, whereas how electrolyte chemistry collectively regulates the interfacial microenvironment, molecular stabilization and the resulting iodine conversion pathways remains less understood. This work establishes a mechanistic framework that integrates anionic chemistry with halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, strong PAs establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interface, whereas KAs weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding to facilitate halogen-bond stabilization of I+. These complementary effects underpin the halogen-free KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, whose composition was subsequently optimized (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4) and exhibits sufficient electrochemical stability (Supplementary Fig. 5) for four-electron iodine conversion.

a, Molecular interplay governed by anionic chemistry and halogen bonding. b, Cyclic voltammetry profiles of iodine conversion reaction using urea as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. c, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using acetamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. d, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using nicotinamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. e–g, Corresponding GCD profiles for b–d at 1 A g−1, respectively. All electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework was validated in aqueous Zn–I2 batteries across four different Nuc (Supplementary Fig. 6). Electron-deficient I+ can interact with two electron-rich Nuc molecules to form linear Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. These halogen bonds provide the molecular basis for I+ stabilization, as supported by Nuc-free controls, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and theoretical calculations23 (Supplementary Figs. 7–11). Using urea (U) as a representative Nuc, KA–U exhibits only the I−/I0 redox process, whereas PA–U enables further I0/I+ oxidation but with poor reversibility (Fig. 2b,e). The excessive capacity at the second charge plateau is attributed to irreversible iodine oxidation coupled with parasitic water oxidation (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Combining KA and PA in KA–PA–U produces two reversible redox peaks and corresponding charge–discharge plateaus, demonstrating their synergistic role in enabling reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion (Supplementary Fig. 14). Replacing U with acetamide (AE), nicotinamide (NA) or pyridine (PD) shows the same phenomenon, with reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion achieved only in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes, including under identical ionic strength conditions, indicating the broad applicability of this electrolyte framework (Fig. 2c,d,f,g and Supplementary Figs. 15–18).

To isolate the role of PAs in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, SO42− was maintained as the KA, whereas structurally related CF3SO3−, CF3COO− or CH3COO− was introduced as the second anion. Density-functional-theory calculations reveal a polarity sequence of CH3COO− > CF3COO− > CF3SO3− (Supplementary Fig. 19), providing a basis for examining how anion polarity influences interfacial behaviours24,25. Molecular-dynamics simulations show similar water-enriched bulk environments across the three electrolytes (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), but distinct interfacial structures (Fig. 3d). CH3COO− reduces the interfacial water density while increasing anion enrichment, whereas CF3COO− and CF3SO3− retain high interfacial water intensity (Fig. 3e,f). In situ attenuated total reflection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy further supports this interfacial redistribution. The δ-HOH vibration at 1,640 cm−1 remains pronounced with CF3SO3− or CF3COO− (Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Fig. 23), but is suppressed with CH3COO− alongside pronounced anion-associated signals26,27,28,29 (Fig. 3i). Notably, highly concentrated ZnCl2 retains a water-enriched interface despite its water-deficient bulk environment (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Differential capacitance measurements indicate stronger interfacial adsorption of CH3COO− than of CF3COO− and CF3SO3− (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27), linking preferential adsorption of strongly PAs to the formation of a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment30.

a, Cyclic voltammetry profiles in electrolytes with different anions. b, GCD profiles in electrolytes with different anions. The rising and falling voltage curves correspond to charging and discharging processes, respectively. c, Cycling stability in electrolytes with different anions, with upper and lower curves representing Coulombic efficiency and specific capacity, respectively. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, Schematic snapshot of the interfacial structure in the electrolyte with CH3COO−. e, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of H2O in electrolytes with different anions, with the grey shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. f, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of anions in electrolytes with different anions, with the pink shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. g–i, In situ ATR-IR spectra in the electrolytes with CF3SO3− (g), CF3COO− (h) and CH3COO− (i).

These polarity-dependent interfacial structures lead to distinct iodine conversion behaviour. CF3SO3− shows a negligible I0/I+ process, whereas CF3COO− enables I0/I+ oxidation but with limited reversibility. By contrast, CH3COO− supports reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion with improved stability and capacity (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 28). In situ ultraviolet–visible spectra and micro-computed-tomography analyses further link these differences to iodine species distribution, showing that CH3COO− confines iodine species within the electrode and suppresses their migration into the bulk electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Together, these results establish a mechanistic relationship between anion polarity and the resulting water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment that governs the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Building on the understanding of PAs, the critical role of KAs in the KA–PA–Nuc framework was further explored. Nuc stabilize I+ through electron-rich nitrogen or oxygen centres, which also interact with water through hydrogen bonding and therefore compete with halogen-bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 31). Inspired by anion-specific effects on water–solute interactions, SO42−, CH3COO−, NO3−, CF3SO3− and ClO4− were compared in the same PA–Nuc baseline31,32,33,34 (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these anions have little effect on the initial capacity, they produce different cycling stability (Supplementary Fig. 33). SO42− maintains nearly overlapping galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) profiles, whereas CH3COO− and CF3SO3− show intermediate cycling stability and ClO4− undergoes rapid deterioration (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 34), giving a stability sequence of SO42− > CH3COO− > CF3SO3− > ClO4−. NO3− deviates from this sequence owing to its limited electrochemical stability within the applied voltage range35 (Supplementary Fig. 35a,b).

a, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing SO42− at different cycles. b, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing CF3SO3− at different cycles. c, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing ClO4− at different cycles. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, 2H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. e, 1H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. f, 13C NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. g, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing SO42−. h, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing CF3SO3−. i, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing ClO4−.

NMR spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations reveal the molecular origin of these electrochemical differences. The 2H chemical shift follows SO42− > CH3COO− > NO3− > CF3SO3− > ClO4− (Fig. 4d), indicating progressively stronger anion-induced water polarization and restructuring of the aqueous hydrogen-bond network36,37. These differences in water–anion coordination translate into distinct water–Nuc interactions. The corresponding 15N chemical shifts, together with the inverse trends observed in 1H and 13C chemical shifts, indicate that KAs such as SO42− polarize hydration water and thereby weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding, whereas chaotropic anions such as ClO4− interact directly with the Nuc backbone and facilitate Nuc hydration32 (Fig. 4e,f, and Supplementary Figs. 32 and 36–38). Nuc solubility measurements, two-dimensional 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) NMR spectra, and calculated Nuc–water distances and hydrogen-bond populations further support this interpretation (Fig. 4g–i, and Supplementary Figs. 35c, 39 and 40). By weakening Nuc–water interactions, SO42− increases the availability of Nuc for halogen-bond stabilization of I+, thereby promoting reversible iodine conversion. These results reveal how anionic chemistry regulates molecular water–Nuc interactions to govern the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Having established the complementary roles of PA and KA in interfacial and molecular regulation, we next examined how these effects manifest in the electrochemical processes governing iodine conversion. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis was used to decouple the complex impedance response and identify individual electrochemical processes38,39,40 (Supplementary Figs. 41–43). In the absence of either KA or PA, the DRT responses evolve distinctly with additional competing interfacial processes, whereas their combined presence maintains stable interfacial electrochemical behaviour throughout iodine conversion41,42 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Rate-dependent analysis identifies charge transfer, rather than ion transport, as the dominant kinetic contribution to iodine conversion in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 44–50). In situ Raman spectroscopy further links these electrochemical processes to iodine chemistry, revealing the reversible evolution of the Nuc–I+–Nuc species during cycling (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52).

The KA–PA–Nuc framework supports four-electron iodine conversion across different operating conditions and cell configurations. Zn–I2 cells retain 96% of their capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g−1 and 94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g−1, while sustaining four-electron conversion at iodine loadings up to 12.2 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. 53–55, 58a and 59). This electrolyte framework is also compatible with different current collectors and pouch-cell configurations and extends to aqueous Al–I2 cells using Al–Zn alloy negative electrodes (Supplementary Figs. 56–58b,c, 60 and 61). A techno-economic analysis under standardized modelling assumptions further illustrates its theoretical cost-reduction potential by avoiding highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes and costly current collectors (Supplementary Fig. 58d–f and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Mechanistic and post-mortem analyses further reveal that the apparent low Coulombic efficiency and capacity fading involve coupled reversible and irreversible iodine inventory loss, with the latter becoming more pronounced at increased iodine loading (Supplementary Figs. 62–67 and Extended Data Figs. 2–4). Together, these results clarify the iodine conversion pathways while defining the applicability and remaining limitations of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, showing that sustained reversible four-electron iodine conversion requires not only stabilization of hypervalent iodine species but also broader management of the entire iodine inventory.

All chemicals were used as received without further purification unless otherwise stated. The manufacturer and purity of each material are specified at its first occurrence in Methods and are not repeated thereafter unless a different source or purity was used.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes were prepared by dissolving KA, PA and Nuc into deionized water at room temperature. For aqueous Zn–I2 batteries, KA and PA were 1.5 M ZnSO4 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M Zn (CH3COO)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich), respectively. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, various Nuc were used, including 2 M urea (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 M acetamide (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 M pyridine (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) or 0.4 M nicotinamide (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). To explore the role of PAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 1.5 M ZnSO4 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. Zn(CH3COO)2, Zn(CF3COO)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) or Zn(CF3SO3)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 0.5 M to obtain electrolytes containing different PAs. To evaluate the role of KAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. ZnSO4, Zn(NO3)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), Zn(CF3SO3)2 or Zn(ClO4)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 1.5 M for comparative analysis. To compare electrolytes performance under a standardized ionic strength condition, the ionic strength of each electrolyte was calculated according to the equation:

where Ci and Zi represent the molar concentration and charge number of ion i, respectively. For aqueous Al–I2 batteries, the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 1.5 M Al2(SO4)3 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 Mg (CH3COO)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M nicotinamide into deionized water.

Iodine-activated carbon (I2–AC) composites were prepared using an evaporation–adsorption method. In brief, 0.5 g iodine (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) and 0.5 g activated carbon (AC; YP-80F, purity not specified, Kuraray) were manually ground in an agate mortar with a pestle for 10 min under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was sealed in a Teflon reactor and heated at 120 °C for 6 h. For the preparation of iodine positive electrodes using titanium (80 mesh, >99.5%, Hebei Conway Metal Products) or stainless steel mesh (80 mesh, 316L, Hebei Conway Metal Products) as the current collector, I2–AC, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% dispersion H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P (purity not specified, Canrd) were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 40 mg I2–AC, 5 mg Super P and 5 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using a roller press (Etelux) and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The areal iodine loading was controlled by adjusting the thickness of the composite film. The dried film was then pressed onto the titanium or stainless steel mesh using the roller press. The resulting electrodes were punched into 12 mm disks using a manual disk punch (T07, ‌Hefei Kejing Material Technology).

For iodine positive electrodes using carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray) as the current collector, I2–AC, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, weight-average molecular weight, Mw ≈ 534,000 g mol−1 by gel permeation chromatography, powder, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg I2–AC, 20 mg PVDF and 20 mg Super P were manually mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) using an agate mortar and pestle in ambient conditions. The resulting slurry was manually and uniformly spread onto the carbon paper using a laboratory spatula. The coated electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 8 h and subsequently cut into 12-mm disks using the manual disk punch. Commercial Zn foils (70 µm, >99.99%, ‌Qinghe Haoxuan Metal Materials) were used as negative electrodes as received.

To assess the potential of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, a Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl (Beijing Jingke Instrument Science Instrument) was used as the reference, and AC electrodes were prepared as the counter electrode. The measured potentials are reported directly versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. For the preparation of AC electrodes, AC, PTFE and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg AC, 20 mg Super P and 20 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle at ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using the roller press and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The dried film was then pressed onto titanium mesh using the roller press. By adjusting the electrode thickness, the capacity of the AC electrode was controlled to be much higher than that of the iodine working electrode, ensuring its capability as the counter electrode for evaluating the electrochemical performance of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte. To further validate the applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, Al–Zn alloys were fabricated as negative electrodes following a previous study43. In brief, symmetric cells were assembled using Zn foils (70 µm, 16 mm in diameter) as electrodes and 2 M Al (CF3SO3)3 (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) as the electrolyte. During charging, Al3+ in the electrolyte deposited on and reacted with the metal Zn substrate, forming the Zn-supported Al–Zn alloys.

Halogen-bond complexes were synthesized via a cation-exchange reaction using corresponding silver analogues, following a previously reported procedure with some modifications44. All operations were carried out under a standard Schlenk line. In a typical synthesis, 0.94 mmol of the corresponding silver salt (Ag2SO4, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCH3COO, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3COO, >98%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3SO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgNO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; or AgClO4, >97%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a 20-ml vial equipped with a stir bar. The vial was sealed with a rubber septum and evacuated. Subsequently, 6.0 ml dry CH2Cl2 (purity not specified, VWR Chemicals) and 1.90 mmol pyridine (3.80 mmol for Ag2SO4) were added at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was stirred for 10 min to form the Ag(I)–pyridine bis-coordination complex. Next, 2.00 mmol of iodine (4.00 mmol for Ag2SO4) was added, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for an additional 20 min under continuous stirring. The supernatant was then carefully transferred to another vial via cannula filtration, followed by the addition of 15 ml dry n-hexane (>99%, Macron Fine Chemicals) to induce precipitation of the halogen-bond complex. The mixture was stored at −20 °C overnight to complete precipitation. Afterwards, the supernatant was removed using a syringe, and the resulting solid was washed with 20 ml dry n-hexane to remove any residual I2. Finally, the product was dried under vacuum on the Schlenk line.

In situ ATR-IR spectra were recorded by a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. Gold-coated silicon plates were used as working electrodes, with Zn foils (70 µm, 10 mm in diameter) and glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter, Whatman) used as reference electrodes and separators, respectively. To assess the critical role of the PA in the interfacial environment, 1.5 M KA electrolyte was maintained as the baseline, and 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2, 0.5 M Zn(CF3COO)2 or 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 was separately added. An electrolyte volume of 500 μl was used for each measurement. During tests, the assembled batteries were connected to a Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat to run a cyclic voltammetry programme at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1 for a full charge and discharge cycle. All spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm−1, with 50 scans per measurement. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

Raman spectra were recorded using a Bruker Senterra II Raman spectrometer with a 532-nm excitation wavelength. The in situ Zn–I2 cell comprised an iodine positive electrode (12 mm in diameter, iodine mass loading 2.2 mg cm−2), a Zn negative electrode (70 µm, 12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter). An electrolyte volume of 200 μl was used. Raman spectra were collected during GCD cycling using an external Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

FTIR spectra of various electrolytes were obtained using an ATR-FTIR spectrometer (BRUKER, Platinum-ATR). Scanning electron microscopy characterization of electrodes was performed using a JEOL 7600 microscope. Ultraviolet–visible measurements were conducted on a Shimadzu UV-3600i Plus spectrophotometer. For in situ ultraviolet–visible measurements, a two-electrode Zn–I2 cuvette cell was connected to a Neware battery test system for GCD cycling. NMR analyses, including 1H, 13C and 1H–15N HMBC spectra, were carried out on a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 500). 15N spectra were collected using a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 700). Deuterium oxide (>99.9%, Fluorochem) was used as the solvent for electrolyte characterization, and dideuteromethylenechloride (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the solvent for characterizing halogen-bond complexes. Micro-computed-tomography imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a ×4 objective, operating at a tube voltage of 80 kV and an exposure time of 8 s, achieving a voxel resolution of 0.8 μm. For each sample, a disk with a diameter of 2 mm was prepared to balance X-ray attenuation and representative sampling volume. The acquired computed-tomography datasets were subsequently processed and analysed using Avizo software.

Electrochemical studies of halogen-free electrolytes were performed using CR2025 coin cells, whereas those of halogen-containing electrolytes were performed using Swagelok cells. For CR2025 Zn–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode, Zn negative electrode (70 µm) and separator (GF/D) had diameters of 12 mm, 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively. For Swagelok Zn–I2 cells, corresponding electrodes and separators had the same diameter of 12 mm. For CR2025 Al–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode had a diameter of 12 mm, the Al–Zn alloy negative electrode had a diameter of 16 mm, and a GF/D separator with a diameter of 19 mm was used. An electrolyte volume of 100 μl was used for each cell. Coin cells were mechanically crimped at 50 kg cm−2 using a hydraulic crimping machine (MSK-110, Hefei Kejing Material Technology) during assembly. Swagelok cells were manually tightened during assembly.

For the 1.1-Ah pouch cell, 2 double-side coated iodine positive electrodes (10 × 15 cm), and 3 Zn negative electrodes (70 µm, 10 × 15 cm) were stacked alternately. The areal iodine loading of positive electrodes is controlled at 10 mg cm−2. Four glass fibre separators (GF/D, 10.1 × 15.1 cm) were utilized, and 1.5 ml electrolyte was added to each separator. The electrolyte consisted of 1.5 M ZnSO4, 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide. Titanium foils were connected to electrodes as tabs. After lamination, the assembled battery was encapsulated in an aluminium–plastic film and mechanically constrained using a customized model during electrochemical measurements. The applied pressure was not specifically quantified.

GCD tests were conducted using a Neware battery test system in a room maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 25–28 °C. All other electrochemical measurements described below were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C. Cyclic voltammetry, linear sweep voltammetry and EIS measurements were performed using a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat. For the electrochemical stability window analysis, linear sweep voltammetry measurements were performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of a titanium mesh working electrode (1 × 2 cm), an AC counter electrode (1 × 2 cm) and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode at a scan rate of 2 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to an exposed geometric area of 1 cm², and the potentials are reported directly versus Ag/AgCl. The polarization measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti CR2025 coin cells using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter), titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter) at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to the geometric area of the titanium electrode. For in situ EIS tests, a thin Zn wire was inserted into the coin cell as an additional reference electrode to establish a three-electrode configuration. This reference electrode was placed between the positive electrode and negative electrode, separated by two layers of separators (GF/A, Whatman). For measurements of the individual iodine positive electrode, the potential is reported versus the Zn reference electrode as potential (V versus Zn/Zn²+), whereas the full-cell and Zn negative electrode responses are reported as voltage (V) owing to the voltage was applied on full cell. For peak assignment, the assembled cells were connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat to perform staircase potentio EIS with a potential range of approximately 0.6–1.8 V. For rate-step identification, the assembled cells simultaneously connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat and a Neware battery test system to conduct potentio EIS and GCD cycling, respectively. All Nyquist plots were fitted using EC-Lab software based on the equivalent circuit (R1 + Q2/R2 + Q3/R3 + W4). DRT data were calculated from EIS data using MatlabR2019 with the DRT tool developed by Francesco Ciucci’s research group. The differential capacitance was calculated using the following equation:

where C is the differential capacitance, ω is the angular frequency and Zim is the imaginary component of the impedance. In this work, a specific frequency of 1,000 Hz was used. Measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti cells assembled in CR2025 coin-cell configuration, using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter) and titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) as the two electrodes and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter). The potential was varied from 1.0 V to 1.7 V versus Zn/Zn2+. No ohmic-drop (iR) correction was applied to the potentials or voltages reported in this work.

All molecular-dynamics simulations were performed using the LAMMPS package45 to investigate the bulk solvation structure of various aqueous electrolytes. The initial configurations were constructed using Packmol46, which randomly packed electrolyte components into a periodic cubic box according to the target molar ratios, ensuring no initial atomic overlaps. The simulation cell was then relaxed by energy minimization before subsequent equilibration. Force-field parameters for organic molecules were taken from the OPLS-AA family47,48, whereas others were adopted from validated aqueous zinc salt parameter sets in the literature. To partially account for polarization effects in concentrated electrolytes, the atomic charges were uniformly scaled (scaling factor 0.8)49. Interaction of water was represented by TIP3P50, and all X–H bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm51. Each system was first energy-minimized and equilibrated in the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (300 K, 1 atm) using a Nosé–Hoover thermostat until both the density and potential energy were stable. Subsequently, production runs were performed in the canonical ensemble for 5 ns (5,000 ps) with a 1-fs integration step to ensure complete equilibration while avoiding structural drift.

Radial distribution functions gij(r) were computed to analyse ion pairing and solvation structure. Coordination numbers were obtained by integrating gij(r) up to their first minimum. Both radial distribution functions and hydrogen bonds were identified using the hydrogen-bond analysis tools implemented in VMD52. Average hydrogen-bond numbers and distributions were determined over the equilibrated trajectories to characterize the reorganization of the hydrogen-bond network by different anions.

To probe field-induced ion and molecular redistribution, an additional set of simulations was conducted in the canonical ensemble with a uniform static electric field applied along the z axis. The field strength corresponded to the experimentally estimated potential gradient.

Density-functional-theory calculations were performed using the Gaussian16 program package, using the M06-2X exchange-correlation functional53. Geometry optimizations were conducted using a mixed basis-set approach: the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set was applied to all elements excluding iodine54. Iodine was described using an effective core potential from the Stuttgart/Dresden group55. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model, with water selected as the solvent56.

#1261. Official: Mbappé out of Italy vs. France, as Zidane warns ‘we won’t risk him’

France coach Zinedine Zidane confirms Kylian Mbappé is out of tomorrow’s Nations League match against Italy. ‘He is injured, so we will not risk him.’

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

Les Bleus are top of the Nations League group with 10 points, followed by Italy on seven and Belgium six, so the two spots going into the quarter-finals are all to play for.

There had been reports in L’Equipe that Mbappé had skipped training today with a hamstring issue and was therefore a major doubt to feature in this Matchday 5 fixture.

When Zidane arrived for his press conference this evening, he spoke to RAI Sport and confessed the decision had already been made.

“No, Mbappé will not be there tomorrow,” said the coach and former Juventus midfielder.

“He is injured, so we will not risk him. We’ll see if he can recover in time for the next game.”

France will face rock bottom Turkiye in the final Nations League fixture on Sunday evening, while Italy go head-to-head with Belgium in Brussels.

Les Bleus are already missing Marcus Thuram, Pierre Kalulu, Aurelien Tchaouameni, Manu Koné, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Ousmane Dembélé, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

Italy should field youthful players to conquer France and leave out veterans

I do not expect Italy to defeat France, more likely a 2-2 draw…

It’s the Belgium match which will decide the fate of the Gli Azzurri, and I have full confidence that we will win that game either 3-2 or 2-1.

#1260. Pocognoli fears Scottish Premiership 'identity crisis' over lack of homegrown stars

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 17:55 EST, 11 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli believes the Premiership has an identity crisis caused by a lack of Scottish players pulling on the jersey at our top clubs.

Just six of the 26 players the newly appointed national team manager initially selected for the Nations League double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland play their football in this country’s top division.

And while the Belgian understands the attraction and the benefits of top talents moving to some of Europe’s top leagues, he’s concerned that the division which should be his first port of call when it comes to making selections is now a barren land.

‘The Scottish league misses Scottish players in the biggest teams,’ he said.

‘The league is intense and competitive, but I am not looking at this. I am looking at who is performing at the big clubs.

‘I believe that’s the most close to international level. And for that you need to play Champions League, Europa League, Conference League in some stage of the competition.

‘That is what I’m looking at. I hope that players who are performing well, let’s say in the bottom (half), can bounce to the next step to a top club inside the country.

Pocognoli has been alarmed by the lack of Scottish talent in the SPFL Premiership

Pocognoli has been impressed by the progress of young Celtic full-back Colby Donovan

‘That will make the competition more competitive, maybe you will go through after the winter into the Champions League or Europa League.

‘That gives the experience to the young Scottish players and in the end, we’d get the benefit.

‘That’s what I’m looking at more in Scottish football rather than the clubs and the style of play of clubs, that kind of thing.

‘It’s not easy because if you look at the Scottish competition, there’s not many young lads who are getting an opportunity to shine compared to Belgium, France, Germany.’

The specific issue of a lack of opportunities being afforded to players who are eligible for the Scotland under 21 side was highlighted at the recent summit at St Andrews which all 42 clubs attended.

With Turkey the only nation which currently gives fewer minutes, the SFA’s chief football officer Craig Mulholland has tabled two proposals which would see clubs obliged to offer more chances to emerging talents in both league and cup matches.

Optimistic that such changes to the rules would lead to a brighter picture further down the line, Pocognoli added: ‘Hopefully, we can see the benefits in future.

‘I follow all of the young lads, not only from the Premiership in Scotland, but also the Championship and League One because some of them are on loan.

‘My job is not only to win the next game, it’s also to prepare for what’s coming next season.

‘In one year, a lot can change. I try to support all the decisions of the clubs in Scotland regarding the fact they play Scottish players and young ones especially.

‘Colby Donovan is a good example, he played some good games for Celtic and I tried to help to accelerate his progress, then he signed a new contract and plays week after week.

‘He is not selected this time, but I think we will get the benefit later on.

‘For Findlay Curtis it’s the same, he’s not playing a lot at Rangers but I believe in his quality.

‘We need to support those type of players because we need them, but hopefully it can help his pathway at Rangers to get some minutes.

‘I hope some other players will be on the same pathway this season.’

#1259. Zidane: ‘France competitive, Lippi a master and I’d love to be Juventus coach one day’

Zinedine Zidane is sure France will be ‘competitive’ against Italy even without Kylian Mbappé, and admits Marcello Lippi ‘taught me so much about tactics’ at Juventus, so he’d love to be their coach one day.

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

Only the top two go through to the quarter-finals of the Nations League, and currently Les Bleus lead Group A1 with 10 points, followed by Italy on seven and Belgium with six.

Considering Italy and Belgium go head-to-head in Brussels for the final match, and France host rock bottom Turkiye, they are practically guaranteed at least second.

There was a heavy blow with news Mbappé will not even be on the bench tomorrow due to a hamstring issue, especially after the likes of Marcus Thuram, Esteban Lepaul, Ousmane Dembélé, Aurelien Tchouameni, Manu Koné and Pierre Kalulu pulled out.

“Mbappé will not be there, he felt some pain and we generally try to avoid risks for the players, but we hope to have him on Sunday,” said Zidane in his press conference.

“We sent Tchouameni and Thuram home because they were not in any condition to play on Thursday or Sunday, so I appreciated their decision to come to the training camp even when not fully fit, it was good to see their desire to represent France.

“Obviously, Mbappé wanted to play tomorrow as well, but we have to adopt a policy of zero risks. The good news is that he could be available on Sunday. It’s November, there are lots of games, it’s a complicated month, so players have to safeguard their health.”

With so many absentees in attack, who will start upfront against Italy?

“The objective is to pick the best possible line-up, and despite the absences, we have a squad capable of doing well. We will be able to field a competitive team,” added Zidane.

The coach has made a habit of adapting some of the players to roles they are not accustomed to at club level, such as Inter’s Andy Diouf going from right-sided wing-back to a left-back for France.

“We know that he plays in a different position at Inter, but he can cover various roles. When he is with us, it is to play on the left. I want to see players up close and I do try to use them in their natural positions. I can confirm Warren Zaire Emery will play in midfield, for example.”

Zidane has only failed to win one game so far on the France bench, and that was the 1-1 draw in Paris against Italy.

A former Juventus midfielder, he is no surprised by the rebirth of the Azzurri under Roberto Mancini.

“We had a complicated night there because we know that when Italy want to put in a good performance, they certainly can, especially when defending. I played at Juventus for four or five years, so I know that for an Italian coach, defence comes first, then the attack. It’s something Italy does so well.”

Zidane was asked in the press conference if he would like to be the coach of Juventus one day, a role Didier Deschamps already took.

“Yes, but you never know. Marcello Lippi taught me we must never stop, we’ve always got to keep pushing. At the start I didn’t play well in Turin, the fans and the media didn’t love me.

“I suffered a little, but Lippi told me I would play for his Juve. I owe him everything. I’d love one day to be at Juventus, why not, if I continue working as a coach.”

Although Zidane hit the heights of his playing career at Real Madrid, he assures the seeds were sowed at Juventus first.

“We spent so much of our day working on tactics with Lippi in training, so for someone like me who always wants the ball at his feet, it means a steep learning curve.

“A master like Lippi taught me so much on a tactical level. He also put so much faith in me, and I tried to repay him on the field.”

Of course, Lippi went on to win the World Cup with Italy in 2006, beating France in the Final with Zidane sent off.

#1258. 'He always wanted to play for Scotland'. Alex McLeish recalls the moment the national team found their new talisman in Scott McTominay

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 18:02 EST, 11 November 2026

While Alex McLeish’s second stint as Scotland manager clearly did not go to plan, the compensations from that period proved to be significant for the national team.

Without a struggling side earning a play-off spot in the Nations League, a famous night in Serbia under Steve Clarke would never have been possible.

For all we know, the years in international exile may have rolled on. The ongoing improvement which led to participation at the World Cup this summer might never have happened.

McLeish’s greatest legacy, however, was surely to persuade Scott McTominay to pull on a dark blue shirt after he travelled to Carrington in 2018.

Alerted to the Lancaster-born player’s eligibility by then Manchester United manager Jose Mourinho, the man who won 77 caps for his country could have been forgiven for feeling that the coup he pulled off was just never meant to be.

‘The beast from the east,’ McLeish recalled with a grin.

Scott McTominay (left) and Alex McLeish in 2018 ahead of a friendly against Belgium

McLeish and McTominay together in a Nations League encounter against Albania in 2018

‘When I was forced off the train in Newcastle, they said “it’s not going any further, the weather’s knackered.”

‘So, I had to wait for a train down south. And I thought “at this point will I go home?”

‘And I thought, “no, I’ve come this far, so I’m going all the way”. Then I got to my hotel at five in the morning, the guy says, “oh, I thought you were a no-show, son.”

‘I said - “no - I’ve arrived and I’m needing a room.”

‘I didn’t go in for the breakfast as Mourinho said “just come in at lunchtime, get some food and we’ll have a chat.”

‘But he said he (McTominay) definitely wants to play for Scotland.

‘So, it was good to hear that from Jose.’

Mourinho liked what he saw the minute he set eyes on the player. It’s fair to say that not everyone at the club around that time was similarly enthused.

‘He was still just a kid, quite raw,’ McLeish recalled. ‘But he had the physique, speed and skill on the ball.

‘He was good in the air and also with the ball at his feet. It made it a no-brainer.

‘I’d gone to a couple of Man United games and they were just kind of breeding him into the system.

McTominay in training ahead of the Nations League clash against North Macedonia on Friday

‘Listen, anyone would have done it and brought him into the squad.

‘The only problem we faced was that England were in the frame as well. But when I said to Scott, “I’d love you to play for Scotland,” he said “That’s the only team I want to play for.”

‘And all of a sudden we had a brand new young superstar.’

Truth be told, it would be some time before Scotland supporters began to place McTominay in such a bracket.

He had his moments early on for his country, but his deployment as a defender – by both McLeish and Clarke – did him no favours.

It was only in the qualifiers to Euro 2024 that the futility of that approach was accepted.

McTominay was outstanding as a central midfielder in the qualifiers, his performance and two goals in the famous win against Spain topping the lot.

In little over a year, he’d be a Napoli player. And within a season, he’d become a Serie A winner and voted Italy’s best player.

Many Manchester United fans were outraged that the club had sold him for just £25.7million.

Even some England supporters voiced their displeasure about the player slipping through their hands.

‘They have such a massive pot to pick from in England,’ McLeish reflected.

‘But I’m sure that privately, in some of their chats behind the scenes, they will have said ‘we should have got McTominay.’

‘But he chose Scotland. He wanted to to come. He wasn’t saying anything about England at all.

‘And that was the best news I could have got in that era of rebuild.’

While Clarke rightly got the plaudits for taking the team to three tournaments, McLeish has taken a huge amount of pride from the part McTominay has played in it all.

‘It’s incredible how he’s grown and grown,’ he added.

‘In the first few games, he was just trying to feel his way into the international scene. But he gave everything from that first call-up.

Scott McTominay in action against Haiti in the 2026 World Cup

‘He’s played in just about every position in the team down the years. He was in the back four at one stage.

‘But he’s mainly operated in the middle of the field and he’s a real threat in the box and moving from middle to front.

‘The way he runs with the ball is just superb because he really knows what he’s doing.

‘He’s got massive confidence and I hope that a lot of young Scottish players coming into the game can take inspiration from what Scott has done.'

In a rare media conference this week, McTominay put his underwhelming displays at the World Cup in context.

Two days before the opener against Haiti in Boston, he underwent a controlled electric shock in hospital to restore a normal heart rhythm. Since then, he’s undergone a medical procedure to deal with the arrhythmia.

He returns to the Scotland squad a month after pulling on a Napoli shirt again against Frosinone.

With five goals in his past six matches, it feels like the player the Tartan Army grew to love is back with them.

Sebastien Pocognoli may soon feel he owes McLeish a word of thanks, too.

‘It’ll be a massive relief for the manager to get Scott back into the squad,’ he said.

‘You always want your best players available.
