Data are the mean ± s.e.m. (a–d,f). Significance was determined using two-sided Student’s t-test (a) or two-way analysis ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test (b–d,f).

PANX1 is a channel that can conduct ions and other small molecules67,68. Previous work has implicated Panx1 in NLRP3 activation in vivo69; however, in vitro studies have discounted a role for Panx1 in NLRP3 activation69,70,71,72. To investigate a link to ECM stiffness, we used macrophages generated from WT and CMV-cre;Panx1f/f (Panx1−/−) animals73. WT BMDMs produced IL-1β when cultured on soft ECM, whereas Panx1−/− BMDMs cultured on soft ECM were defective for IL-1β (but not pro-IL-1β) production (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 10b). We confirmed previous results of the effects of Panx1 on macrophages grown on plastic plates72, as Panx1−/− BMDMs retained normal two-signal activation of NLRP3 (Extended Data Fig. 10c). Similar results were obtained when cells were treated with the Panx1 inhibitors probenecid and trovafloxacin69,72 (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). Panx1 conducts ATP; however, culturing cells with oxidized ATP (oxATP; which blocks ATP signalling via P2X7) did not affect LPS-stimulated IL-1β release (Extended Data Fig. 10g). As a control, oxATP suppressed the effects of exogenous ATP on IL-1β production by these cells (Extended Data Fig. 10h). To determine whether increased Panx1 expression is sufficient to enable macrophages to activate NLRP3 in response to LPS, we overexpressed Panx1 in iBMDMs and cultured the cells on plastic plates. Notably, LPS stimulated the production of IL-1β from Panx1-overexpressing iBMDMs but not in control cells (Fig. 4d,e). MCC950 inhibited LPS-stimulated production of IL-1β in Panx1-overexpressing iBMDMs (Fig. 4d). Overexpression of Panx1 did not affect two-signal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome when cells were treated with LPS + nigericin (Extended Data Fig. 10i). To determine whether Panx1 overexpression can bypass the requirement of NRF2 for NLRP3 activation, we overexpressed Panx1 in Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs. Overexpression of Panx1 in Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs enabled LPS to stimulate production of IL-1β when BMDMs were cultured on soft ECM or plastic plates (Fig. 4f,g). Overexpression of Panx1 minimally increased IL-1β release induced by treatment with LPS and ATP (Extended Data Fig. 10j). No genotype-specific differences in pro-IL-1β production were observed (Fig. 4g). The induction of Panx1 by NRF2 is therefore necessary and sufficient for one-signal activation of NLRP3.

Our findings suggest that macrophages that exist in high stiffness organs should display functional NRF2 and NLRP3 deficiencies. On the basis of this prediction, we examined NRF2 functions in osteoclasts, as bone is the stiffest organ in the body. RNA sequencing analysis was performed on osteoclasts and BMDMs. Osteoclasts displayed lower Nfe2l2 expression and NRF2 target gene expression than BMDMs (Extended Data Fig. 11a). To confirm these findings, we re-analysed a publicly available RNA sequencing dataset74 and similarly found that osteoclasts had lower Nfe2l2 expression and NRF2 target gene expression than BMDMs (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Osteoclasts also had reduced NRF2 protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 10l). Activation of NLRP3 in osteoclasts through LPS + nigericin treatment led to minimal IL-1β release (Extended Data Fig. 11b) compared with BMDMs. Osteoclasts therefore display a functional deficiency in NRF2 and consequently NLRP3.

As KEAP1 does not control Nfe2l2 expression, yet osteoclasts display low Nfe2l2 transcript abundance, KEAP1 may not regulate NRF2 or NLRP3 activities in osteoclasts as it does in BMDMs. Consistent with this idea, Keap1∆M osteoclasts did not display increased NRF2 protein levels, and Keap1∆M osteoclasts did not display increase NLRP3 inflammasome activities (Extended Data Figs. 10l and 11c). Thus, although BMDMs control NLRP3 via KEAP1-mediated NRF2 regulation, osteoclasts regulate NRF2 at the level of Nfe2l2 expression.

Mutations in NLRP3 cause systemic autoimmune diseases, the most severe of which is neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID)75,76. We recognized the similarity between macrophages with NOMID NLRP3 mutations and WT macrophages cultured on low-stiffness ECM. In both instances, LPS is sufficient to promote IL-1β production. This symmetry in phenotypes raised the possibility that disease-associated NLRP3 mutants may be prone to autoactivation because they bypass the NRF2 checkpoint.

To address this possibility, we investigated NRF2 activity in BMDMs from mice with macrophage-specific expression of one allele of the NOMID NLRP3 mutation: D301N (Nlrp3CA/+)77. As previously reported, Nlrp3CA/+ BMDMs cultured on plastic plates activated the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to LPS alone77, as evidenced by IL-1β secretion and cleavage of IL-1β, caspase-1 and GSDMD (Extended Data Fig. 11d,e). WT and Nlrp3CA/+ BMDMs did not differ in NRF2 protein abundance or the expression of NRF2 target genes, nor did they show any difference in the ability of LPS to regulate the known NRF2 target gene Slc7a11 (Extended Data Fig. 11e–g). These data demonstrate that despite the low NRF2 activities in Nlrp3CA/+ BMDMs, these cells can activate NLRP3 inflammasomes in response to LPS. Consistent with the insensitivity of NLRP3D301N cells to low NRF2 activities, ECM stiffness did not affect NLRP3 activities in Nlrp3CA/+ BMDMs (Extended Data Fig. 11h). On the basis of these data, we reasoned that NOMID mutant cells may retain NLRP3 stimulatory activities under conditions of NRF2 deficiency. To address this possibility, we generated mice with macrophages expressing NLRP3(D301N) and deficient in NRF2 (Nlrp3CA/+;Nfe2l2∆M mice) (Extended Data Fig. 10m). Nlrp3CA/+;Nfe2l2∆M BMDMs retained the ability to release IL-1β after LPS stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 11i). Consistent with these in vitro data, in vivo analysis demonstrated no difference in survival in Nlrp3CA/+;Nfe2l2∆M mice compared with Nlrp3CA mice (Extended Data Fig. 11j). These data suggest that NOMID mutations bypass NRF2 regulation of NLRP3.

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a chronic, fibrotic disease of the lung that increases tissue stiffness27. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a subtype of ILD characterized by increased ECM protein abundance, thickened alveolar septa and stiffening alveoli78. We obtained publicly available spatial transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets of lung tissue explanted from patients with ILD and from individuals without lung disease79,80,81. In the spatial transcriptomic dataset79, several subsets of macrophages from patients with fibrosis had lower NRF2 transcriptional activity than macrophages from individuals without lung disease (Fig. 5a). Similar findings were made after pseudobulk analysis followed by gene set variation analysis (GSVA) using NRF2 target genes as the gene set82,83 (Extended Data Fig. 12a). Further analysis determined that patients with ILD had increased fibroblast COL1A1 and COL3A1 expression, which indicated increased collagen production and tissue stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 12b). SPP1+ macrophages from patients with ILD did not show differences in expression of TNF, IL1A or IL1B (Extended Data Fig. 12c). In both single-cell RNA sequencing datasets80,81, alveolar macrophages from patients with IPF demonstrated a reduction in NRF2 transcriptional activity compared with alveolar macrophages from individuals without lung disease (Extended Data Fig. 12d,e).

a, NRF2 module score calculations from a previous study79 in four macrophage subtypes in patients with pulmonary fibrosis and from individuals without lung disease (unaffected). The grey box represents 25–75% the interquartile range (IQR) with the line at the median, and whiskers represent the minima and maxima. The total number of cells analysed was as follows: SPP1+ macrophages n = 2,909 (unaffected) and n = 12,492 (fibrosis); FABP4+ macrophages, n = 5,546 (unaffected) and n = 4,079 (fibrosis); interstitial macrophages, n = 25,097 (unaffected) and n = 10,497 (fibrosis); other macrophages, n = 7,975 (unaffected) and n = 25,892 (fibrosis). b, Representative immunofluorescent images of the NRF2 transcriptional targets GSR, HMOX1 and SLC7A11 in human lung tissue from unaffected individuals and patients with lung fibrosis. Scale bar, 10 µm. c, Quantification of alveolar macrophage sum of cellular fluorescence for each NRF2 target. The grey box represents 25–75% the IQR with the line at the median, and whiskers represent the minima and maxima. Data were quantified from five fields of view for two unaffected individuals and two patients with lung fibrosis. The total number of alveolar macrophages analysed was as follows: GSR, n = 83 (unaffected) and n = 138 (fibrosis); HMOX1, n = 119 (unaffected) and n = 292 (fibrosis); and SLC7A11, n = 104 (unaffected) and n = 271 (fibrosis). Data are the median with IQR (a,c); for a, lines were calculated using the Tukey method. Significance was determined using two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test (a) or two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test with Holm–Šídák multiple-comparison test (c).

To validate these findings, we obtained tissue samples from individuals without lung disease and from individuals with IPF and performed immunofluorescence for three NRF2 targets in macrophages: GSR, HMOX1 and SLC7A11 (Extended Data Fig. 12f). Alveolar macrophages from patients with fibrosis had reduced expression of each NRF2 target (Fig. 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 12g). Similarly, analysis of interstitial macrophages revealed decreased expression of each NRF2 target (Extended Data Fig. 12h). These data suggest that macrophages exposed to high stiffness in vivo (from patients with fibrotic lung disease) have decreased NRF2 activity.

On the basis of the data presented, we propose that the in vitro to in vivo disconnects long associated with NLRP3 biology can be explained, at least in part, by differences in ECM stiffness. Underlying NLRP3 regulation is the mechanistic link between ECM stiffness, the actin cytoskeleton, and ROS generation, which regulates NRF2 activity and the induction of Panx1. All of these factors promote one-signal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Our finding that NRF2 supports NLRP3 activation is consistent with previous reports that used genetic deficiency to assess the effect of NRF2 on NLRP3 activity46,47,48. However, previous work using chemical activators of NRF2 reported that NRF2 has anti-inflammatory effects. Although our transcriptional data suggest that some effects of NRF2 activators may be off target, both models can co-exist, and we propose that the relationship between NRF2 and inflammation depends on the context. Indeed, our finding that NRF2 is required for alum-induced peritonitis and for hyperactivator-mediated antitumour immunity (both NLRP3-dependent processes) contrasts with the NRF2-independence of MSU-crystal-induced peritonitis. The contexts in which NRF2 are most important for regulation of NLRP3 require further investigation, and there may be scenarios in which different NRF2 regulators control pathway function. For example, although KEAP1 (and its oxidation state) is likely to be a general regulator of NRF2, other factors such as GSK3 may regulate NRF2 in specific contexts84. Regardless of the mechanism of NRF2 regulation, our findings highlight ECM stiffness as a foundational regulator of NRF2 functions in macrophages. NRF2 may therefore operate as a mechanosensitive checkpoint that controls one-signal NLRP3 activation. The evidence presented herein provides a mandate to consider ECM stiffness as a determinant of immune cell functions in diverse contexts of health and disease.

No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Experiments were not randomized, and investigators were not blinded during experiments or during outcome measurements. Details of specific statistical tests are included in the figure legends. All unique and newly generated materials (cell lines and mice) are available from the authors upon request. All other materials are commercially available.

All mice used in these studies were on the C57BL/6J background. Both male and female mice were used throughout the studies and no differences were noted based on sex. WT C57BL/6J (000664), Nlrp3−/− (021302), Casp11−/− (024698), Casp1−/−;Casp11−/− (016621), Gsdmd−/− (032410), Nfe2l2−/− (017009), LysM-cre (004781), Keap1f/f (037075), Nlrp3D301NneoR (017971) and Nfe2l2f/f (025433) mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory. LysM-cre;Keap1f/f mice were generated in the Kagan Laboratory; LysM-cre;Nlrp3D301NneoR and LysM-cre; Nlrp3D301NneoR;Nfe2l2f/f mice were generated in the Mbalaviele Laboratory. Bone marrow samples from CMV-cre;Panxf/f mice were provided by H.B.d.S.73. Mice were maintained on regular chow and in a specific pathogen-free environment on a 12-h light–dark cycle with continuous access to food and water in a room at approximately 22 °C and 35–70% relative humidity. All animal studies were approved by the Boston Children’s Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conducted under the supervision of the department of Animal Resources at Children’s Hospital.

E. coli LPS (serotype O:111 B4) was purchased from Enzo Biosciences as a ready-to-use stock solution of 1 mg ml–1 or purchased from Invivogen and reconstituted in LAL water at a stock concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a working concentration of 100 ng ml–1 for in vitro experiments. R848 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in LAL water to a concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at 1 µg ml–1. MCC950 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. zVAD-FMK was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 10 µg ml–1. Nigericin was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile ethanol to a concentration of 6.7 mM and used at a final concentration of 5–15 µM. CL097 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in LAL water to a concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 µg ml–1. OVA EndoFit was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 10 mg ml–1 and used as described below. IFNγ was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 50 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 50 ng ml–1. IL-4 was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 20 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 ng ml–1. IL-13 was purchased from Sino Biological and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 20 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 20 ng ml–1. FLT3L was purchased from Miltenyi Biotec and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 100 µg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 100 ng ml–1. ATP was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, and fresh stock solutions were made at the time of each experiment by resuspending in PBS to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 5 mM. PGPC was purchased from Cayman Chemical as a solution in ethanol, solvent was evaporated under gentle nitrogen stream, dried lipids were resuspended in serum-free medium to a final concentration of 1 mg ml–1 and used at a final concentration of 100 µg ml–1 for in vitro experiments or 65 µg per mouse for in vivo experiments. Recombinant human M-CSF (CHO expressed, carrier-free) was purchased from R&D Biosystems and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a concentration of 100 µg ml–1. NAC was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS to a concentration of 500 mM, pH adjusted to 7.4 using sodium hydroxide and used at a final concentration of 5 mM. MitoTEMPO was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 15 mM and used at a final concentration of 15 µM. Cytochalasin D was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 20 µM. Jasplakinolide was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich as a stock solution of 1 mM in sterile DMSO and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. Y-27632 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. ML-7 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. 4-Octyl itaconate was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 125 mM and used at a final concentration of 125 µM. Dimethyl fumarate was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 25 µM. Sulforaphane was purchased from Cayman Chemicals and resuspended in sterile ethanol to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 5 µM. Tert-butylhydroquinone was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 100 µM. KI696 was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 1 mM and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. MDIVI-1 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. Drpitor1a was purchased from MedChem Express and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 10 mM and used at a final concentration of 0.5 µM. Probenecid was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a final concentration of 100 mM, pH adjusted with NaOH, and used at a final concentration of 1 mM. Trovafloxacin was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile H2O to a concentration of 25 mM and used at a final concentration of 25 µM. oxATP was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile PBS pH 7.4 to a concentration of 100 mM and used at a final concentration of 300 µM. ML171 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 1 µM. GSK2795039 was purchased from Tocris Biosciences and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. GKT137831 was purchased from Cayman Chemical and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 µM. MG132 was purchased from Invivogen and resuspended in sterile DMSO to a concentration of 20 mM and used at a final concentration of 10 μM.

The following primary antibodies for were used for immunoblotting: polyclonal goat biotinylated anti-mouse IL-1β and polyclonal goat biotinylated anti-human IL-1β (both from R&D Biosystems); polyclonal rabbit anti-mouse IL-1β and polyclonal rabbit anti-human IL-1β (both from GeneTex); monoclonal rabbit anti-mouse cleaved GSDMD-NT and monoclonal rabbit anti-NRF2 (both from Abcam); monoclonal mouse anti-mouse caspase-1 p20 and monoclonal mouse anti-NLRP3 (both from Adipogen); monoclonal rabbit anti-mouse NRF2, monoclonal rabbit anti-KEAP1, polyclonal rabbit anti-lamin-A/C, monoclonal rabbit anti-pS172 IKKε, monoclonal rabbit anti-pS172 TBK1, monoclonal rabbit anti-pT180/Y182 P38, polyclonal rabbit anti-pT183/Y185 JNK, monoclonal mouse anti-pT202/Y204 ERK and monoclonal rabbit anti-pS536 P65 (all from Cell Signaling); monoclonal mouse anti-β-tubulin (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank); and monoclonal mouse anti-actin (Sigma-Aldrich). All primary antibodies were used at a 1:1,000 dilution in TBS pH 7.4 and 0.1% Tween-20 and 5% BSA, except for mouse anti-actin, which was used at 1:5,000 in the same buffer. Uncropped and unprocessed scans of all western blots in this study are available in the Source Data.

For assessment of macrophage depletion, anti-mouse/human-CD11b (clone M1/70) and anti-mouse-F4/80 (clone BM8) were purchased from BioLegend, whereas mouse FC Block was purchased from BD Biosciences. In brief, 1 × 106 peritoneal lavage cells were resuspended in 70 µl FACS buffer (PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA, 2% FBS) containing FC block and incubated on ice for 15 min. Subsequently, fluorescently conjugated primary antibodies were added to a final dilution of 1:200 and cells were incubated on ice for 30 min. Cells were washed with FACS buffer and resuspended in FACS buffer containing 1 µg ml–1 DAPI (Biotium) to stain dead cells and passed through a 30 µm strainer. Data were acquired on an LSR II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analysed using FlowJo software (Tree Star). The gating strategy is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Age-matched male or female C57BL/6J, Nlrp3−/−, Casp11−/−, Casp1−/−;Casp11−/− and Nfe2l2−/− mice were ear tagged and weighed the day before an experiment. The next day, mice were injected (i.p.) with E. coli LPS (serotype O111:B4) at a dose of 10 mg kg–1 in a final volume of 200 µl (or equal volume PBS pH 7.4 as a control). Plasma was collected by retroorbital bleeding using microhaematocrit heparinized capillary tubes (Fisher Sciences) and placed in microtainer tubes with lithium heparin (BD Biosciences). Red blood cells (RBCs) were pelleted by centrifugation at 6,000g for 5 min at 4 °C. Plasma was removed and stored at −80 °C until assay. To isolate peritoneal fluid, mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation, sprayed with ethanol and the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 5 ml ice-cold PBS pH 7.4. The peritoneal lavage was collected and cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C. Peritoneal lavage supernatant was transferred to a separate tube and stored at −80 °C until assay.

Age-matched male or female C57BL/6J mice were ear tagged and injected (i.p.) with 100 µl Clodrosome or control Encapsome liposomes (Encapsula Nanosciences). Three days after injection of clodronate, mice were either injected with LPS as described above or euthanized, and peritoneal lavage cells were collected in PBS pH 7.4 with 2.5 mM EDTA as outlined above to assay macrophage depletion by flow cytometry.

All cells were cultured in humidified incubators at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Primary BMDMs, iBMDMs and HEK293T cells (obtained from the American Type Culture Collection, not authenticated and not tested for mycoplasma) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) with 10% FBS (R&D Systems), penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco), l-glutamine (Gibco) and sodium pyruvate (Gibco), hereafter referred to as complete DMEM (cDMEM). BMDCs were cultured in IMDM (Gibco) with 10% FBS, penicillin–streptomycin, l-glutamine and sodium pyruvate, hereafter referred to as complete IMDM (cIMDM). Human monocytes and MDMs were cultured in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, penicillin–streptomycin, l-glutamine and sodium pyruvate, hereafter referred to as complete RPMI (cRPMI). Cytosoft plates corresponding to normal tissue (soft, 2 kPa, 5141) or fibrotic tissue (stiff, 32 kPa, 5144) were purchased from Advanced Biomatrix. Cytosoft plates and plastic tissue culture (TC) plates were coated with fibronectin (Advanced Biomatrix, 5050) at 1 µg cm–2 in PBS according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Plates were washed twice with PBS and cells were seeded in 3 ml medium.

BMDMs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nlrp3−/−, Casp11−/−, Casp1−/−;Casp11−/−, Gsdmd−/−, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f, LysM-cre;Keap1f/f and CMV-cre;Panxf/f mice. In brief, mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation and leg bones were surgically removed and cleaned of surrounding muscle and tissue. Bones were washed once in 70% ethanol, washed in PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA with penicillin–streptomycin and then stored in a solution of PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA and penicillin–streptomycin until processing. All future steps were undertaken in a Biosafety Cabinet. Bones were scraped clean of tissue using sterilized razor blades, the ends of the tibia and femurs were cut and bones were placed into a sterile 0.6 ml tube with perforations at the base. The 0.6 ml tube with bones was placed into a sterile 2 ml tube and the nested tubes were spun at 12,000g for 15 s in a tabletop centrifuge. Cell pellets were resuspended in PBS pH 7.4 and 2.5 mM EDTA and spun at 400g for 5 min followed by RBC lysis using ACK buffer (Gibco) for 1 min at room temperature. Lysis was stopped by adding a 10-fold volume of PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and cells were pelleted at 400g for 5 min. A total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC-treated plate and differentiated in cDMEM supplemented with 30% L929 supernatants containing M-CSF for 6 days. Immortalization of WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs was performed using J2 virus supernatants as previously described85.

Primary BMDCs were differentiated from whole bone marrow derived from tibia and femurs of C57BL/6J, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-cre;Keap1f/f mice isolated as described above. For in vitro experiments testing R848 and PGPC, a total of 4 × 106 cells were seeded per 10 cm non-TC treated plate and differentiated in cIMDM supplemented with 30% B-16 supernatants containing GM-CSF for 6 days. For in vivo experiments using adoptive transfer of BMDCs, a total of 10 × 106 cells were seeded per non-tissue culture treated 6-well plate and cultured in cIMDM supplemented with 100 ng ml–1 FLT3L (Miltenyi) for 8 days.

Panx1 cDNA was ordered as a gBlock (IDT) and cloned using Gibson Assembly into pMSCV-IRES-GFP. Effective cloning was confirmed using restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing. Generation of retrovirus was done in 293T cells.

For transduction of iBMDMs, 293T cells were plated in a 6-well dish at one well per construct. Cells were then transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g. The next day, supernatants containing virus were collected, clarified by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the viral supernatants at a 1:2,000 dilution. Viral supernatants were then placed on top of iBMDMs in 12-well plates which were spinfected at 1,250g for 1 h at 30 °C. iBMDMs were transduced again the following day. iBMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting.

For transduction of primary Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs, primary BMDMs were generated from the bone marrow of Nfe2l2−/− mice as described above. Generation of virus was done in 293T cells plated in 10 cm dishes at one dish per 10 cm dish of differentiating BMDMs. 293T cells were transfected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP or pMSCV-Panx1-IRES-GFP alongside the helper plasmid pCl-Eco and VSV-g and viral supernatants were collected the next day, clarified by centrifugation, and filtered through a 0.45 µm PVDF filter. Viral supernatant was added to BMDM cultures on day 3 of differentiation alongside additional L929 supernatant. BMDMs were differentiated for another 3 days and BMDM transduction was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy (evaluating for GFP expression) and by western blotting. BMDMs were plated for experiments as described elsewhere.

Bone marrow was isolated as described above and cultured in the presence of a 1:10 dilution CMG supernatant (a source of M-CSF) for 4–5 days. BMDMs were then seeded at the following concentrations: 1 × 104 cells per well of a 96-well plate, 4 × 105 cells per well of a 6-well plate or 8 × 105 cells per P60 dish. Osteoclast differentiation was induced in a 1:50 dilution of CMG medium with addition of receptor activator of NF-κB ligand (RANKL) at 50–100 ng ml–1 for 5–6 days. For NLRP3 activation, cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h followed by 15 µM nigericin for 1 h, after which supernatant was assayed for IL-1β.

For prophylactic immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were subcutaneously injected near the shoulders with 200 µg per mouse OVA (EndoFit OVA, Invivogen), 5 µg per mouse R848 (Invivogen) and 65 µg per mouse of PGPC (Cayman Chemical) emulsified in incomplete Freund’s adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich). Mice received a booster dose 14 days later. Seven days after receipt of the booster immunization, mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank.

For adoptive DC immunization experiments, 7-week-old female C57BL/6J WT mice had 3 × 105 B16-OVA cells subcutaneously implanted on the flank. On day 8 of BMDC differentiation, FLT3L–BMDCs were stimulated with 500 ng ml–1 R848 for 3 h and then treated with 100 µg ml–1 PGPC for 18 h. BMDCs were subsequently loaded with 500 µg ml–1 OVA for 1 h, washed and resuspended in PBS. A total of 1 × 106 DCs per mouse was subcutaneously injected between the shoulders. BMDC injections were performed 7, 14 and 21 days after implantation of B16-OVA cells.

For all experiments, tumour sizes were measured every other day by recording the length and width using a caliper. Mice were euthanized when the humane end point was reached, which was defined as tumour area >2 cm2 or tumour ulceration.

MSU-induced peritonitis was performed as previously described86. In brief, a 10 mg ml–1 solution of MSU (Invivogen; tlrl-msu) was prepared in sterile PBS. Mice were injected (i.p.) with 180 µl of 10 mg ml–1 MSU using a 29 G insulin syringe. Similarly, alum-induced peritonitis was performed by injecting mice (i.p.) with 200 µl of a 1:9 dilution of Alhydrogel (Invivogen; vac-alu-50) in PBS. At 3 h (MSU) or 16–24 h (alum) after injection, peritoneal lavage was performed on the mice using 5 ml sterile PBS. Lavage fluid was collected through a 25 G needle and immune cells were pelleted. Cells were stained with a Live/Dead fixable stain (Invitrogen) and Fc block (BioLegend; clone S17011E) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Cells were then stained with CD45 (BV711; clone 30-F11), Ly6G (FITC; clone 1A8) and Ly6B.2 (PE; clone REA115). Neutrophils were defined by flow cytometry as live, CD45+Ly6G+Ly6B.2+ and represented as a proportion of CD45+ cells. Alum-treated mice with <11% neutrophils (non-responders) were excluded from the analysis (two mice per group, four mice in total excluded).

Mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation, sprayed with 70% ethanol and the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 5 ml PBS containing 2.5 mM EDTA. The peritoneal lavage containing resident peritoneal macrophages was centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and the pellet resuspended in cDMEM. For experiments evaluating the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in plastic TC plates, peritoneal lavages from 2–3 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 12 wells of a 96-well dish. For experiments evaluating the role of stiffness on inflammasome activation, peritoneal lavages from 5 mice were pooled and cells were plated across 9 wells of 6-well dishes (3 wells for each stiffness). After 2 h, cells were washed 3 times with PBS to remove contaminating non-macrophages and cultured in cDMEM overnight. Cells were then stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 24 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 30 min. Cell culture supernatants were saved for ELISA and IL-1β immunoprecipitation. Cells were lysed in 1× SDS loading buffer containing 2% β-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) and heated at 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

Human buffy coat was purchased from BioIVT and shipped on ice on the day of collection. All buffy coat samples were anticoagulated with EDTA and were confirmed to be free of common viral infections. Buffy coat was mixed 1:1 with PBS and 2.5 mM EDTA and overlaid on 15 ml Ficoll-Paque Plus (Cytiva). The sample was spun at 800g for 35 min at 22 °C without break. The plasma was aspirated and discarded. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were placed in a fresh conical tube and washed in MACS buffer (PBS, 2.5 mM EDTA, 2% FBS and penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were spun at 300g for 10 min, pooled together and washed a second time in MACS buffer. RBCs were lysed in ACK buffer for 5 min and the reaction was stopped with fivefold addition of MACS buffer. PBMCs were washed an additional time to remove residual ACK buffer and the final pellet was resuspended in 10 ml MACS buffer and filtered through a 30 µm filter. Monocytes were isolated using human anti-CD14 beads (Miltenyi Biotec) and MACS LS columns (Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the pellet was resuspended in 80 µl MACS buffer per 107 PBMCs and 20 µl anti-CD14 beads were added per 107 PBMCs. Cells were incubated on ice in the dark for 15 min, washed with 20 ml MACS buffer followed by centrifuging at 300g for 10 min. The cell pellet was resuspended in 2.5 ml MACS buffer per buffy coat and applied to an equilibrated LS column. The column was washed 3 times with 2.5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer and cells were eluted in 5 ml ice-cold MACS buffer. Next, 2 × 107 CD14+ cells were cultured on a tissue culture treated T75 flask in 15 ml cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 recombinant human M-CSF. The medium was exchanged every 2 days and cells were considered differentiated into macrophages on day 6. Cells were lifted using Macrophage Detachment Solution DXF (PromoCell) per the manufacturer’s protocol and plated at 1 × 106 cells per well in variable stiffness plates or 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well plates.

C57BL/6J WT mice were subcutaneously immunized with 100 µg OVA emulsified 1:1 in incomplete Freud’s adjuvant (Invivogen) on one shoulder and boosted on day 7 on the opposite shoulder. On day 14 of immunization, spleens were collected and CD8+ T cells were isolated by negative selection (BioLegend) and resuspended in cRPMI containing 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 10 µM β-ME. FLT3L-derived BMDCs were generated and activated overnight using R848 and PGPC as described above. Activated BMDCs were collected, counted and plated at 1 × 104 cells per well in 96-well round-bottom plates, pulsed with 1 mg ml–1 OVA for 1 h and washed with PBS. Enriched CD8+ T cells from OVA-immunized mice were added at 1 × 105 cells per well (10:1 ratio of CD8+ T cells to DCs) in a final volume of 100 µl and cultured for 7 days. Supernatants were collected, clarified by centrifugation and stored at −20 °C for IFNγ ELISA analysis.

Primary BMDMs or human MDMs were typically seeded at the following numbers according to the assay being performed: 1 × 106 cells per well in fibronectin-coated 6-well Cytosoft or plastic TC plates or 0.5 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC plates for RNA isolation; 0.25 × 106 cells per well in 24-well TC plates for ELISAs; or 0.1 × 106 cells per well in 96-well TC plates for LDH assays. Cells were incubated overnight in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants or in cRPMI and 30 ng ml–1 human M-CSF for MDMs. iBMDMs were seeded at 0.5 × 105 cells per well in a 96-well TC plate and incubated overnight in cDMEM. The next morning, the medium was exchanged to cDMEM with or without inhibitors (or vehicle control), and cells incubated for 30 min. A subset of cells were left unstimulated whereas others were stimulated with LPS at 100 ng ml–1 for up to 6 h followed by inflammasome activation with 5 mM ATP for 2 h (for LDH release or GSDMD oligomerization assays), 5 mM ATP for 30 min (for IL-1β ELISA and IP), 5 µM nigericin for 30 min (ASC specks), 5 µM nigericin for 2 h (for IL-1β ELISA and LDH release) or 20 µg ml–1 CL097 for 2 h.

For examination of oxidized lipid activation of the inflammasome, BMDMs or BMDCs were seeded at 1 × 105 cells per well in 96-well TC plates and incubated overnight. Cells were primed with R848 at 62.5 ng ml–1 for 3 h followed by stimulation with PGPC at 100 µg ml–1 for an additional 24 h.

Lytic cell death was quantified using a LDH-release assay with a CyQuant LDH cytotoxicity assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In a 96-well plate, 25 µl cell-free supernatants was mixed with 25 µl LDH assay buffer and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C in the dark. The reaction was stopped by addition of 25 µl stop solution. Absorbance at 490 nm and 680 nm was measured on a Tecan Spark plate reader and the signal was normalized to equivalently treated control samples in which cells were lysed using a detergent-containing lysis buffer.

Cytokine release into cell culture supernatants, mouse plasma or mouse peritoneal fluid were assayed for mouse IL-1β and TNF using uncoated ELISA kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific), human IL-1β using a Lumit Human IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega) or human TNF using ELISA MAX Deluxe kit (BioLegend) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. For experiments using PGPC, mouse IL-1β was assessed using a Lumit Mouse IL-1β Immunoassay kit (Promega).

Primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 2 × 106 cells per well on soft and plastic plates and cultured overnight. A total of two wells were used per stiffness and treatment condition. Cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h and then lysed in-well with 600 μl NP-40 lysis buffer (TBS pH 7.4, 1% NP-40, 5% glycerol and protease inhibitors) per well. The lysate was spun at 20,000g for 5 min. Next, 120 μl clarified lysate was saved as input whereas the rest was incubated protein G Sepharose beads (GE Healthcare) loaded with anti-NRF2 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, 12721S) at 4 °C for 1 h. Afterwards, 2 µg NRF2 antibody was added to each sample. After incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with NP-40 lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted in 120 μl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. Samples were heated to 95 °C for 20 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE.

Cell culture supernatants were transferred into microcentrifuge tubes and depleted of cells and debris by centrifuging at 400g for 5 min. Peritoneal lavage fluid was prepared as described above. Equal volumes of cell-free supernatants or peritoneal lavage fluid were mixed with 0.5 µg biotinylated goat anti-mouse IL-1β or anti-human IL-1β antibody and 20 µl dry weight neutravidin agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, washed 3 times with PBS pH 7.4 and protein was eluted in 50 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer and served as lysate control. Samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by separation by SDS–PAGE. IL-1β was detected by immunoblotting using Bio-Rad Image Lab. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

For analysis of inflammasome activation in cells cultured on variable stiffness plates, primary mouse BMDMs were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM (Gibco) and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. The cell culture supernatant was removed, cleared of debris by centrifugation at 400g for 5 min at room temperature and then protein was precipitated by adding trichloroacetic acid to a final concentration of 10%. Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C while rotating, protein was pelleted by centrifugation at 13,000g at 4 °C for 15 min and was washed twice with 400 µl ice-cold acetone. Protein pellets were air dried at 65 °C for 5 min. Protein was solubilized in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. The remaining cells in the well were lysed in 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME and served as lysate control. All samples were heated to 65 °C for 10 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

For analysis of inflammasome activation in WT, Nfe2l2−/−, Keap1f/f and LysM-Cre;Keap1f/f primary BMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured overnight in cDMEM. For analysis of inflammasome activation in iBMDMs, 1 × 106 cells per well were plated in a 24-well dish and cultured for 1 h in cDMEM. Cells were then left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, medium was removed and OptiMEM containing nigericin was added for 1–2 h. Cells and supernatant were lysed together by addition of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME, lysates were needle homogenized and samples were heated to 95 °C for 5 min followed by protein separation by SDS–PAGE.

Primary mouse BMDMs from WT and Gsdmd−/− mice were plated at 3 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic plates and cultured overnight. The medium was exchanged for OptiMEM and cells were left untreated or treated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 6 h or 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h followed by 5 mM ATP for 2 h. Protein was precipitated as outlined above and solubilized in 1× sample buffer without reducing agent. Protein was solubilized by incubating at 65 °C for 5 min, after which samples were split equally into two tubes and β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O was added to generate reducing and non-reducing samples, respectively. Whole-cell lysate was generated by adding 1× sample buffer to the remaining cells, solubilizing at 65 °C for 5 min, splitting the sample equally and adding either β-ME or an equal volume of ddH2O to generate reducing and non-reducing samples. The final concentration of β-ME was 2%. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE on a 4–12% acrylamide gradient gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and GSDMD was detected by western blotting. The assembled GSDMD pore is resistant to SDS under non-reducing conditions and thus oligomerization was indicated by a gel shift towards a higher molecular weight. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

Fractionation was performed as previously described87. In brief, primary BMDMs derived from WT and Nfe2l2−/− mice were seeded in variable stiffness plates at 3 × 106 cells per well. A total of 3 wells were used per genotype and stiffness and BMDMs were cultured overnight. Cells were placed on ice and washed once with ice-cold PBS. Cells were scraped into ice cold PBS, spun at 10,000g for 10 s, and PBS was aspirated. Cells were lysed in 900 µl PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors by trituration with a P1000 pipette. A total of 300 µl of this was saved as whole-cell lysate. The remaining 600 µl lysate was spun at 10,000g for 10 s and 300 µl of the supernatant was saved as the cytoplasmic fraction. Next, 75 µl of 5× sample buffer containing 10% β-ME was added to the whole-cell lysate and cytoplasmic fractions to denature the protein. The remaining supernatant was aspirated, and the nuclear pellet was washed with 1 ml PBS, 0.1% NP-40 and protease inhibitors. The nuclear pellet was lysed in 300 µl 1× sample buffer containing 2% β-ME. All fractions were needle homogenized and then boiled at 100 °C for 5 min. Tubulin and lamin A/C served as markers for the cytosol and nucleus, respectively. Cell-associated actin was detected as the loading control.

Cells were seeded at 1 × 106 primary BMDMs per well in 6-well 2 kPa Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin. One well was left without cells as a blank. Cells were cultured overnight in the presence or absence of NAC (5 mM, pH 7.4), MitoTempo (15 µM), ML171 (1 µM), GSK2795039 (10 µM) or GKT137831 (10 µM). The next morning, cells were incubated with 20 µM H2DCFDA in 1× HBSS without phenol red for 30 min. Cells were then washed 3 times with HBSS without phenol red and bottom read fluorescence was read using a TecanSpark with an excitation wavelength of 490 nm, emission wavelength of 535 nm and bandwidth of 20.0. Cells were then lysed in 350 µl RNA lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored at −20 °C until further processing.

iBMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 2.5 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes and left to adhere for 1 h. Primary BMDMs were seeded on glass coverslips at 1 × 105 cells per well in 24-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants, left to adhere overnight. The next morning, medium was removed and replaced with cDMEM. Cells were stimulated with 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 4 h, after which medium was aspirated and replaced with 450 µl OptiMEM containing zVAD-FMK with or without nigericin for 30 min. Cells were fixed by the addition of 150 µl of 16% EM-grade aqueous paraformaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed twice with PBS pH 7.4 and stored overnight at 4 °C. The next morning, cells were permeabilized and blocked for 30 min in PBS pH 7.4 containing 0.2% BSA and 0.05% saponin (blocking buffer). Cells were washed 3 times in PBS pH 7.4 and primary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing polyclonal rabbit anti-ASC antibody (Adipogen) at 1:100 dilution in a humidified chamber. Cells were washed 5 times in PBS pH 7.4 and secondary antibody staining was performed for 1 h in blocking buffer containing Alexa Fluor 488-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 1:200 dilution, Alexa Fluor 647-tagged phalloidin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 1:400 dilution and DAPI (Biotum) at 1 µg ml–1 in a humidified chamber in the dark. Cells were washed 5–10 times in PBS pH 7.4, mounted on glass slides using prolong glass antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and left to cure overnight at room temperature in the dark. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM 880 with Airyscan and processed using Zeiss Zen Blue (v.2.3SP1). ASC specks were manually counted, and nuclei were counted in Fiji (v.2.16.0) using the Analyze particles algorithm.

Tissue samples for these experiments were isolated from discarded explanted human lung tissue specimens collected at Massachusetts General Hospital. Patients provided informed consent, and discarded tissue samples from non-diseased donors were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2016P001890. Discarded tissue from patients with ILD were collected under Massachusetts General Hospital IRB number 2013P002332. Samples were fixed in 4% buffered paraformaldehyde and then embedded in paraffin. The following primary antibodies were used for immunofluorescence: monoclonal mouse anti-human CD68 (Abcam, ab955), polyclonal rabbit anti-human SLC7A11 (Abcam, ab37185), polyclonal rabbit anti-human HMOX1 (Proteintech, 10701-1-AP) and polyclonal rabbit anti-human GSR (Proteintech, 18257-1-AP). Paraffin-embedded tissue was sectioned at 5 µm slices onto glass slides, deparaffinized and then rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed using Tris-EDTA pH 9 for 5 min in a pressure cooker, after which samples were cooled and tissue was circled using a hydrophobic pen. Sections were permeabilized and blocked using sterile filtered PBS, 1% BSA and 0.3% Triton X-100 (blocking-staining buffer). Sections were stained with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight at the following dilutions: CD68, 1:100; HMOX1, 1:50; GSR, 1:50; and SLC7A11, 1:100. Sections were washed 5 times in blocking–staining buffer and then left in blocking–staining buffer for 10 min. Secondary antibody staining was performed at room temperature in blocking–staining buffer containing Alexa Fluor 594-tagged polyclonal goat anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-tagged polyclonal goat anti-mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:400) along with Hoechst (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:2,000) for 2 h. Samples were then washed 5 times with blocking–staining buffer, submerged in PBS pH 7.4 and 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, dipped in deionized water and mounted with Fluoromount-G mounting medium (Southern Biotech). Samples were imaged on a Zeiss Axio Imager.M2 widefield microscope and a Zeiss LSM 780 confocal microscope.

Cells were detected using Cellpose (v.2.0) and the implemented model ‘Cellpose fluorescence’ (CP) with the following parameters: average cell diameter 50 pixels (12.2 µm), flow threshold 2.0 and cell probability threshold –3. Segmentation was performed on the stained cells using nuclei as a secondary channel for detection. The resulting labels were filtered for a minimum size of 600 pixels (35.4 µm2), and the resulting labels were used to calculate fluorescence values of the corresponding cells. An empirically determined threshold for the average CD68 fluorescence intensity was used to discriminate alveolar macrophages from interstitial macrophages and stromal cells following histogram normalization of the underlying imaging data. The mean fluorescence intensity and sum of fluorescence per cell were plotted in PRISM (GraphPad).

BMDMs were grown on Cytosoft 2 kPa plates or glass cover slips, both coated with fibronectin as described above. BMDMs were immersion-fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences), 2% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) and 0.3% picric acid (Sigma-Aldrich) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate (Sigma-Aldrich) pH 7.4 for 1 h at room temperature. BMDMs were washed with 0.1 M sodium cacodylate and then post-fixed for 1 h at 4 °C in 1% osmium tetroxide (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate. BMDMs were then washed in DI water and incubated in 2% aqueous uranyl acetate (Electron Microscopy Sciences) overnight at 4 °C. The following day, BMDMs were washed with DI water and then dehydrated at 4 °C in a graded ethanol series. BMDMs were then brought to room temperature and dehydrated with 100% ethanol (Sigma-Aldrich). Infiltration with LX112 resin (Ladd Research) was followed by embedding in flat-bottom Beem capsules (Electron Microscopy Sciences) cut to form a cylindrical mould on the growing substrate. The resulting blocks were separated from the culture plates using liquid nitrogen and then sectioned using a Leica Ultracut E ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems). Sections were then placed on formvar and carbon-coated grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences). The sections were contrast stained with 2% uranyl acetate followed by lead citrate (Sigma-Aldrich) and imaged in a Jeol 1400 transmission electron microscope (Jeol) equipped with a Gatan Orius SC1000 digital CCD camera (Gatan). Mitochondrial length was manually measured in Fiji (v.2.16.0).

RNA was isolated using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). In brief, cells were collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −20 °C until processing. Equal volumes of 70% ethanol were added to each sample, which were then applied to PureLink RNA columns and processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Total RNA was eluted using 50 µl RNAse-free H2O. RT–qPCR was performed using a Taqman RNA-to-Ct 1-step kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on equal amounts of RNA per the manufacturer’s protocol. The following Taqman probes were used: Gsta3 (Mm00494798_m1), Nqo1 (Mm01253561_m1), Gsr (Mm00439154_m1), Hmox1 (Mm00516005_m1), Gclm (Mm01324400_m1), Slc7a11 (Mm00442530_m1), Srxn1 (Mm00769566_m1), Txnrd1 (Mm00443675_m1), Nfe2l2 (Mm00477784_m1), Keap1 (Mm00497268_m1), Il1b (Mm00434228_m1), Panx1 (Mm00450900_m1), Il6 (Mm00446190_m1), Nos2 (Mm00440502_m1), Arg1 (Mm00475988_m1), Retnla (Mm00445109_m1), Nox1 (Mm00549170_m1), Cybb (Mm01287743_m1) and Tbp (Mm01277042_m1). Data were normalized to Tbp, analysed using Microsoft Excel and plotted in GraphPad Prism.

For determination of Nfe2l2 deletion, RNA was collected purified from cells using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Life Technologies) and PureLink DNase I (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The quality and quantity of RNA were assessed using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg RNA using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems). Gene expression was analysed by qPCR using a SYBR Green gene expression assay (Applied Biosystems) and primers were synthesized from IDT. The following mouse Nfe2l2 primer sequences were used: forward 5′-TAGATGACCATGAGTCGCTTGC-3′, reverse 5′-GCCAAACTTGCTCCATGTCC-3′. The following mouse cyclophilin B primer sequences were used: forward 5′-AGCATACAGGTCCTGGCATC-3′, reverse 5′- TTCACCTTCCCAAAGACCAC-3′. Data were normalized to cyclophilin B, and relative mRNA expression was calculated using the \({2}^{\Delta \Delta {C}_{t}}\) method.

BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 6-well Cytosoft or plastic Petri dishes coated with fibronectin and cultured overnight. Cells were washed once with PBS, collected in lysis buffer containing 1% β-ME and stored frozen at −80 °C until processing. RNA was processed using the QIAsymphony RNA protocol according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, RNA was extracted using QIAsymphony RNA Isolation kits (Qiagen) on a QIAsymphony SP instrument using the RNA CT 400 protocol. The elution volume for RNA samples was 100 µl. RNA sequencing libraries were constructed from 500 ng total RNA using a KAPA RNA HyperPrep kit (Kapa Biosystems). Library preparation was tested manually and subsequently fully automated on a Biomek i7 Workstation (Beckmen Coulter). Libraries underwent paired-end 75 base-pair sequencing on a NovaSeq6000 (Illumina) at a depth of 50 million reads per sample. Raw reads were aligned to the mouse genome (GRCm39) using the STAR aligner (v.-2.7.5c). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using the FeatureCounts function from the subread package (v.1.6.0). The count matrix was imported into R (v.4.1.3) and low-expressed genes were filtered out (included genes required ≥1 CPM in at least 20% of samples). Trimmed mean of M-values was computed using edgeR (v.3.38.0). Differential gene expression analysis was computed using the limma package (v.3.52.0). Differentially expressed genes were loaded into ingenuity pathway analysis (Qiagen, v.01-22-01) and upstream regulator and canonical pathway analysis was conducted on samples with an absolute value log2 fold change > 1 and a corrected P < 0.05. Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

For effects of stiffness on the NRF2 transcriptional program, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in soft (2 kPa) or plastic 6-well dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. For the effect of NRF2 activators on LPS-stimulated transcription, WT and Nfe2l2−/− BMDMs were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 12-well TC dishes in cDMEM and 10% L929 supernatants and incubated overnight. The next morning, medium was replaced with fresh cDMEM containing 1 µM KI696, 5 µM sulforaphane, 100 µM tert-butylhydroquinone, 25 µM dimethyl fumarate, 125 µM 4-octyl itaconate or DMSO as a control, and BMDMs were incubated for 30 min. Half of the cells were left unstimulated and the other half had LPS added to a final concentration of 100 ng ml–1 and were cultured for 6 h.

For all samples, supernatants were aspirated and cells were lysed in 350 µl RNA Lysis buffer from a PureLink RNA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). RNA was isolated as described in the RT–qPCR section above. Technical triplicates were combined to create one sample per condition per mouse, DNA was degraded using a TURBO DNA-free kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and RNA was quantified using a Nanodrop instrument. RNA was kept frozen at −80 °C and paired-end 150 base-pair sequencing was conducted by Azenta at a depth of 20 million reads per sample. Raw sequencing data processing was done with the Galaxy server, whereas differential gene expression analysis was performed in R (v.4.3.2). Raw reads were trimmed using fastp (Galaxy v.0.23.2) and aligned to the mouse genome (mm10) using RNA STAR aligner (Galaxy v.2.7.11a). Reads mapped to genomic features were counted using FeatureCounts (Galaxy v.2.0.3). Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0) and heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.18.0).

WT BMDMs were cultured for 5 days in 2% CMG, then left untreated or treated with RANKL to generate osteoclasts. On day 5, cells were treated with or without 100 ng ml–1 LPS for 3 h. RNA was extracted using a PureLink RNA Mini kit (Invitrogen) with on-column DNase treatment (Ambion). RNA quality and quantity were assessed using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Libraries were prepared using a NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep kit and sequenced on an Illumina platform to generate paired end reads. Raw reads were cleaned using fastp and aligned to the reference genome, mm10 using STAR. Gene expression was quantified with Feature Counts, and RPKM values were calculated. Differential expression was analysed using DESeq2 with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted P < 0.05). Heatmaps were generated using ComplexHeatmap. Three biological replicates were used per group.

Spatial transcriptomic data from human lung tissue were downloaded from the NIH Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) platform (identifier GSE250346)79, whereas single-cell RNA sequencing data were downloaded from NIH GEO (identifiers GSE122960 and GSE136831)80,81. All analyses were performed using Seurat (v.5.0.1). Data from ref. 80 (GSE122960) required integration, which was performed using the IntegrateLayers pipeline in Seurat. Data from ref. 81 (GSE136831) were available as a sparse matrix and a Seurat object was manually created using these data. Data from ref. 79 (GSE250346) were available as a Seurat object. In brief, cells were re-clustered and individual cluster annotations were confirmed manually. NRF2 transcriptional targets were used to generate an NRF2 module score across all cell types using the AddModuleScore. The NRF2 activity score was then compared between samples from unaffected individuals and samples with more fibrosis on a per-macrophage-subtype basis. Significance was assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis test and Dunn’s multiple comparisons test, and P values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Violin plots were generated using scCustomize (v.2.0.1). Pseudobulk analysis was performed by creating an aggregated count matrix followed by differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2 (v.1.42.0). Normalized counts were extracted and GSVA (v.1.50.0) was performed using NRF2 target genes as the target gene set. Significance was assessed using the Mann–Whitney U-test. All data analyses were performed using R (v.4.3.2).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Notable software package versions are listed in the relevant sections above. No new software pipelines were developed or used in this study. Bulk RNA sequencing data generated in this study are available from the NIH GEO (GSE274019, GSE274020, GSE274336 and GSE298028). Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic data were downloaded from the NIH GEO (GSE250346, GSE122960 and GSE136831). All data supporting the findings of this study are available in the paper.  Source data are provided with this paper.

#1255. Pio Esposito impressed Upamecano ahead of Italy vs. France

France international Dayot Upamecano is impressed by Italy striker Francesco Pio Esposito, noting it is ‘not easy to mark him,’ but won’t change his style for this Nations League clash.

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

This is the penultimate round of the group stage, with France leading on 10 points, followed by Italy with seven and Belgium on six.

In Matchday 6, France will host rock bottom Turkiye, while it is a head-to-head between the Azzurri and Red Devils in Brussels on Sunday.

“Italy are a very good team, they changed coach and have players at top clubs,” said Upamecano in his press conference.

“Our concentration is always the same, we are focused entirely on doing well for France. There is no reason to change our style of play, we want to replicate what we do in training, and hope to do so tomorrow.”

France have dropped points only once in this Nations League campaign, in the 1-1 draw with Italy in Paris on October 2.

Inter striker Pio Esposito started that match and he is expected to lead the attack again tomorrow evening.

“Esposito is a very good player, very physical, we saw in the first match it was not easy to mark him. I would prefer not to concentrate on a single player, though, because we are taking on the whole Italy team,” noted Upamecano.

It was not an easy match for Upamecano, who was sent off for a second bookable offence against Italy.

“France try to keep a high defensive line, to press and recover the ball quickly. I like this style of play, and we’ll try to keep that going tomorrow against Italy.”

Like the first leg in Paris, France are again without injured Kylian Mbappé, while Marcus Thuram, Esteban Lepaul, Ousmane Dembélé, Aurelien Tchouameni, Manu Koné and Pierre Kalulu are also among those who withdrew from the squad.

“It’s true, we are missing a lot of players and I wish them all a speedy recovery, but we are still ready to face Italy, that goes for all those who start and can come off the bench.”

Jeremy Jacquet has been tipped to step into the defence with Upamecano in a reshuffle tomorrow.

“I don’t know, you’d have to ask Zidane. He is a young lad, very motivated, and we hope he can keep going like this.”

The Bayern Munich full-back was asked if he would like to play in the Premier League in future.

“I’ve lived in Germany for a while and I am happy there. We’ll see what happens in future, but I am happy at Bayern Munich,” he replied.

“I am always ready to improve, try to listen to the advice I receive, and give my all. I think there’s a lot that I can do better.”

#1254. USA pulls out of U-17 World Cup just days before it starts… amid war in the Middle East and 'risk of armed conflict'

Published: 18:48 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 18:48 EST, 11 November 2026

The US Soccer Federation is withdrawing its team from the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Qatar amid growing security concern over the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, according to multiple reports.

The American State Department currently has a travel advisory for the country at a Level 3, with guidance telling travelers to 'reconsider travel to Qatar due to risk of armed conflict.'

Athletes who were set to compete in the tournament - held from November 19 to December 13 - were informed of the decision via an e-mail.

'We are writing to inform you of the difficult decision to cancel our World Cup pre-camp and our planned participation in the World Cup,' the letter stated.

'We are extremely proud of the preparation by our players and coaches to represent the US in the World Cup.

'Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances including the US State Department's Level 3 Travel Advisory for Qatar and related directives for Embassy staff and families, we are no longer able to participate in the tournament. The well-being of our players and staff will always be our top priority.'

The United States has told players they will not participate in the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Qatar

The US State Department has a Level 3 travel advisory for the country amid ongoing conflicts

The USA won their CONCACAF qualifying group in order to reach the tournament

This announcement comes one week after coach Alex Aldaz announced his roster for the competition. The team was set to take part in a training camp this week at US Soccer's new headquarters outside Atlanta.

Players were set to open their tournament on November 21 with a match against Montenegro. They were also scheduled to face Chile and Algeria.

The United States earned the right to compete in the tournament by winning their group and outlasting the Dominican Republic on goal difference in CONCACAF U-17 World Cup qualifying.

The Baby Nats drew the Dominicans after beating Saint Kitts and Nevis as well as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

At last year's tournament, the Americans reached the Round of 32 before being eliminated by Morocco.

The best finish for the United states at the tournament came in New Zealand in 1999, when they came fourth - losing to Australia on penalties. Landon Donovan was named as the competition's Best Player.

FIFA made changes to the tournament last year, making it an annual event rather than once every two years. Qatar won the rights to host it from 2025 to 2029.

It is not clear which team will replace the United States at the tournament. The Daily Mail has contacted FIFA for comment on the matter.

#1253. Milan reunion for Maldini, Theo Hernandez and almost Rafael Leao

There was a special reunion between former Milan figures Paolo Maldini and Theo Hernandez today, with Rafael Leao adding his envy of the get-together.

Some Rossoneri supporters will have seen the moment Maldini was sacked as technical director in June 2023 as a crossroads for the club, a moment when different paths were taken and it is a side still trying to rediscover that level.

Maldini’s departure was also viewed as a catalyst for players to walk away, as Theo Hernandez never disguised that he felt Milan fundamentally lost something when the legend left.

He followed suit to Al-Hilal in the summer of 2025 and continues to play for the Saudi club, but made a return to Italy during the break for international duty.

“Respect and admiration, always,” was the message Theo Hernandez wrote when posting an image of himself having a reunion with Maldini.

It wasn’t just the Rossoneri supporters who flooded the Instagram post with messages expressing love, regret and frustration.

A post shared by T H E O H E R N Á N D E Z (@theo3hernandez)

“I’m on my way,” replied Rafael Leao, who also left San Siro only a few months ago for a new adventure at Galatasaray.

Zona Milan summed it up for many of the supporters who still follow Theo Hernandez: “A knife in my heart would’ve hurt less than this image.”
